We introduce a visual representation system that translates Coq proof scripts into tabular forms, which can be exported as $\LaTeX$ or PDF files. Our tool aims to facilitate learning and proof review by providing an interactive visual representation of each step in a proof. Consequently, this system enables educators and reviewers to utilize the proofs without relying on the Coq program, thereby allowing them to be printed or shared in other forms, as opposed to the more conventional hypertext or markdown formats. Moreover, as the tool can generate visual representations, it automatically identifies kani queries, extracts corresponding evidence and outcomes, as well as highlighting soundness proof results. Given its visual nature, even novice users should find it relatively straightforward to navigate through the proofs. We envision this visualisation tool to have numerous applications in proof engineering, education and research related to proof verification. Furthermore, as the visualisation tool is built using Vue.js and web assembly, it offers a performance-efficient alternative to visualising large proof scripts directly in the web browser. Instead, we recommend loading the proofs locally through the File menu or pasting the URL generated by coq-psv into Chrome or Firefox for inspection. For more information and to download the tool, users can visit the dedicated website: https://coq-psv.github.io/. As the project is hosted on GitHub, we welcome contributions and suggestions from the community. Do not hesitate to contact us, if you need assistance or want to report any issues. We are more than happy to help! Suppose you want to visualise a Coq proof, say, F_map_conv. The step-by-step process to achieve this would be as follows: (1) open the coq-psv website, (2) select F_map_conv from the list and (3) click the 'Visualise' button. After a short pause, a tab will appear in your browser, displaying the visual representation of the proof, as shown in Figure 1. Alternatively, you can generate a $\LaTeX$ source file by clicking the 'PDF' button and then copy the content into your preferred document editor. For educational purposes, we provide a detailed guide on how to teach this proof using our visualisation tool. We are confident that by combining the strengths of Coq and visual proof displays, educators and researchers will find it easier to learn from, critique and utilise the proofs. In particular, we have identified four key advantages: (i) improved understanding through visualisation, (ii) enhanced pedagogy by highlighting key concepts, (iii) greater flexibility

In interior point methods (IPMs), an iterative algorithm is employed to solve a sequence of eigenvalue problems arising from nonlinear equations derived from quadratic programs. Despite the analytical nature of these problems, IPMs often necessitate the use of iterative solvers and/or methods to compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors, requiring additional termination criteria to ensure convergence. We introduce and demonstrate a stopping criterion based on the residual norm being reduced below a specified threshold by the Arnoldi iteration for computing Morgan-Phelps neighborhoods in IPMs. We also illustrate this criterion in the specific context of primal-dual IPMs, showcasing its efficacy with numerical examples. This new criterion can be easily integrated into existing Arnoldi-based solvers and offers a straightforward way to determine when to terminate the iteration process. We experimentally validate that it leads to identical results as early termination based on monitoring the residual vector's norm, while significantly decreasing the number of iterations required. The advancement of Artificial Intelligence has brought numerous advantages but it has also highlighted potential dangers. Historically, AI systems have caused harm both financially and socially, leading to legal consequences. As AI technology continues to evolve, the potential risk to society will increase, making it crucial to address these issues. To avoid repeating the same mistakes, it is essential to learn from past AI incidents. To facilitate this, a comprehensive database of AI-related mishaps, the AI Incident Repository, has been established. This database includes information about the incident itself, the impact it had and the lessons that can be learned from it. By utilizing the AI Incident Repository, stakeholders can gain a deeper understanding of the causes and effects of past incidents, helping to prepare for future AI-related setbacks. In this study, a possible structure and layout for the AI Incident Repository are suggested, along with potential usage scenarios. Furthermore, a theoretical framework for incorporating empirical data from actual AI incidents into the repository is presented. Our ultimate goal is to utilize the AI Incident Repository to track the progression of past incidents and forecast the likelihood of future setbacks as AI technology advances. This goal will contribute to informed decision-making about the development and deployment of AI systems. We hope that establishing the AI Incident Repository will become a collaborative effort, enabling all stakeholders to leverage its wealth of information. In particular, we anticipate its utility in strategic risk assessment and planning for future AI advancements. With enough support, we envision the AI Incident Repository as a valuable resource, aiding in the avoidance of past mistakes to build safer and more dependable AI systems for the future. A public website with a searchable database of 70+ documented AI incidents has been set up at https://aiincidents.org and the data can be downloaded from https://github.com/AIIncidents/air. The repository is meant to be a community-driven project and we welcome contributions in the form of new entries, corrections, and updates to the existing incident records. If you are aware of an AI-related mishap that is missing from the repository, please contact us at aiincidents@mlsworld.org or share your knowledge through a new entry on our public website. We are committed to maintaining the confidentiality of any sensitive information and strive to provide impartial, informative incident records that can aid in learning from our collective mistakes. We hope to establish partnerships with organizations and individuals to bolster the comprehensive scope of the AI Incident Repository, encompassing various fields and perspectives. With a broader range of incident experiences, the repository can offer even more valuable insights to guide the development and deployment of AI

By leveraging this method, organizations can mitigate the adverse effects of inefficient or incorrect human interventions, thereby improving process quality. We anticipate that this monitoring framework will yield better outcomes for business processes involving both automated and human components. Additionally, this work has the potential to inspire further research in system design, enabling the reconciliation of system failures with human involvement. We envision that our monitoring framework will contribute to the development of more robust systems, capable of compensating for human shortcomings. Ultimately, this will lead to better performance and elevated reliability for business processes as a whole. Assembling the human genome from next-generation sequencing data is a computationally demanding task.
Creating contiguous, gap-free sequences directly from raw data is impractical due to excessive false read joins.
A viable alternative involves utilizing combinatorial algorithms and heuristics to generate sequences, although this approach also incurs significant time and space costs.
To overcome these challenges, we developed Ares, a parallel memory allocator that addresses sequential inefficiencies by efficiently placing raw reads.
Ares optimizes memory usage on node memory, eliminating data replication and model memory on distributed-memory architectures.
By doing so, Ares enables the assembly of small genomes on multi-node clusters with scalable, parallelized contiguous assembly.
We showcase Ares's effectiveness in assembling the S. cerevisiae genome, demonstrating up to 4x speed improvements with reduced memory usage compared to single-threaded approaches. Ares's documentation is available at https://ares-contiguous-assembly.readthedocs.io/en/latest/. Ares is based on MUMmer4 and can be used with other assembly tools. We are open to collaboration and invite the community to utilize Ares in assembling genomes and environmental microbiomes. A suitable concept to convey the reliability of this order is the statistical depth, which can be viewed as a generalisation of the half-space depth. By applying a specific transformation, pointwise, to the data and using the resulting values to determine a linear order, we define statistical depth. To efficiently process and analyze data, businesses often tag their text-based information with structured elements such as dates, names, and addresses. The TOTEM experiment employs the infrared mode of the LHC to study interactions between individual particles within proton-proton collisions. However, analyzing interactions involving multiple nucleons in the target presents analytical challenges due to the complexity of nucleon-nucleon interactions. To overcome these difficulties, the cross-section of proton-lead collisions is investigated through the observation of lead-like secondaries in the forward region of the STU detector at $\sqrt{s}=900$ GeV. A total of $1191 \pm 167$ events consistent with the formation of a lead nucleus at $z=3.30\pm0.13$ were recorded along the STU detector's 13.2 unit range, corresponding to a measured cross-section of $\sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}=64.8\pm5.8$ mb. Third-order Coulomb effects were also observed in the experiment, yielding a total Coulomb barrier of $B_c=17.2\pm2.2$ GeV/c^2. Furthermore, the cross-section for the formation of lead nuclei at various values of $z$ was also investigated, revealing an anisotropic distribution of lead secondaries in the range of $z=2-4$. A total cross-section of approximately $\sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}\approx 110$ mb was recorded at $z=2$, whereas this value significantly decreases to $\sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}\approx 5$ mb at $z=4$. A description of these findings in accordance with the quark formation of top quarks within nucleon-nucleon interactions is proposed, exemplified by the generation of top quark triplets (t, b, $\bar{b}$) in proton-lead collisions. A detailed theoretical analysis of this phenomenon, incorporating proton-lead interactions at $\sqrt{s}=900$ GeV, reveals the possible formation of top quark generation at $x\sim 10^{-3}$ with high virtuality $Q^2\sim 10^{3}$ GeV$^2$, exhibiting third-order Coulomb behavior. A further examination of nucleon-nucleon interactions at lower scales revealed the possibility of re-encountering top quarks at lower energies, specifically at $\sqrt{s}\sim 1.5$ GeV with high virtuality $Q^2\sim 10^{2}$ GeV$^2$. A total cross-section for this process was estimated to be in the range of several millibarns.

This mechanism allows relevant database columns to be incorporated into the parsing model, thereby enhancing its ability to accurately translate spoken language into SQL queries. To illustrate our point, consider the phrase "pick the largest house". Without context, the model might confuse "house" with "car", but the supplementary task clarifies the intent, enabling the parser to correctly rephrase the input as "the biggest houss". As a result, the supplementary task boosts the parsing model's performance, achieving higher accuracy in translating spoken language to SQL queries. Notably, the best performance is achieved by combining a moderate level of supplementary information with the inherent instructions, not overwhelming the model with too much data. In social networks centered on security, trust plays a key role in influencing individual behavior, particularly when individuals make decisions based on limited information available to them. This study examines how complete structural equilibrium outcomes and shorter-term views impact social interactions among network participants. We begin by defining views as predictive models that estimate payoff predictions, after which we demonstrate the existence of a forward-looking Nash equilibrium in networks. Subsequently, we show that views converge to a structural equilibrium in networks that adhere to regular graph topologies, albeit this outcome may be hindered by specific network features. Notably, we find that views can diverge over time in certain networks, even in scenarios where all participants adopt the same viewing strategy. This result highlights the significance of understanding both short- and long-term decision-making dynamics among individuals in social networks. Chiral gauge theories without supersymmetry serve as a major non-supersymmetric framework for establishing duality, particularly Planar Chiral Gauge Theories which have an established duality theory. This paper introduces additional chiral theories that could potentially be dual: Chern-Simons-Higgs theories featuring defect systems such as domain walls and surface defects, and SU(N) chiral gauge theories with matter fields representing fundamental, anti-fundamental, and a mixture of both. By exploring various asymptotic regions and applying the Coset Construction, we establish dualities for each of these theories, extending and generalizing prior studies on dualities in 2d chiral theories. We examine SU(N) chiral Yang-Mills theory and discuss multiple approaches to construct dualities. Additionally, we consider Generalized Double Field Theory as a distinct framework for addressing chiral dualities, which in some cases yields the same outcomes as the Coset Construction. This method, however, also provides novel dualities. We use multiple examples to demonstrate that various chiral dualities can be expressed through GFPT, a recent framework. Lastly, we explore the M-theory framewirk and establish novel dualities for M2-brane systems corresponding to chiral dualities. This includes a dual for SU(N) chiral Yang-Mills theory and three different duals for SU(N) chiral QCD. All M-theory dualities are confirmed by analyzing brane configurations in two distinct asymptotic regions. An appendix supplements the paper with an application of GFPT to a 7d chiral QCD with three different matter field configurations. GFPT yields three distinct duals for 7d chiral QCD. Lastly, an alternative method is provided in an accompanying letter for constructing dualities: explicitly utilizing Coset Construction in a framework independent of Chern-Simons theory. This involves a novel generalization of the Coset Construction in a framework that we call CKP. This method, however, also yields the same outcomes as the Coset Construction when utilized for the same theories, whereas CKP provides novel insights into the dualities of four chiral theories whose dualities were established by the Coset Construction. CKP potentially holds a broader scope of applicability. CKP may apply to numerous chiral dualities that were not explored in the paper. It is uncertain whether CKP can be used to construct dualities for gauge theories featuring matter fields that are not asymptotically free. It is also unclear if dualities can be constructed for such theories.

In complex graphical models, precise Multiple-Instance Search (MIS) solutions require thorough derivation of probability functions or their partial optimizations. We introduce a streamlined explanation of probability functions, reducing the associated computational burden. Our method, known as Brief Function Depiction (BFD), notably enables the precise matching of partial optimization results by comparing function summaries. We develop an algorithmic framework, BFD-MIS, which leverages BFD to efficiently exact MIS solutions for smaller models and, in certain cases, also finds optimal solutions for #SAT problems. We also introduce a simplified miscoverage function, Brief Miscoverage Depiction (BMD), which rapidly generates approximate MIS solutions and, in certain instances, also provides optimal solutions for #MONTECARLO problems. Our experimental findings demonstrate that BFD-MIS and BMD outperform competing algorithms and often match performance of the leading exact algorithm, Hero. Furthermore, BFD-MIS often matches Hero's performance even when Hero's parameters are tweaked to exploit its vulnerabilities. We also observe that BFD-MIS and BMD exhibit comparable results for specific problem instances due to their shared functional summaries, known as functional equivalents. We utilize an online tool to generate (i) precise MIS solutions for difficult instances; (ii) ground truths for evaluating approximate #SAT solvers; and (iii) optimal solutions for #MONTECARLO problems, surpassing current standards. To address this challenge, we develop a camera-based system capable of detecting the position of supine and prone individuals. Asynchronous AVF, a technique where visual and audio signals are processed separately and combined, presents an opportunity for efficient signal fusion. However, it can also introduce significant latency, rendering it less suitable for high-criticality applications. To overcome this limitation, we explore the possibility of utilizing asynchronous fusion in real-time locating devices. Our proposed location-detection method combines visual and audio signals to identify prone individuals, leveraging pre-recorded audio clips and incorporating motion detection for added reliability. Pertinent information that can be obtained through the Customized Web search results may be obscured from view, leading to the notion of 'information darkness'. This phenomenon has theoretical underpinnings, supported by recent laboratory studies that demonstrate its occurrence. In this paper, we present further evidence for the existence of information darkness by examining how Customized Web search results affect users' knowledge gains during online information retrieval. In our study, 80 participants were divided into four groups and provided with different sets of search results by Google. Our findings reveal that users may fail to notice up to 90% of relevant information due to the Customized Web search. This led to the development of the information darkness coefficient (IDC), representing the minimum proportion of relevant information that can be overlooked. In our study, an IDC of 0.83 was achieved, surpassing our initial expectation of 0.58. This research highlights the significance of considering information darkness in studies on Customized Web search, and offers possible solutions to decrease IDC and enhance users' online information retrieval experiences. Furthermore, the concepts of information darkness and IDC may be applied to various fields such as information science, social network studies, and information systems, to evaluate the overall efficiency of search engines and retrieval systems. By employing informational darkness, researchers can gain a deeper understanding of how Customized Web search influences the dissemination of information and the shaping of public opinion. Moreover, IDC can potentially replace traditional media metrics, such as reach and frequency, to assess the impact of online information dissemination. By combining IDC with statistical models, researchers can analyze the underlying mechanisms of information spread and examine the influence of various factors on information darkness. Ultimately, IDC may be utilized to develop strategies for decreasing information darkness and enhancing the overall quality of information retrieval. Specifically, searches for "2019 US population" were conducted to demonstrate the practical application of IDC. Google Customized Web search results failed to reveal information from reputable sources, including the US Census Bureau, due to their low PageRank. The development of wise computed tomography (CT) has significantly enhanced radiological images' clarity, allowing for the detection of various diseases, including gastrointestinal cancers. Nevertheless, CT scans' standardization is hindered by the time-consuming and labor-intensive process of manually tracing organs on scan data. In this research, we utilize a publicly accessible deep learning algorithm, specifically the U-Net model, to automate the segmentation of the gastrointestinal tract in CT scans. A total of 1,600 CT scans containing the gastrointestinal tract were collected from the Radboud University Medical Center and divided into a training set of 1,200 scans and a validation-set-examination cohort of 400 scans. The algorithm's performance was assessed using the Dice score, sensitivity, specificity, and the Hausdorff distance. Results revealed that the U-Net model achieved Dice scores exceeding 0.85 for the stomach and colon, demonstrating satisfactory performance. Further investigation into reducing U-Net-related errors showed that incorporating a gastrointestinal tract priori decreased U-Net-related errors by 15%. As such, the proposed workflow, integrating the U-Net model and enhanced by a gastrointestinal tract priori, presents a viable solution for standardizing CT data. This could contribute to optimizing radiation dosages, enhancing image quality, and integrating data from multiple institutions, ultimately facilitating more robust clinical research. With further refinement, this technique holds potential for widespread clinical applications. The exoplanet sample from CORALIE/HARPS (Mayor et al., 2011), which is renowned for having the largest collection of super-Earths and sub-Neptune masses (Price-Whelan et al., 2018), has led scientists to wonder if such a planet population might be the result of a disfavoring process, notably core accretion followed by photoevaporation (Goulet et al., 2019). We aimed to explore this idea by comparing the observed distribution of exoplanets from CORALIE/HARPS with simulated planet populations obtained through core accretion and migration mechanisms. Notably, we discovered a significant discrepancy between the observed and simulated distributions: the latter exhibits a notable shortage of planets with masses between Earth and Neptune (deserted planets), whereas the former displays a substantial number of such planets. Using statistical tests, we found that the discrepancy is highly significant (p-value ~ 10^-5). We propose an explanation for the discrepancy by pointing out that the suppression of planets with masses between Earth and Neptune is largely due to the over-estimation of post-migration losses in the core accretion model. Consequently, we suggest that the lack of planets with masses between Earth and Neptune is largely an artifact of the core accretion model, and the transition to giant planet formation is typically smooth rather than biphasic. Our study is consistent with recent findings (Bueno-Caballero et al., 2020) and our analysis also sheds light on the role of gravitational spreading in shaping planetary mass distributions, an effect that is particularly evident in the CORALIE/HARPS sample around the boundary of terrestrial and giant planets. An important consequence of our study is that the core accretion model, which is widely regarded as the dominant planetary formation process, is unable to explain a key observation of the exoplanet population, prompting us to speculate that an alternative mechanism (e.g., streaming instability) might be responsible for the initial growth of planetary cores. Furthermore, we also explored the role of gravitational shear in the core accretion model using numerical simulations, which might be able to reproduce the observed planet mass distribution, and found that this effect is able to partially alleviate the discrepancy between the observed and simulated distributions by reducing the width of the planet mass range at lower masses. To prevent the deterioration of attention performance in computer vision tasks, we present a novel mutational knowledge acquisition approach called Mutual Knowledge Enhance (MKE). This method starts with a initial "tough" attention pool derived from optimal data features. Then, through an iterative process of mutual enhancement, it continuously refines the pool until satisfactory attention pools are generated for a variety of tasks. Unlike existing attention pools such as PoolFormer, MKE-based models can learn high-quality attention pools adapted to different scales and types through mutual enhancement. As a result, a simple MKE-PoolFormer model achieves superior performance in convolutional vision tasks while reducing the complexity and weight count significantly. The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated by experimental results showing improved robustness and superior performance on large-scale image classification, semantic segmentation, and object detection tasks under both regular and adversarial conditions. We analyzed the 40.5-minute eclipsing binary system SDSS J082239.54+304857.19, utilizing data from the Kepler space telescope. Our research revealed distinct temporal stages of the binary system's orbit during an eclipse. These stages are characterized by non-repetitive changes in the optical flux. Observations indicate that the hottest stage occurs shortly after the eclipse begins, followed by a rapid decline in brightness. A partial mass accretion disk forms during this phase, attributed to the white dwarf's irregular spin. A notable temperature drop is observed for the hottest stage (around 1800 K) and the coolest stage (around 700 K) of the binary system. Based on our findings, we constructed an simplified diagram that incorporates our observed temperature variations. Additionally, we estimated a 0.08-inch elevation of the mass accumulation disk (or ring) above the primary white dwarf during the hottest stage. An approximate outer radius of this disk is proposed to be 0.017 parsec (or 0.009 R_sun). Further research using high-resolution X-ray telescopes is recommended to detect any potential X-ray emission resulting from the formation of this disk or other inherent binary system phenomena. Our research offers novel insights into the binary system's characteristics, essentially painting a picture of the double white dwarf binary system's physical structure and behavior. We re-explore the process of global aggregation in climate models using a method called optimal transport. This approach allows us to identify an ideal transport strategy that minimizes the cost of interacting atmospheric masses while an equilibrium state is achieved. To understand the current climate system, we apply our transport method to global carbon dioxide and ocean current data. Carbon dioxide data reveals two distinct carbon pools: one that responds quickly to changes in the atmosphere and another that is more slowly absorbed. This double-response pattern correlates with the North American and Antarctic regions. Ocean currents also exhibit various circulation patterns that affect heat transport in different areas. By analyzing the climate system through optimal transport, we uncover several key processes, including carbon sequestration and ocean heat transport mechanisms, that were previously unidentified. These findings highlight the potential of using optimal transport to model various physical systems and identify an ideal transport strategy that may inform climate model improvements and carbon management policies. To achieve this, we develop a version of the optimal transport method that accounts for carbon absorption rates and use it to estimate the impact of altering carbon prices and efficient transportation costs on global carbon distribution. Our study shows that optimal transport can provide accurate models and inform policies that result in optimal climate distribution scenarios. Deep neural network training necessitates considerable computing resources, prompting researchers to explore preprocessing techniques, such as utilizing transfer learning. A common approach involves leveraging image classification models, often trained on a vast and easily accessible dataset (ImageNet), to achieve this. The surge in access to time-series data from various sources has led to an increasing need for automated storytelling systems that can effectively convey this data's inherent temporal nature and meaningful patterns. To address this, we present TCube, a novel neural approach that transforms time-series data into engaging, chronological stories. TCube's innovative architecture combines two key features: 1) a domain-agnostic neural network for time-series synthesis, allowing for numerous possible stories; and 2) a unique selection method using latent representations to optimize the coherence and diversity of the generated stories. Through our experiments, we demonstrate TCube's superiority over existing methods on multiple datasets, achieving a remarkable 44% improvement in coherence and 32% improvement in diversity, while also showcasing its ability to create high-quality stories in various domains. The generated stories undergo rigorous evaluation by both automated metrics and human assessors. This study examines well-posed Cauchy problems with coefficients that exhibit sublogarithmic growth and possess a specific hyperbolic complexification. By leveraging specific properties of these coefficients and their spatial variation, we extend existing research on Lp-type problems (where p > 1) to include coefficients with logarithmic or faster growth rates. Our findings specifically validate the Lp-type space as a universal space of integrable coefficients for well-posed problems of this type, without requiring any smoothness assumptions on these coefficients. Moreover, we analyze the universal space's continuity and conjugacy properties within this context. Our research notably encompasses various special cases, including problems with coefficients exhibiting polynomial growth that is subcritical (i.e., less than a certain threshold) and problems with bounded coefficients that vary rapidly. Our study also compares the universal space to other relevant spaces, ultimately demonstrating its optimality as the smallest space of integrable coefficients that guarantees well-posedness. Additionally, we investigate the continuous and conjugate embedding properties of the universal space, particularly its relationships with other spaces within a certain family. Our research notably establishes the optimality of the universal space as the largest space of compactly supported smooth functions within this family, thereby providing further insight into its characteristics. Lastly, we expand our analysis to consider not just existence, but also uniqueness and continuity of solutions in the weak sense, thereby defining and characterizing the universal space of integrable coefficients for weak solutions. Our study explicitly demonstrates the universal space's conjugacy to another space derived from the Besov norm and, using certain equivalences between norms, relates it to the space of Hölder continuous functions with exponent less than one-half. Ultimately, our research resolves a certain conjecture regarding the space of Hölder continuous functions, thereby providing further confirmation of our findings and shedding light on their optimality as the smallest space of integrable coefficients that guarantees well-posedness. Additionally, we extend our research to examine certain generalizations of the Cauchy problem, including a set of differential equations involving operators with certain symbolic properties and smooth coefficients that vary rapidly. This research examines the method through which software developers establish connections with other professionals under the "Related" section on the Stack Overflow question-answer platform, and how these established connections influence expert specialization, as measured by user reputation. Our analysis reveals two key patterns: first, developers often share users with other professionals under the "Related" section based on users' shared tag endorsements, and second, there is a positive correlation between the reputation of experts specializing in related areas and the number of external connections shared by other professionals. These findings could contribute to further research on information dissemination among software development communities and the creation of more effective knowledge management systems. The current study is confined to examining the visual representations of shared connections, and future research could build upon these findings by exploring other aspects of Stack Overflow's link structure. A potential drawback of neural architecture search lies in the challenge of diverse model architectures, limiting their performance on complex problems. This difficulty, known as the galaxy variety problem, occurs when searching architectures that are similar to existing models, rather than exploring innovative ones. This study aims to rectify this issue by reviewing various approaches addressing the galaxy variety problem and evaluating their efficacy. A comprehensive evaluation framework is established to compare the various remedies, utilizing benchmark tests on AmoebaNAS-Bench and real-world image classification tasks. Results demonstrate that incorporating diversity into the search process through regularization and population management significantly enhances the quality of discovered models. Notably, regularizing the accuracy of child models and prioritizing diverse parent models in population management showcase the most promising outcomes. A key observation from our analysis is the relative underperformance of certain previously established remedies when evaluated systematically. This extensive examination contributes to the understanding of potential biases in NAS benchmark suites and offers insights for future NAS research. Code implementation can be accessed via https://github.com/hjdw2/NAS_Remedies. This research is expected to guide researchers in neural architecture search to tackle the critical issue of the galaxy variety problem. A comparative table of evaluated remedies is available in Appendix D. Additional details are available in the supplementary material. Three important findings of this research are the relative underperformance of remedy 14 (pruning), the effectiveness of remedy 10 (regularize parent), and the promise of remedy 1 (evaluation regularization) and remedy 9 (evaluation-based sorting), all of which are highlighted in the conclusion. A key contribution of this research involves establishing a comprehensive and systematic evaluation of various remedies to address the galaxy variety problem in neural architecture search. This research paves the way for a thorough exploration of neural architecture search and sheds light on potential biases in NAS benchmark suites by examining the relative underperformance of certain remedies. By comparing different remedies in NAS, this research identifies evaluation regularization and population management as crucial approaches and highlights their potential to discover more diverse and better-performance architectures. This research further investigates the relative underperformance of remedy 14 (pruning) and remedy 5 (path-based regularization), and demonstrates the effectiveness of remedy 10 (regularize child) and remedy 9 (evaluation-based sorting). Two scenarios are examined - regulating the accuracy of child models and prioritizing diverse parent models - and reveal significant improvements in performance and diversity. Medical sign events documented in clinical notes hold significant value for medical research and development. However, their utilization is hampered due to limitations in their accessibility and interpretability resulting from unstandardized notation and contextual dependencies. To overcome these obstacles, a novel approach called SignEventNet is proposed, aiming to capture the diverse expressions of medical sign events across different healthcare systems and to decipher their underlying meanings. It accomplishes this through a dual process of obscuring the variability across different domain datasets and uncovering the intrinsic semantics of medical sign events. Extensive experiments conducted on three distinct datasets demonstrate that SignEventNet surpasses current state-of-the-art models in sign event extraction and representation. Moreover, the model's generalizability and semantic awareness enable researchers to discover previously unobserved sign event patterns. This research outcomes will be made available, enabling developers to build upon this research and utilize the extracted data for future studies. Lastly, the research highlights potential avenues for further exploration, including the application of vision and human-generated data to enhance sign event extraction and representation. It also potentially enables researchers to build more informed clinical systems directly utilizing unstandardized clinical data. Our profound reinforcement learning system is designed for autonomous driving and serves as a comprehensive vehicle control framework, with subsidiary systems in place for navigation and sensor management. The vehicle control aspect is handled by a series of modules including steering, gear shifting, and speed adjustments. An essential feature of our system is its use of significant reinforcement learning with Multiple Intelligent Pathways (MIP), where a central controller funnels information to various module controllers through an autoencoder. This modular structure facilitates vehicle function optimization, with each module optimized independently but coordinated through the central controller via pathway assignments. Additionally, our driverless vehicle network relies on a Subsidiary Manager for Sensor Management, which ensures optimal quality of incoming data to the vehicle's decision-making system by regulating the activation of various sensors based on the current scenario and scene interpretation. With this framework, we achieve a substantial boost in overall performance and efficiency for autonomous driving operations. Experimental results show our system to be highly effective in comparison to existing solutions, with notable improvements seen in driving straight, gear shifting, and robotic navigation capabilities. This profound reinforcement learning system is positioned to be a leading solution for autonomous driving operations, with a strong foundation for future growth and development. This research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of spin-aligned strange quark matter under a strong magnetic field, applying the MIT bag model. We derive the equation of state for spin-aligned strange quark matter in the presence of a strong magnetic field and calculate various thermodynamic properties, such as pressure, energy density, specific heat, speed of sound, gravitational redshift, and radial over axial instability. Furthermore, we establish a numerical solution for the equation of state in the canonical formalism and plot isothermals on a pressure-energy density grid. We demonstrate that as temperature increases, quark matter becomes less stable in terms of radial over axial instability, but this phenomenon can be mitigated by a strong magnetic field. We also find that as temperature grows, the mass radius of spin-aligned strange quark stars expands, but remains stable in the presence of a strong magnetic field. Our findings are applicable to stars like PSR J0737-3039.

A surge in complex computations from fields like AI, physics, chemistry and biology is outpacing current processing capabilities, making it necessary to enlist computational resources from millions of available CPUs, GPUs, TPUs and JavaScript engines to accelerate complex simulations and train sophisticated models efficiently. The traditional model of maintaining large-scale supercomputing clusters is increasingly impractical due to the cost, infrastructure requirements and energy consumption. To bridge this gap, we introduce Pando, a novel volunteer computing platform that leverages decentralized networks of available computational resources from various devices, including desktops, laptops, mobiles, smartphones, servers and browsers, to accomplish complex simulations and model training quickly and effectively. The effectiveness of Pando is demonstrated through a range of real-world tasks including simulating the spread of diseases, training image classification models and exploring chemical compound properties, all of which show significant time savings when compared to running these tasks on local machines or using cloud computing services. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that there are numerous opportunities for further improvement in volunteer computing through technical advancements that can effectively tap into unused computational resources. Deciding which tree in an ensemble to consider is a difficulty encountered when attempting to understand decision tree ensembles such as random forests. Due to the randomness of their creation, the order of trees can vary, which makes it difficult to analyze them. We introduce a novel approach to analyzing random forests by examining the data points' relationships with assigned trees, rather than focusing on individual trees. This method utilizes assignment curves, a dynamic representation of data point assignments across various trees, to uncover patterns and trends within the data. It also provides insights into how trees are crafted using feature importance maps, which serve as a dynamic representation of how data points are assigned to trees as the forest evolves. Furthermore, we show that by combining this method with previous approaches to analyzing random forests, we can attain higher prediction accuracy when reducing the complexity of deep neural networks. This method is made available through an open-source Python package called disentangle. Experimental analysis of random forests and gradient boosted machines using pseudo-ensembles, small and large datasets reveals that it is possible to accurately identify key features and model parts, as well as distinguish between random forests and deep neural networks. This was achieved by employing multi-scale assignment curves, dynamic feature importance maps, and a novel embedding technique called embedding assignment curves. Our research challenges the conventional wisdom that analyzing random forests necessitates examining individual trees. Instead, we argue that it is possible to derive insights from the ensemble as a whole. This claim is backed by our experimental findings. Additionally, we show that it is feasible to analyze and interpret complex model parts, such as layer 25 of a 100-layer deep neural network, using assignment curves. This is an area of research that has not been extensively explored, particularly when it comes to model parts. We propose the concept of pseudo-ensembles, dynamic feature importance maps, and a novel method for visualizing binned assignment curves. This method enables researchers to derive new insights from neural networks by treating data points as temporal entities. It also allows them to model parts as temporal sequences. We demonstrate that it is possible to derive insights from model parts by employing assignment curves. In recent years, the concept of collaborative machine learning has gained popularity, facilitating the secure exchange of information among parties. Unfortunately, current implementations are often hindered by insecure data transfers and unreliable trust assumptions. To address these challenges, we present an efficient framework, called Flatee, for managing collaborative machine learning operations within secure environments known as Trusted Execution Enclaves. By integrating both remote execution and cryptographic techniques, Flatee ensures that data is protected throughout the entire processing cycle. Specifically, Flatee comprises two key components: TEKM (Trusted Encrypted Knowledge Migration) and TCE (Trusted Confirmed Evidence). TEKM is responsible for secure data transmission between partners, using a combination of Trusted Execution Enclaves and cryptographic protocols, while TCE focuses on validating the results through a unique combination of zero-knowledge proofs and Truncated Binary Arithmetic Code. By combining these tools, we achieve a robust solution for remote execution of neural network training, striking a balance between efficiency and security. Our experimental results show that Flatee offers exceptional security benefits, along with acceptable performance slowdown. For instance, the training of a ResNet50 model on the ImageNet dataset within a Trusted Execution Enclave takes around 35 minutes, while the same process outside of this environment takes approximately 52 minutes, resulting in a considerable security gain at minimal cost. Furthermore, Flatee substantially surpasses contemporary collaborative machine learning solutions in data confidentiality. Our work is expected to contribute to the advancement of collaborative machine learning operations within secure environments. A detailed evaluation of Flatee is available online. To examine the dynamics of diverse species in diverse environments, researchers have been using complex models to simulate how different species interact and affect each other. A particular model being studied is the voter model, which has various modifications to account for species competition and movement. One such model, featuring chaotic network structure and asymmetrical competition, is being analyzed to determine the long-term effects on the number of coexisting species. Our findings show that this model results in two possible outcomes: either all species eventually go extinct or exactly one species persists in the given population. The probability of finding only one dominant species increases as the number of species increases. The species' diversity, represented by the number of different species present, peaks at an intermediate level of competition. This maximum diversity is found when the level of competition is neither too high nor too low. In our research, we utilize computer simulations to explore the complex behavior of this model, with particular focus on the complex long-term population configurations that emerge. Our simulation results reveal that the long-term population configurations are often linear or hierarchical in structure and exhibit various patterns of species coexistence. The probability of finding each specific population configuration varies greatly, depending on the initial conditions and the number of species. Our research shows that the one-species-dominant outcome is more common when the initial conditions favor a single dominant species. In contrast, the diverse population configurations are more likely to occur when the initial conditions are diverse. Our simulation results also suggest that the maximum diversity is often found in populations that have a hierarchical long-term configuration, where one species dominates and the other species act as "supporting cast." The one-species-dominant outcome is also associated with populations that have a linear long-term configuration. In our research, we identify two distinct types of species: the dominant species and the "underdog" species. The dominant species is highly competitive and eventually becomes the sole species in the population, while the underdog species is less competitive and is often found in the losing end in any interaction. For an $n$-dimensional abelian quantum dual model with a base space divided into finite, mutually exclusive, bounded regions, the algebra of von Neumann is generated by local observables within each separate area. The algebras of these individual regions form a category, denoted as $\mathcal{C}$, whose morphisms are identity mappings of the base space's partition. This category is called the category of regional von Neumann algebras. It's important to note that the algebras within this category aren't commutative unless the base space is partitioned into single-particle dimensions. Using the category of regional von Neumann algebras, the quantum dual model is extended to a larger structure, allowing description of nonlocal properties of the system. Specifically, for a given number of dimensions, the extension results in a monoidal category, allowing interpretation of the model within the framework of extended quantum operations if the base space is partitioned into single-particle dimensions. This includes a specific realization of a free compact automorphism monoid, providing a formal description of the model's algebraic structure and its relations to the compact automorphism group of the torus. Further investigation involves classifying all subcategories, denoted as $\mathcal{C}_\dim r$, where the base space is partitioned into $r$ single-particle dimensions, for a given number of dimensions. These subcategories are found to be equivalent to the category of continuous functors from the lattice ordering of finite continuous subspaces in $r$ dimensions to the category of continuous functors from the lattice ordering of finite continuous subspaces in $r$ dimensions. This process results in a weakly compact monoidal structure for these subcategories, allowing potential application in modeling the behavior of composite systems. Moreover, the monoidal closed structure of these subcategories is found to be equivalent to the category of functors from the lattice ordering of finite continuous subspaces in $r$ dimensions, which is partially compact and monoidal closed. These results imply a formal description of the model within the framework of extended quantum operations, and potentially classify all possible categories of regional von Neumann algebras. An important observation is made that the model's algebraic structure and its relations to the compact automorphism group of the torus are formally described by a free compact automorphism monoid. Potential applications and further investigations are considered. An important connection is made between the model's extension to a nonlocal structure and the quantum dual model's own underlying nonlocal nature

We investigate the magnon-photon-phonon entanglement in a chamber magnomechanics system, enhanced by a coherent feedback circuit. This study involves analyzing the ground state properties and the entanglement characteristics of the system, via the logarithmic negativity measure. Conventional magnomechanics suffer from limited entanglement due to decoherence effects, primarily stemming from phonon radiation pressure. Nevertheless, the integration of a coherent feedback circuit, facilitated by an additional beam splitter, enables the generation of an effective two-mode squeezing effect. This effect, produced by the accretion of phonons in opposite modes, significantly boosts magnon-photon-phonon entanglement. This research presents detailed analytical findings on the logical negativity and its relationship with parameters in the system, particularly the twinpeak structure. This unique structure reveals the optimal operating points for maximum entanglement and may hold potential for applications in magnomechanics and quantum information processing. Additionally, the study examines the effects of temperature and feedback strength on the entanglement characteristics. Notably, the entanglement exhibits an inverse temperature dependence and a unique critical value, above which it rapidly increases. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that a minimal level of magnon-photon entanglement can be maintained even in the presence of phonons, solely through the coherent feedback circuit. This research contributes to the understanding of entanglement in complex systems and may pave the way for the development of entangled magnons and photons in magnomechanics and quantum information processing. Additionally, it sheds light on the role of the coherent feedback circuit in enhancing entanglement and may be extended to other systems, yielding key insights into the entanglement properties of both classical and quantum systems. Finally, the study presents a comparison with previous research on the ground state properties of the system, revealing the unique entanglement characteristics of chamber magnomechanics and its applications in quantum information processing. A sundial is a historical clock that relies on Earth's shadow to track time, linking ancient cultures to modern societies via timekeeping methods. As a legacy of traditional technology, sundials are significant cultural artifacts that reflect a community's history, societal development, and technological capabilities. In Indonesia, sundials served as time-telling tools before the advent of mechanical clocks, with examples dating back over 700 years. Although still standing, many of these sundials have undergone restoration due to neglect, with limited documentation available about their existence, location, and cultural value. A recent study sought to record and evaluate the cultural significance of Indonesian sundials, referred to as the Suryakala project, with a focus on Winukoro, a district in Central Java renowned for its sundials. We conducted field research, involving local community members, students, and experts in astronomy, architecture, and conservation, to gather information about the sundials' state, history, and cultural impact. Our approach incorporated participatory methods and introduced a novel tool for assessing the cultural significance of sundials, which served as a template for evaluating other historical structures. Our findings highlighted the sundials' influence on local traditions, community activities, and education systems, with suggestions provided for restoring and conserving these sundials, such as organizing community-based restoration programs and integrating them into the education curriculum. By documenting the cultural significance of Indonesian sundials, we contributed to raising public awareness about these historic clocks and advocated for their preservation as significant cultural artifacts. We also made available a database and design guidelines for cultural impact assessments, which can be accessed through a dedicated website. Ultimately, our research facilitated collaboration among experts, local communities, and students in appraising the cultural value of sundials and addressing the challenges facing these historic structures. We are now expanding the Suryakala project, referred to as the Suryakala-Nusantara program, to record and evaluate sundials throughout Indonesia, featuring a comprehensive database and online platform for facilitating community-led restoration efforts, educational integration, and promoting public awareness about these historic clocks. We are excited to share our new findings and invite experts, local communities, and students to join us in this endeavor, with opportunities for mutual benefit and collaboration. We consider the Suryakala-Nusantara program a pioneering initiative in recording and evaluating sundials nationwide, with a cultural significance perspective that fosters community engagement, expert collaboration, and educational incorporation of these historic clocks. We are now in the initial stage of this project, with a comprehensive database of sundials

This research proposes a novel intelligence surface-assisted technique that integrates power and data transmission in coexisting D2D communications. In response, we've developed a specialized receive technique that integrates power and data reception using a shared receive chain, achieving BER performance on par with dedicated chains. The integrated power and data transmission are then formulated as an optimization problem, with the objective of maximizing the total network sum-rate. Notably, the optimization problem has a unique saddle-point solution, enabling efficient integration of D2D communications and wireless power transfer. The integration of power and data transmission also enables a significant reduction in power consumption. Theoretical analysis and simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, with an average throughput increase of nearly 30% in dense networks. Furthermore, the integration of power and data transmission enables a 70% reduction in energy consumption while maintaining an acceptable BER. The proposed technique has potential applications in emerging technologies like D2D wireless comms and wireless power transfer. The integration of power and data transmission can be generalized and may appear in future 6G systems. The use of a phase plate in the transmission electron microscope is increasing, particularly in observations of cryo-electron microscopy, due to its ability to enhance contrast and resolve higher-order lattice structures. Despite its benefits, the phase plate poses challenges, such as limited availability, difficulty in programming, and potential contamination which can cause out-of-focus images. Programmed phase disks, used to bypass these issues associated with conventional phase plates, are gaining recognition for their ability to overcome these obstacles. However, the potential of these disks to compensate for aberrations in the TEM is largely unexplored. This study delves into the capabilities of a programmable phase disk as an aberration compensator by analyzing its effectiveness in correcting astigmatism through simulations and comparisons with established methods. The results demonstrate that a specially designed disk can mitigate astigmatism to a satisfactory level, surpassing the performance of other aberration correction methods. This research reveals the potential of these disks to not only replace conventional phase plates but also to extend the resolution beyond the $\beta_{min}$ limit set by the phase plate's program and improve image resolution by mitigating star bursts. This study opens the door to utilizing programmable phase disks as versatile tools for resolving diffraction patterns to their full potential, ultimately contributing to advancements in cryo-electron microscopy and structural cell biology. The programs utilize a simplified model and disregard electron Nondispersive Nibro's as their influence is minimal and can be accounted for through a more complex program. A conventional mathematical approach to measuring progress is through the use of metrics such as achievement scores and gain scores. The latter, gain scores, are essentially the difference in performance scores from before and after a specific period. This report seeks to highlight potential issues with relying on these metrics for evaluating growth, particularly in contexts where students do not complete all assessments as required. For example, in the case of standardized testing, students may refuse to take the exam due to various reasons or may not be ready for it at the prescribed time. What appears as a low gain score for such students can be misleading, as their actual improvement might be unclear due to not participating in the initial assessment. This problem is compounded in studies examining retrospective assessments of educational interventions. Interventions are often aimed at enhancing students' performance, but their effectiveness can be difficult to determine if students do not show up to the counterfactual outcome. In this context, we explore alternative methods for estimating intervention effects, such as among students who might have participated in both the pre- and post-intervention assessments. These estimates could serve as a lower bound on the actual impact. Another area of focus is predictive analytics, specifically its applications in fairness considerations. By regulating the influence of predictive variables on predictive models, organizations aim to minimize disparities in treatment allocation based on protected attributes. We delve into one possible constraint, norm-based fairness, and demonstrate how it can result in situations of optimal treatment allocation, including instances where the optimal action for every individual variable differs from the overall best course of action. This illustrates challenges in developing fairness constraints that balance individual and collective considerations. Finally, we analyze data from online advertising platforms, specifically the behavior of advertisers who use target audiences based on reader demographics, and find that doing so may result in disparities in ad distribution among certain groups. These groups include races other than white and individuals across various age groups. Additionally, we examine ad distribution disparities based on audience demographics and find that some of these disparities coincide with disparities in ad distribution based on audience income. We discuss the implications of our findings for companies operating online advertising platforms, highlighting the need for them to monitor and manage their advertising practices to ensure they do not perpetuate inequalities. Furthermore, we explore the broader context of these disparities in ad distribution and their potential consequences, including their impact on social interactions and relationships. This discussion focuses on the particular heat within doped graphene sheets, specifically its temperature-dependent behavior. It's notable that this discussion only considers the changes taking place within doped graphene, excluding any related changes occurring in the surrounding environment. In doped graphene, electron-phonon interaction exhibits a distinct characteristic, evident from the way the particular heat is linked to the speed of long-wave phonons. Additionally, electron-phonon coupling in doped graphene results in a wave-like decrease in temperature-dependent specific heat. This decrease is particularly evident from low-temperature levels all the way to temperatures exceeding the phonon dissipation point. In doped graphene, electron-phonon coupling is the primary factor influencing temperature-dependent specific heat. This effect is seen across doped graphene temperatures, regardless of the type and concentration of dopants present. It's also worth noting that this understanding of temperature-dependent specific heat, driven by electron-phonon coupling, is applicable to single layers and concentrated concentrations of doped graphene. This phenomenon is a distinct thermal characteristic of two-dimensional materials like doped graphene. This unique property sets it apart from conventional three-dimensional materials. In conventional three-dimensional materials, the impact of electron-phonon coupling on temperature-dependent specific heat is relatively minor. This distinction highlights the significance of electron-phonon coupling in doped graphene, resulting in a noticeable reduction of temperature-dependent specific heat. This phenomenon is a direct result of the speed at which long-wave phonons travel within doped graphene. This understanding can potentially be extended to other two-dimensional materials that exhibit similar properties. It's also worth noting that the speed of phonons in doped graphene is influenced by the concentration of dopants. This concentration plays a crucial role in determining the thermal properties of doped graphene. At concentrated concentrations of dopants, the speed of phonons is relatively low. This phenomenon is distinct from quantum thermal properties, typically observed in doped graphene with low concentrations of dopants. In doped graphene with low concentrations of dopants, the speed of phonons is relatively high. This high speed results in doped graphene exhibiting quantum thermal properties. Neural speech synthesis models are highly capable of producing high-quality speech, but current approaches rely on lengthy training transcripts that include speaker information, leading to a gap between synthetic speech and real-life speech. The primary challenge here is incorporating speaker identity into the speech representation. Our proposed model, MaskedSpeech, addresses this concern by using a masking technique that inserts speaker-specific cues, represented by speaker IDs, into the speech representation. This approach not only adds speaker ID phonology but also employs a set of well-designed mask tokens that embed speaker semantic information. Through experiments, we found that MaskedSpeech outperforms baseline models, as evidenced by higher ratings in subjective evaluations and more accurate parse graphs in automatic metrics, showcasing its ability to effectively incorporate speaker IDs into the speech representation. Additionally, the model's ability to learn speaker ID phonology endures even after removing the masking operation, and the use of mask tokens enables the synthesis of speaker ID phonology. Crucially, the model's design allows for varying degrees of masking intensity, enabling a balance between inserting too much or too little speaker ID information. Code and pre-trained models are available on GitHub. Our work contributes to the development of context-sensitive speech generation methods that effectively insert speaker ID information into the speech representation. Specifically, we explored the feasibility of inserting speaker IDs into the speech representation through masking, which can insert a range of cues, from phonology to semantics. The success of this approach suggests that masked tokens can serve a meaningful purpose in speech synthesis. Ultimately, we believe that a more nuanced approach to speaker ID information in speech will lead to more natural-sounding speech synthesis outputs. Our proposed model, therefore, represents an important step in the development of context-sensitive speech generation methods. While we primarily tested our model in the speaker ID synthesis setting, we found that varying the masking intensity also affects non-identity speakers, leading to potential applications in voice conversion scenarios. Our model, therefore, represents a valuable resource for researchers working in voice conversion. Subjective and objective evaluation metrics revealed that our model produced high-quality speech synthesis outputs, with ratings comparable to state-of-the-art baselines. Notably, we found that increasing the masking intensity led to greater similarity between synthetic speech and real speech. Code and pre-trained models are available on GitHub. Our work contributes to the development of context-sensitive speech generation methods that effectively insert speaker ID information into the speech representation. Specifically, we explored the feasibility of inserting speaker IDs into the speech representation through masking, which can insert a range of cues, from phonology to semantics.

Artificial intelligence's capacity to learn from data can significantly benefit the medical field, but there are challenges to overcome. Firstly, there's the issue of data accessibility - medical datasets are often restricted and non-transferable. Additionally, there's the problem of interpreting the predictions made by black-box models. To tackle these obstacles, researchers have explored techniques such as transferring knowledge across similar datasets and utilizing attention mechanisms to refine predictions. Although these methods show promise, they fail to address all concerns when working with large datasets and complex black-box models. This paper introduces a novel technique, HSPI, which harnesses the power of hidden space representations to provide transparent predictions. The hidden space is mapped through a series of transformations applied to the input data. By analyzing the characteristics of the mapped space, HSPI accurately identifies sample similarities and classifies data, often surpassing the performance of black-box models. Moreover, HSPI's success can be achieved with significantly less computing power, making it an efficient tool. The benefits of HSPI were demonstrated through experiments involving synthetic data sets and actual imaging data. The research has the potential to contribute to future medical AI applications, particularly in scenarios where data is scarce, and interpretation of results is crucial. The proposed technique can be found on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/AsinMoghtaderi/Hidden-Space-Predictive-Inference. A new and potentially devastating threat has emerged for machine learning classifiers, involving a person-in-the-middle (PitM) attack that occurs outside of the standard training, deployment, and query phases. During this type of attack, an adversary intercepts data en route from its origin to the classifier and alters it with the help of AI-generated fake data before sending it to the classifier, allowing them to manipulate classification results. We refer to this type of attack as the Generative Person-in-the-Middle (GitM) attack. In this research, we seek to address two critical questions: 1) How effective are machine learning classifiers in detecting modified data and 2) How much fake data generated by AI is required to alter classification results? Our investigation into these questions reveals that current machine learning classifiers are susceptible to the GitM attack, particularly when processing data under limited computational resources and possessing simple architectural designs. Moreover, we find that AI-generated data as minimal as 5% can alter classification results and that various data augmentation techniques can significantly reduce the amount of fake data required to alter classification results. Finally, we derive mathematical expressions for determining the minimum amount of fake data required to alter classification results and conduct experiments across different domains, yielding an average ratio of modified data to total data of 4.54%. This research offers valuable insights into the vulnerability of machine learning classifiers to the GitM attack and could potentially inform the development of more robust classification systems. Furthermore, this research poses new challenges to researchers working in the areas of machine learning, data generation, and security. These challenges include exploring new training methods that can withstand the GitM attack, developing novel data generation algorithms capable of resisting detection, and identifying existing data augmentation techniques that can significantly reduce the amount of fake data required to alter classification results. Additionally, we make available our implemented attacks, as well as detection and data augmentation methods, on the GitHub platform. This research could potentially be applied to various domains such as computer vision, natural language processing, and reinforcement learning. However, the extent to which it could be applied to these domains remains to be investigated in future research. In particular, image classification is a potential candidate for further study. By substituting the Deepfake generation tool 'deepfakepy' with an image classification tool, we find that around 16% of modified images generated by AI are required to alter classification results. This research offers new avenues for research and could potentially lead to novel machine learning applications that can effectively counter the GitM attack. The first direct investigation into the production of dark matter in association with a single top quark or a top quark pair is reported. The analysis uses 36.1 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton data collected at 13 TeV center-of-mass energy by the CMS experiment at the LHC during 2015-2016. A prominent signal region specifically designed to identify the dark matter interaction is created by comparing observed results to simulated data from standard model processes. At a specified top quark pair kinematic configuration, a notable excess of 0.6% or 0.6-0.7 expected signatures is observed above the predicted background level. This excess could potentially be explained by dark matter interaction involving a scalar or pseudoscalar mediator with mass between 600 and 700 GeV for kinematic orientation, or by vector mediators with mass between 700 and 800 GeV. The dark matter mass accounts for approximately a 20% fraction of the vector mediator mass. This study offers new constraints on the dark matter interaction cross-section scaling with inverse masses, specifically lepton-associated dark matter: $\sigma N / (100 \text{ GeV})^2 < 0.4$, monolepton dark matter: $\sigma N / (100 \text{ GeV})^2 < 0.3$, and missing energy dark matter: $\sigma N / (100 \text{ GeV})^2 < 0.5$, with the exclusion levels expressed in GeV$^{-2}$. Additionally, this study introduces new lower limits on the mediator mass based on the invariant mass distribution in the dark matter resonance search channels. For both scalar and pseudoscalar mediators at rest, the lower limits are respectively at 1.1 and 1.2 TeV. This study also introduces new dark matter interaction cross-section constraints across various simplified models with the dark matter particle coupled to a top quark and a top anti-quark. These models primarily yield upper limits under 10$^{-41}~\text{cm}^2$ per GeV, with one model, where the dark matter particle couples to a top quark and a top anti-quark with equal strength, yielding a limit of 6-20~fb. Its members maintain constant orbital patterns despite the black hole's gravitational influence. Furthermore, one of the stellar members is assumed to have a surrounding disk, causing it to slow down due to friction with the disk. This interaction leads to an uneven distribution of speeds among the stellar members as well as other orbital irregularities. As a result, researchers identify scenarios in which the system's rotation accelerates at an increasing rate under specific conditions, a phenomenon not observed in similar systems without disks. This analysis contributes to our understanding of these types of stellar systems and their potential applications in astrophysics. It also sheds light on the creation of these systems following the loss of a binary's companion in various environmental contexts. In particular, researchers find that certain systems with disks embedded in them exhibit distinct behavioral patterns compared to those without disks. These differences become most apparent under highly eccentric conditions, a phenomenon consistent with recent observations. This work represents a significant advancement in our knowledge of these types of stellar systems and their behavior under different astronomical conditions. Its findings have potential implications for the observation and analysis of these systems using data from astronomical surveys in the future. Ultimately, researchers identify essential areas for further investigation and development in the study of these stellar systems and their associated dynamics. A previously reported method, which leverages Taylor series, allows for the training of neural networks without gradient calculations. However, this method's expansion to tackle complex functions is hindered by the degree of polynomial series and network depth. To address this limitation, a novel neural network structure called GSNNS is presented, capable of approximating any continuous function with a single hidden layer, similar to traditional neural networks. GSNNS achieves this by utilizing a series of localized Taylor bases within its hidden layer, along with a derivative estimator that eliminates the gradient calculation requirement. Additionally, the model's non-convergence theorem and stable learning rate is established to guide GSNNS training. With improved efficiency and fewer parameters, GSNNS surpasses or equals the performance of state-of-the-art methods in regression tasks. essential for creating immersive experiences that have a lasting impact.  The
research discussed in this paper explores how user perceptions change in response
to variations in certain key factors, specifically the frame rate, resolution,
and movement system.  By examining these alterations, we can gain a deeper
understanding of the user's visual experience and ultimately improve the
overall feeling of presence in VR.  According to our analysis, users are more
sensitive to changes in motion than in other aspects, and interestingly, high
levels of motion can actually make users less noticeable small changes in the
other areas.  This discovery has significant implications for the design of
optimal rendering systems, and suggests that overloading the visual system
with excessive motion may not be an effective strategy, and could potentially
negatively affect the user's experience.  In particular, our research
demonstrates that while an ideal frame rate is difficult to achieve but
necessary, there is some flexibility in terms of image quality settings.  By
prioritizing motion above other factors, developers may be able to create
more efficient and responsive experiences, and potentially even find a
balance between motion and image quality that is more user-friendly.  This
research was conducted using a custom-designed laboratory setup, and is
supported by a significant body of experimental results and statistical data.

Focusing on a theoretical model, they consider how a protostellar core, assumed to be a homogeneous object, undergoes mass redistribution as it forms twin planets. This redistribution is simulated through a process called radial fragmentation, which is driven by the core's rotation. As the core's total mass increases, it undergoes fragmentation, resulting in planet pairs that are chemically equivalent and increasingly distant from their parent core as the core's mass grows. This planetary development mechanism is compared to observations of exoplanetary systems, including the mass range of their constituent planets, to see how it correlates with characteristics of the systems. Specifically, researchers find that planet development mass, which increases with the core's mass, aligns with the observed mass range of planetary systems. This would allow researchers to examine how the spatial distribution of mass within systems influences planetary development, and make more precise predictions based on radial fragmentation. In cases where this data cannot be precomputed due to performance constraints, an alternative approach is to derive valid inputs from a smaller set of precomputed inputs. This results in a new problem, verifying whether a given program output is within a specified range for a particular input, given a smaller set of precomputed inputs. An efficient solution to this problem is crucial for achieving substantial speedups in program stabilization. Specifically, our study investigates how to achieve fast stabilization for programs comprising a single recursive function, particularly when evaluating integer or bitvectors. Our analysis reveals that certain assertions from Clight, a C language subset, can be successfully explored, while others can be reduced to known problems. Notably, our results demonstrate that 42% of Clight assertions meet specific criteria, enabling rapid input selection, while an additional 41% can be reduced to comprehensible input, although this requires a deeper understanding of program components. Ultimately, input derivation proves to be the bottleneck, accounting for 75% of overall computation time. Consequently, future work will focus on improving input selection, whereas the current solution effectively handles input derivation.
