Our tool has been thoroughly tested, verifying correct outcomes for all assertions in Clight and our own experimental dataset of 1,016 assertions. For Bayesian estimation to be reliable, it's essential that learned models remain unaffected by deliberate attempts to deceive, a challenge that has garnered little research attention. We tackle this problem by developing robust Bayesian networks that can withstand various forms of tampering. By framing this problem as a misclassification game and employing principles of strategic equilibrium, we outline specific boundary conditions that safeguard Bayesian estimation from both targeted and unforeseen attacks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that enhancing model resilience often results in simpler architectures. Our framework has broader applications and can be used to devise more secure learning algorithms as well as improve the reliability of existing Bayesian estimation methods. Specifically, we apply this framework to fundamental problems of parameter estimation and manifold learning, successfully defending against real-world attacks and providing predictable outcomes. Dimensionality reduction techniques, such as principal component analysis, are widely used in hyperspectral image processing to enhance data visualization and efficiency. This study examines the effects of reducing the spectral dimensionality of hyperspectral images on pixel categorization tasks. A hyperspectral image of a citrus orchard is used as a test dataset, and various methods for combining reduced spatial and spectral dimensions are compared to identify the optimal strategy. Our findings suggest that using principal component analysis for dimensionality reduction can negatively impact pixel categorization performance in certain scenarios. As a result, we recommend selecting the optimal number of reduced spectral dimensions based on specific conditions and combining it with other dimensionality reduction techniques, such as region growing, to ensure the best results. The optimal strategies identified in this study can guide the development of more effective hyperspectral image processing techniques. Residual water molecules within protein structures can provide insight into their true form, revealing details previously obscured by high-resolution resolutions. Calculations of amide proton chemical shifts in proteins, made possible by advancements in quantum computing, enable researchers to refine protein structures. Chemical shifts for every amide proton are determined and used to resonate frequency-resolved NMR data, allowing the distinction of near-protein water molecules. This methodology is used to verify and improve protein structures by identifying and correcting errors, particularly misaligned regions, using a global refinement protocol. By applying this protocol to 19 GPCR-related proteins, researchers demonstrate the ability to improve some models by up to 5 Angstroms, underscoring the utility of quantum-derived chemical shifts in enhancing protein structures. Additionally, the integration of quantum-derived chemical shifts with existing resonance assignments and NMR constraints in RefineSOPHIA enhances protein structure refinement. This hybrid approach, RefineSOPHIA+QC, leads to improved protein structures, specifically in complex regions, ultimately contributing to a more accurate understanding of GPCR biology. To address challenges in describing quantum many-body systems, we have enhanced our ab initio method for exciton condensation to include electron-hole interactions. This improvement enables us to utilize the scheme within the density functional theory framework. As an application of the advancement, we have investigated the possibility of exciton condensation in the 2H polytype of TiSe2, a material exhibiting a topological Bragg insulator phase. Through computational analysis based on density functional theory and excitonic density functional theory, we have identified an anomalous mode in the phonon spectrum of TiSe2, suggesting the presence of electron-phonon coupling that could lead to exciton condensation. However, the outcome differs from recent experimental and theoretical findings claiming the emergence of a charge density wave in TiSe2, underlining the significance of electron-phonon coupling in the process. Utilizing the newly developed theory, we have described the interplay between excitons, electron-hole pairs, and phonons within TiSe2, yielding results consistent with density functional theory. These results demonstrate that the charge density wave in TiSe2 arises from exciton condensation of a particular combination of electron and hole states that shares a particular symmetry with the phonon mode involved, as well as an additional process occurring via electron-phonon coupling that leads to charge transfer. Conversely, the anomalous mode in TiSe2 does not directly contribute to the charge density wave through exciton condensation as initially assumed. This study represents the first instance where an ab initio approach for exciton condensation has been utilized to describe a real material, marking an important milestone in the theory's development. Furthermore, the advancement could be applied to various quantum many-body systems, such as superconductors and ferromagnets, under specific constraints. In particular, it is crucial that the excitons formed do not disrupt the critical symmetry of the system, a standard requirement. A notable exception occurs in the case of ferromagnets, where the critical symmetry is trivial and thus excisions are permitted. Lastly, it is essential to note that the theory's application relies on the presence of well-localized correlation tails within the wave functions of the system, an assumption met by density functional theory. Moreover, the theory's utilization necessitates the presence of distinct quasiparticle states and phonon states, an assumption also met by density functional theory and evidenced by the outcome of our analysis on TiSe2. Ultimately, the theory's development paves the way for the novel application of exciton condensation

To analyze the impact of an external magnetic field on a novel class of quantum coherent states known as nematic quantum phases of superconductivity, we developed a theoretical framework. Our model specifically investigates how this magnetic field influences a novel type of superconducting state characterized by paired electrons that have triplets of angular momentum. In our study, we discovered that the magnetic field's alignment has a significant effect on the paramagnetic behavior exhibited by these triplet-cooper pairs as they interact with the field. The magnetic field's alignment can either facilitate or impede the formation of magnetic associations between the pairs, which in turn influences the observed paramagnetic behavior. In the case of poorly aligned triplet pairs, we discovered that the magnetic field's impact is minimal, resulting in a reduction of paramagnetism that is proportional to the square of the magnetic field. Conversely, when the triplet pairs are well-aligned, the magnetic field's impact is more pronounced, and the resulting paramagnetism exhibits linear proportionality to the magnetic field. Our theoretical findings may be relevant to the analysis of nematic quantum phases of superconductivity in materials such as strontium curium where such a phenomenon has been observed. In typical teacher-student relationships, students strive to maximize their grades, and teachers seek to minimize lax behavior. However, this research explores an alternative dynamic where both the teacher and student seek to outdo each with the most motivated approach. By examining the strategic interactions within these relationships, we identify scenarios in which the teacher can successfully induce enthusiastic students and vice versa. Additionally, we investigate how small changes in the model affecting payoffs can alter the stability of these equilibrium states, potentially shifting from a state of student apathy to a state of mutual engagement. To study these interactions, we utilize game theory applied to sequences, specifically focusing on Fleming and Sondermann's model. Our analysis reveals that when the teacher is committed to 'educating,' the student has a clear preference, and we apply this to investigate the Asymptotic Variation Lemma. Furthermore, we make observations on the local structure of these relationships, and finally, we introduce a novel application of our analysis to model the dynamics of the social phenomenon known as 'keeping up with the Joneses.' Our research is presented in a series of separate papers, with one studying the strategic teacher-student dynamic, another examining the asymptotic properties, and a final paper exploring the local structure and practical implications. Researchers felt that the images conveyed a sense of interactivity and sparked a desire to manipulate objects visually. Nevertheless, they realized that the concept of 'computational playfulness' was too ambiguous and varied greatly according to personal perspectives. This led the research community to call for a more systematic investigation into the underlying factors contributing to the phenomenon. A study was conducted to examine how image properties, specifically lighting effects, influence perceptions of playfulness. A survey was sent out to researchers in the field and a dataset, LIT, was established consisting of 301 pairs of images, each featuring a scene illuminated in two different ways. Participants were asked to rate the playfulness of each pair, and the results showed that modifications to the lighting often had a significant impact. When participants felt a change in the lighting affected their perception of playfulness, the direction of the change was often opposite to what they had initially anticipated. This revealed that personal perspectives on playfulness can sometimes be contradicted by the perceived ambiance created by the lighting. A model was developed to identify the factors in the images that contributed to variations in perceptions of playfulness. Interestingly, the model showed that the most playable and interactivelike images were those that were dimly lit and had shadows. On the other hand, the most playful images were brightly lit and had highlights. This study strives to be the first to investigate how lighting affects the perceived playfulness of computational systems and paves the way for future research in the area. It also highlights the importance of considering the ambiguity in the interpretation of playfulness and the significance of incorporating perspective-taking techniques. Reward learning poses significant challenges to efficient data utilization, typically requiring extensive, time-consuming marking of trial data by human experts. To accelerate this process, reward learning often employs simple tasks such as basic categorization. However, basic categorization offers limited information to guide complex decision-making processes. To boost the informational value of human labeling, we introduce a novel ranking task called Visually Supported Cluster Ranking (VCRR). In VCRR, humans group trial data into visually represented clusters based on their characteristics, providing rich information to guide complex decisions through cluster boundaries. Notably, we utilize VCRR to enhance the robustness of reinforcement learning models against adversarial attacks by modeling the clustering as a probabilistic graph partition. Our experiments involve integrating VCRR into state-of-the-art reinforcement learning training pipelines for Atari games, yielding notable improvements in robustness and efficient exploration of complex environments. The source code is available at https://github.com/yangyangyang/VCRR. Current research limitations are discussed, and potential future developments are proposed to leverage human labeling capabilities further.

### Introduction

Reward learning is an autonomous system that adapts its environment rewards to maximize its effectiveness, but human experts must mark trial data to train it. This labeling process is time-consuming, so we explore visually supported groupings of trial data to boost the informational value of human labeling. We introduce Visually Supported Cluster Ranking (VCRR), a group-ing task where humans categorize data into visually represented clusters based on their characteristics. We utilize VCRR to enhance the robustness of reinforcement learning models against adversarial attacks by modeling the clustering as a probabilistic graph partition. We integrate VCRR into state-of-the-art reinforcement learning training pipelines for Atari games, yielding notable improvements in robustness and efficient exploration of complex environments. We discuss current research limitations and propose future developments to leverage human labeling capabilities further.

We show that a topological space's Smyth powerspace is core-complete if and only if the original space has a cover consisting of core-complete spaces. This leads to the conclusion that core-conciseness is not a necessary condition for the Smyth powerspace, in contrast to the Laski-Merektin powerspace. Moreover, we demonstrate that a space with a core-complete cover does not necessarily have a core-complete Smyth powerspace. This raises the question of whether such a space's Smyth powerspace is at least core-complete if it has a specific cover consisting of core-complete spaces with a certain property. This raises further potential questions for investigation. We also define a type of space called weakly core-complete spaces, and establish that these spaces have core-complete Smyth powerspaces. Furthermore, we examine the core-conciseness of powerspaces derived from these weakly core-complete spaces, specifically in relation to their own core-conciseness. Finally, we analyze the core-conciseness of the T$_0$-refinement of a space's Smyth powerspace, specifically when it has a cover consisting of core-complete spaces with a certain property. We also propose some open questions related to this area of study. We further prove that a space's $\mathcal{K}$-Scott topological powerspace is core-complete if and only if the original space has a cover consisting of core-complete spaces. This leads to the conclusion that core-conciseness is not a necessary condition for the $\mathcal{K}$-Scott topological powerspace, in contrast to the Laski-Merektin powerspace. We also define a type of space called quasi-core-complete spaces, and establish that these spaces have core-complete $\mathcal{K}$-Scott topological powerspaces. Moreover, we examine the core-conciseness of powerspaces derived from these quasi-core-complete spaces, specifically in relation to their own core-conciseness. Finally, we analyze the core-conciseness of the T$_0$-refinement of a space's $\mathcal{K}$-Scott topological powerspace, specifically when it has a cover consisting of core-complete spaces with a certain property. We also propose some open questions related to this area of study. We further investigate a type of space called almost core-complete spaces. We demonstrate that a space's Smyth powerspace is almost core-complete if and only if the original space has a cover consisting of almost core-complete spaces.

This technique is susceptible to model instability and an optimal smoothing parameter value, which can be difficult to determine. A modified EILW method is proposed, addressing these issues by introducing a robust EILW (REILW) technique. The REILW algorithm applies a standardized distribution to neural network forecasts and uses a quantile-based metric to determine the optimal smoothing parameter value. Experimental results on energy demand forecasts demonstrate the robustness of REILW models across varying parameter values, while outperforming EILW models and established ensemble methods in terms of accuracy and future prediction reliability. A typical strategy for modeling extreme events involves considering occurrences within a fixed period of time as realizations of a Poisson process with an unknown rate. However, relying on the "mean of the largest" for estimating the extreme value phenomenon can lead to biased results, particularly when the number of observed events is relatively low. To address this issue, a study explores alternative methods based on the original parameterization of the Poisson process, focusing on approximations that facilitate efficient Bayesian estimation with minimal computational requirements. The proposed approaches are evaluated using real-world data and simulated scenarios, with findings indicating that they offer improved accuracy compared to existing techniques. We've developed methods for pinpointing texts that fall outside a learned distribution during training. Unusually frequent metadata categories are first determined in order to identify unusual data distributions. This is then followed by the creation of models that can recognize these uncommon distributions. As a result, these models exhibit improved out-of-distribution detection abilities when confronted with texts from infrequent metadata categories. Moreover, our methods surpass prior techniques that rely solely on frequency to pinpoint texts from lesser-represented groups, such as underrepresented data variants, texts written in lesser-known languages, and texts containing fewer words. A composed curve, in the context of curve sketching, results from combining two functions through an operation like addition or subtraction. We explore a generalized concept of composed curves, denoted by $\gamma\sigma^n$, where $\gamma$ is a non-constant, rate-nonconstant function and $\sigma$ is a translation operation, and investigate its periodic variants. Specifically, we analyze the implications of function $\gamma$ being linear, quadratic, or a specific type of nonlinear function, and examine the resulting periodic compositions, obtaining key results and examples in each case. We further consider how these compositions behave under specific transformations, such as dilation, and develop a related concept of dilative curves, obtaining essential properties and examples in this realm as well. Ultimately, we study the geometric characteristics of our generalized composed curves, establishing connections to well-known geometric entities like Pasko curves, as well as nonexpansive functions and mappings. We also demonstrate the applicability of our theories to some counterintuitive geometric phenomena, such as shape replication and dilation. Interestingly, our work reveals relationships between some periodic compositions and fractal patterns, particularly under the dilation operation. Furthermore, we identify a connection between dilative curves and the Mandelbrot set, a renowned fractal. We also revisit and refine some periodic compositions of functions previously studied in the field. Additionally, we utilize our generalized theories to analyze the behavior of certain parameterized curves, expressing them in vectorial form and examining their properties in both the Euclidean space and its affine variant. Ultimately, our study caps off with an exploration of the topological characteristics of our generalized composed curves, constructing them from elementary fractal patterns and establishing their equivalence to certain fractal curves. Interestingly, we demonstrate the accessibility of some fractal lines and curves, obtaining this result via the streamlined fractal nature of our generalized composed curves. Lastly, we establish a connection between dilative curves and the Pasko curves, as well as the Pasko fractal, tying together the generalized concepts of composed curves with the iconic Mandelbrot set. This comprehensive study brings together and synthesizes our previous work on fractal curves, presenting it in a streamlined and efficient manner. The findings also reveal that the order of long nonlocal characteristics of motion corresponds to the order of partial derivatives of the Lagrangian. Graphs with planar subgraphs that share edges with the rest of the graph can be rendered upwardly planar by applying certain restrictions. In this study, we explore the parameterized complexity of achieving upward planarity, applying various constraints such as vertex contraction, edge deletion, and vertex coloring. Our research shows that when contracts are the parameter, deleting edges and applying color schemes are essentially equivalent problems in terms of complexity. However, contracting vertices presents a more complex challenge, leading to a partial answer – some cases are solvable in polynomial time, while others are likely NP-hard after a certain threshold. Our techniques involve the development of new parameterized algorithms as well as the application of parameterized reduction techniques. Furthermore, we introduce the concept of bond-cut clause, a new parameterized complexity technique that resembles Boolean constraint programming, and demonstrate its usefulness in characterizing the complexity of upward planarity problems. This study also introduces the BCC technique to the field of parameterized complexity, offering a novel perspective on the subject. In terms of efficiency, our research yields polynomial-time solutions to problems such as finding vertex sets to delete edges for upward planarity and finding vertex coloring schemes that facilitate upward planarity, exceeding the current known time complexities in these areas. Lastly, we prove that contracting vertices is an easily definable (but potentially hard) problem by establishing a straightforward formulation as a Boolean programming problem and showing that its solution yields an upwardly planar graph. In particular, we investigate the complexity of applying vertex contraction for upward planarity, deleting edges for upward planarity with a given outerplanar structure, and finding vertex coloring schemes for upward planarity, covering a range of $K_k$-free graphs and $P_t$-free graphs. In visual navigation tasks, robots are successful due to their ability to learn from their environment and store observations in their memory. However, storing every detail in memory proves useless, as it is typically only a few insights that ultimately lead to achieving the goal. A limited amount of space in the memory buffer forces robots to decide which experiences to retain and which to discard. Current methods typically rely on experience replay systems, storing all perceptions during one session in the memory, and when empty, adding all new observations to the memory. This approach is inefficient because it incorrectly assumes that all experiences are equally valuable. As a result, robots fail to integrate previously encountered situations that resemble the current state, as all memories are presented equally. To overcome this limitation, we present MemoNav, an advanced experience-retrieval system for visual navigation, capable of selecting the most insightful remembrances. MemoNav assigns importance scores to experiences, selectively stores exceptional moments, and makes the most of the memory buffer. By doing so, MemoNav optimizes the representation of past situations, successfully integrating previously encountered situations that resemble the current state. As a result, MemoNav enhances the overall performance of vision-based navigation. MemoNav does not need human annotations, as it learns to assign weights to experiences during training. By doing so, MemoNav discovers that exceptional moments, such as navigating through unknown areas or overcoming obstacles, require more memory space than routine behaviors. MemoNav outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in evaluation campaigns, as it significantly decreases the number of steps required to reach the goal while successfully reducing the likelihood of getting stuck in dead ends. Moreover, MemoNav's memory buffer is more efficient because it only stores exceptional moments, resulting in a compact and insightful memory that ultimately leads to higher success rates. As a result, MemoNav reaches 100% success rate in navigation tasks that were previously considered challenging, as it effectively stores the most insightful remembrances. MemoNav is now open-source and can be used in a range of applications including service robots and search and rescue scenarios. More information is available at https://epicrobot.ai/memo-nav. The current study focuses on utilizing the Townsend Particle Counter as a highly portable and versatile detector to study the decay of the Hoyle state in natural helium without the need for a medium.  The Hoyle state is generated through 12C+α collisions at an energy of 45.7 MeV, and the resulting 12C transitions are detected by an TPC located at the center of a helium gas atmosphere.  The 12C particles are then analyzed based on their velocity, direction, and penetration depth into the TPC.  The 0+ state of the Hoyle state is confirmed by examining the distribution of 12C velocities on both sides of the TPC, and the 0+ state's branching ratio is calculated based on the 12C penetration depths into the TPC.  The 0+ state's branching ratio is determined to be less than 9×10^-4, significantly lower than the existing limit of 2.6×10^-3.  The portable and medium-free setup of the TPC offers an innovative approach to studying the Hoyle state using a naturally occurring and abundant medium, eliminating concerns about medium effects on the Hoyle state's existence. To address this issue, we examine the effectiveness of two educational methods: (1) inquiry-based learning and (2) a novel testing education framework that incorporates a game-theoretic mechanism design. This study introduces a novel explanation, suggesting that GCNs suffer from an 'over-blurring' effect, resulting from the fusion of graph spatial features and node features within the graph convolutional layer. A fundamental limitation of traditional GCNs exists, which involves the inadequate capture of distinct spatial features in multi-layer stacked models. This inherent flaw renders traditional GCNs susceptible to perturbations and simple gradient-based attacks. It becomes apparent that nodal features and graph spatial structures are interchangeable, enabling adversaries to manipulate attacks from targeting nodes alone. The study further addresses this shortcoming by proposing ExplainGCN, a novel graph convolutional layer that incorporates feature explanation mechanisms to distinguish and separate spatial features. Additionally, the study incorporates various methods to assess feature explanations and their interpretations. Notably, ExplainGCN's effectiveness is verified by evaluations involving natural attacks on the graph structure, demonstrating its capacity to elucidate and mitigate the blurring influence of traditional GCNs. In a remarkable discovery, ExplainGCN achieves superior results and outperforms leading robust and distillation methods, showcasing its potential to address the inherent vulnerabilities of traditional GCNs. A critical issue in auction design revolves around ensuring bidding integrity, specifically preventing bid suppression and manipulation. This study focuses on the Trustworthiness mechanism, an auction format designed to foster honest bidding by incorporating the previous bids of other participants into each bidder's evaluation. This is achieved through a combination of laboratory and field experiments conducted in Australia, involving participants who bid both singly and in pairs. The findings from these experiments indicate that the Trustworthiness mechanism can function effectively in reducing bid suppression and increasing honest bidding, particularly in smaller auction scenarios. The system exhibits resilience to bid manipulation attempts and displays enhanced outcomes when compared to a standard second-price auction. However, there are noticeable difficulties encountered in implementing the Trustworthiness mechanism, primarily stemming from technical challenges related to data privacy and the complexity of bidding calculations. Ultimately, the auction format is deemed feasible but the experiments reveal that bidders may employ simple strategies and the mechanism struggles to differentiate between genuine and manipulative bids. Consequently, the advantages of the Trustworthiness mechanism over standard auction formats are observed but they are limited to specific contexts and do not extend to larger auctions. Potential solutions to these challenges and future research directions are also explored. Additionally, the project contributes to the field of auction design by showcasing a novel idea and making the associated code and datasets publicly available. This information can be accessed via the link: https://www.aueb.it/homepage-drosu-public/Trustworthiness.html. Keywords: Auction design, Trustworthiness mechanism, Bidding integrity, Second-price auction, Bid suppression, Experimental economics.

Ultimately, our study reveals the underlying connection between vertex partitions and these higher-order structures. GANs, bring to creation, along with exploring their visual characteristics.

resemblance of known artworks; using human-like language to describe generated
images, resulting in unique artistic pieces; and leveraging GANs to recreate
artworks based on detailed descriptions, demonstrating the GAN's ability to
interpret artistic cues. Our findings illustrate the artistic delights of

This interaction is believed to be responsible for the irreversibility of the condensation process. This letter investigates the possibility that the observed irregularities in $K$ and $B$ mesons arise from the distinct ways in which these mesons are composed of the fundamental fields responsible for the condensation process. We show that, due to the differences in the composition of these mesons, the spectrum and decay constants predicted by the model vary significantly for $K$ and $B$ mesons, thereby potentially reconciling existing discrepancies in the spectrum and decay constants of these mesons with vectorlike compositeness. We also note that the standard aggregation procedure, used to study composite particles, is not applicable in this case as the process is not perturbative. Therefore, in the context of this model, the observed irregularities in $K$ and $B$ mesons are not seen as anomalies but as a natural consequence of the non-perturbative composition of these mesons. We present KQRNet, a resource of 3.44 million knowledge-seeking queries and their corresponding answers, all based on research papers in natural language processing. We also investigate how KQRNet can facilitate multiple knowledge-related tasks by leveraging the distinct characteristics of queries and responses. Additionally, we explore potential dangers of AI systems that claim to possess human-like knowledge, as they may rely on data like KQRNet that is extracted from research papers rather than genuine human conversations. We utilize supervised learning approaches to assess AI knowledge that is comparable to that found in research papers, and propose evaluating AIs on the basis of their ability to apply existing knowledge rather than solely seeking to expand their existing knowledge base. This differs from current widely-employed evaluation methods. We demonstrate that AIs that prioritize knowledge application outperform those that prioritize knowledge expansion in real-world scenarios. Our findings indicate that IAs can effectively utilize their existing knowledge to address queries that are typical of those found in research papers, and SOTA language models can achieve comparable results, ultimately leading to the development of more practical AI technologies. A portion of our knowledge queries was utilized in the SAIL 2021 data challenge. We now release the full knowledge queries, as well as associated human responses, via an API. This resource is designed to support researchers engaged in AI knowledge-related studies. A user-friendly interface allows for public access to both the data and KQRNet. The code and full dataset can be accessed at https://github.com/ghrua/kqrnet. (From the abstract of the SAIL2021 paper)

Neutrino-driven instability is a short-lived, dense and neutron-rich region created by the rapid transformation of neutrinos into antineutrinos in core-collapse supernovae. This instability, being dense and neutron-rich, leads to the formation of nuclei such as alpha particles and deuterons which significantly alters its composition compared to typical core-collapse supernova models. In a recent study using three-dimensional simulations of core-collapse supernovae, we examine how this instability influences the development of stellar shock. This shock, formed soon after supernova collapse, plays a crucial role in stellar shock behavior and is typically characterized by a slowly expanding outer layer and a centrally located peak in density. This peak in density is initially caused by the original neutrino-driven instability which gradually changes the core's composition, promoting the growth of the instability. Once the instability reaches its maximum, we find that supernova shock expansion patterns vary depending on the density and distribution of core nuclei. This modification to the core results in a significant reduction of the instability's density and pressure compared to models without nuclear reactions. Consequently, we find that supernova models with this altered instability, when subjected to the convection criterion $\nabla\nabla\mathcal{E}<0$, become more extensively convective and affect stellar shock more profoundly, extending its size and making it more irregular in shape. This growth and alteration to stellar shock is primarily attributed to a larger and more irregular structure caused by the changed instability, which further grows and spreads as it collapses and merges with nearby convective structures. This change to stellar shock has notable effects, potentially potentially affecting a range of physical properties including the size and duration of supernova fall back, the size and luminosity of supernova cloud and the type and intensity of supernova light curve. Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a widely diagnosed psychiatric condition, and psychiatric evaluations that rely solely on clinical analysis can be time-consuming and challenging. Recent research combines resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) brain scans with machine learning (ML) to improve diagnosis by analyzing brain activity, but varying ML methods produce distinct results. This study aims to resolve the issue of model selection by investigating several popular deep learning (DL) techniques' performance in classifying ADHD states using rs-fMRI data. Furthermore, in an effort to streamline data processing, we explore two methods to reduce dimensional data, and also examine the reliability of data selection in ADHD classification through the random forest algorithm. Notably, our study differs from existing research by focusing on identifying essential regions of the ADHD-related brain and evaluating the stability of data selection. We utilize popular loss functions, including cross-entropy, categorical cross-entropy, mean squared error, and Charbonnier, along with convolutional neural networks such as VGG19, ResNet50, and SqueezeNet to analyze rs-fMRI data. However, in an effort to improve classification results, we also investigate the performance of transfer learning, data augmentation, and feature selection. Additionally, we report on the computational efficiency of open-source hardware (Graviton2) in comparison to precision benchmark (TPU). Our code is publicly available on GitHub, and we anticipate that our research will contribute to the development of more accurate ADHD diagnosis using deep learning methods by reducing dimensional data and enhancing classification results. Experimental data shows that deep learning models, particularly transfer learning, achieve success rates of up to 90% in classifying ADHD states, and demonstrate stability when trained with data from various regions of the brain. Notably, our study reveals that reducing dimensional data through feature selection yields better results and enhances computational efficiency. Our work may facilitate the development of precise and efficient diagnostic tools for ADHD, and contributes to research in psychiatric diagnosis using deep learning methods. Efforts to reduce dimensional data in ADHD classification may negatively affect data generalizability, but we demonstrate that selecting the right regions of the ADHD-related brain can improve classification results and produce stable outcomes. Our research indicates that deep learning methods can accurately diagnose ADHD, and we advocate for further research on data selection and reduction techniques in ADHD classification. In contrast to the traditional continuous time epidemic SISI model, this paper presents a discrete-time version, exploring its underlying dynamics and deriving mathematical formulas for the epidemic threshold and core outbreak rates. Analytical methods, such as the spectral radius of nonlocal interaction matrices, can help determine these critical values. A numerical study compares the behavior of the distinct-time model to the traditional SISI model, revealing similar qualitative characteristics in the small disease transmission regime, but a more complex transition to the outbreak regime in the distinct-time model. A special case study of the discrete-time SISI model, where the population interacts equally in all directions, shows that the core outbreak region has a simpler shape than in the non-uniform interaction scenario. Numerical simulations demonstrate the distinct-time SISI model's ability to capture the epidemic's persistent behavior, while also investigating the influence of random noise. This is further validated by observing the model's ability to model both outgoing and endemic phenomena. Overall, this discrete-time SISI model contributes to a deeper understanding of core outbreak dynamics and the distinct-time epidemic model's capacity to replicate key epidemic characteristics. Suggestions for future research, such as incorporating heterogeneity into the distinct-time model, are also presented. Knowledge of this discrete-time SISI model's properties could inform the development of novel control strategies, such as targeting core outbreak rates to guide epidemic mitigation policies. Additionally, the distinct-time model's unique features could enable the creation of novel outbreak detection algorithms, such as detecting core outbreak patterns through the analysis of space-time cubes. Researchers in epidemiology, specific to core outbreak rates, may find the discrete-time SISI model's properties particularly relevant and useful in their studies. This work aims to stimulate the exploration of distinct-time epidemic models in mathematical epidemiology, enabling novel and distinct approaches to understanding core outbreak dynamics. In doing so, it bridges the gaps between continuous-time, discrete-time, and graph-based epidemic models, ultimately contributing to the development of distinct-time models that can accurately and uniquely capture core outbreak phenomena. To achieve this, it draws on concepts and techniques from discrete-time Markov chains, equilibrium analysis, and graph-based models, incorporating the epidemic threshold and core outbreak rates into a comprehensive picture of distinct-time core outbreak dynamics. A cutting-edge data storage technology has emerged, utilizing DNA sequences for long-term, high-density data retention. Although individual DNA molecules can efficiently store 24 to 40 bits of information due to replication errors, the traditional binary DNA storage method has a significantly lower information efficiency of around 2.6 bits per base. To overcome these limitations, recent research has focused on developing new coding strategies. We address two key issues in DNA storage: helping the reader navigate complex data hierarchies and keeping DNA data up to date with changing information. Our work introduces a novel combination of guided hierarchical storage and update mechanisms, achieving an information efficiency of 4.17 bits per base. We achieve this by incorporating 2 bits of hierarchy-assistance, utilizing the inherent properties of DNA to eliminate errors and increase storage efficiency. Additionally, our update mechanism allows for the efficient deletion and insertion of nucleotides at specific locations to maintain high information efficiency. Our findings demonstrate the effectiveness of combining these approaches in achieving superior performance. We achieve an information efficiency of 4.67 bits per base when deleting existing data and 4.85 bits per base when inserting new data. These achievements could significantly enhance the overall performance of DNA storage systems. Our research uses the DNA storage framework, guided by the DNA-guided hierarchical storage strategy, and evaluates the performance of the update mechanism within the guided framework, utilizing the Shannan entropy concept to maximize information efficiency. We thoroughly analyzed our results and found that our methods surpass existing state-of-the-art techniques in terms of information efficiency. We expect these findings to contribute to the development of more efficient DNA storage codes and systems in the future. To facilitate future research, we publicly release our code, which is compatible with multiple DNA storage frameworks, and document the design of our efficiency-enhancing storage codes. These resources can be accessed at the provided URL. Our work is the first to address both hierarchical assistance and update mechanisms in DNA storage, achieving an information efficiency of 4.85 bits per base when combining guided hierarchical storage and update mechanisms. We consistently outperform existing state-of-the-art techniques in DNA storage, and our results reveal that our methods can efficiently handle complex data hierarchies and effectively update DNA storage codes. We expect these findings to significantly contribute to the advancement of efficient DNA storage codes and systems in the future. To ensure transparency and facilitate future research, we publicly release our code, which is compatible with multiple DNA storage frameworks, and document the design of our efficiency-enhancing storage codes. These resources can be accessed at the provided URL.

Momentum-space nodal surfaces have captivating properties that bridge abstract topology with real-world physics, exhibiting exceptional behaviors influenced by their topological characteristics. These surfaces, found in momentum space, are distinct from conventional atomic nodal surfaces and offer unparalleled opportunities for manipulating light and its interactions. Although first identified nearly a decade ago, momentum-space nodal surfaces have gained significant interest in recent years, thanks in part to their realization in photonic systems. This review seeks to establish a solid foundation in topological characteristics, momentum-space geometry, and photonic implementations of momentum-space nodal surfaces, providing a thorough understanding of their underlying mechanics and practical applications. Additionally, we examine the realization of momentum-space nodal surfaces in other systems, such as superconductors and ultracold atoms, and discuss their experimental observations. By integrating theoretical and experimental knowledge, this review aims to establish a connection between momentum-space topological characteristics and actual experimental outcomes. These connections will enable researchers to leverage their knowledge of topological characteristics to predict and adapt momentum-space nodal surfaces in various systems. With an extensive range of momentum-space nodal surfaces awaiting discovery, this review provides a comprehensive framework for exploring new momentum-space topological phenomena and implementing them in diverse systems. Furthermore, we outline potential avenues for realizing momentum-space nodal surfaces that are protected by symmetry, spatial spin-orbit coupling, or other mechanisms. By pushing the understanding of momentum-space topology, this review can contribute to the advancement of momentum-space nodal surfaces and inspire novel applications in photonic and other systems. Lastly, we include a detailed description of the momentum-space topological characteristics, followed by an examination of recent implementations in photonic systems, and conclude by discussing the realizations of momentum-space nodal surfaces in other systems and the various avenues for further exploration. These systems include momentum gaps, momentum edges, momentum vertices, momentum zeros, momentum loops, momentum spirals, momentum cylinders, momentum cones, momentum rings, momentum disks, momentum spheres, momentum torus, and momentum donuts. These momentum structures have been successfully implemented in photonic systems, including photonic crystals, integrated photonic circuits, photonic wire networks, and randomized photonic systems, as well as in systems with inverse photonic design and programmable photonic circuits. In oscillatory media, pacemaker-generated waves exhibit a unique characteristic, where the distance they travel is directly proportional to the square of the time they are active. This phenomenon has been observed in numerous biological systems, such as the intestinal tract and the heart's sinoatrial node, where these waves play a crucial role in regulating the body's internal clock. Two analytical methods are employed in this research to verify this velocity prediction, first by applying it directly to known models, and then utilizing a novel approach by slightly modifying the pacemaker's response curve to incorporate a novel, piecewise-linear model. Both analytical techniques yield the same velocity prediction and confirm that it is insensitive to the specifics of the pacemaker's dynamics. This confirms the previously reported velocity prediction and provides a new tool to study these types of waves and their role in biological systems. Additionally, this research highlights the significance of analyzing velocity predictions in piecewise-linear models, which may have various applications in the analysis of relaxation oscillators. It also suggests an alternative method for identifying these waves and proposes conducting further studies on the dynamic interactions between multiple waves in oscillatory networks. Two numerical simulations are also included in this research, where the velocity prediction is tested and verified in the presence of disorder, first by incorporating various types of noise into relaxation oscillators, and then utilizing a model of competing activator and inhibitor chemicals to replicate the dynamic behavior of these waves. Both simulations demonstrate that the predicted velocity remains accurate even under noisy conditions and provide a further understanding of these types of waves and their role in biological systems. In the course of this research, a general method for identifying and confirming velocity predictions in piecewise-linear models is developed, which can be applied to various models of relaxation oscillators. This confirms that the predicted velocity is a universal characteristic of these waves and provides a further understanding of their behavior and the role they play in biological systems. Lastly, this research highlights the potential applications of these waves and suggests conducting further studies on their use in oscillatory networks, particularly regarding their ability to regulate the body's internal clock and maintain healthy heart rhythms. It also proposes an alternative method for reading electrocardiograms by utilizing these waves and predicts that future studies will utilize these types of waves to develop new, pacemaker-generated wave-based treatments for cardiovascular disorders. In the end, this research summarizes the key findings and suggests that the predicted velocity is a universal characteristic of these waves and provides a further understanding of their dynamic behavior and the role they play in biological systems. It also presents two numerical simulations to test the predicted velocity

For a mixed quantum state described by a density matrix ρ, the goal is to approximately calculate its von Neumann entropy, denoted σ(ρ). A quantum algorithm is developed that uses only Õ(log^3(1/ε)|ρ|^3) operations, where ε represents the approximation error, |ρ| signifies the matrix size, and log^3(1/ε) outplays other entropy estimation algorithms. This newly designed algorithm combines techniques from prior studies, integrating a randomly selected unitary transformation (U) into ρ to utilize its spectral decomposition, followed by determining low and high eigenvalues of ρUρ. The algorithm then employs U again to approximate entropy, taking advantage of its diagonalization of ρ without the influence of minor eigenvalues. Consequently, the algorithm restricts entropy approximation to approximately bounding the log of the ratio between ρ's largest and smallest eigenvalues, which are essentially the measures of its entropy. This algorithm showcases robustness in approximating entropy, even in scenarios where entropy distribution is irregular, and it achieves this in a feasible computational cost without the support of additional assumptions. Additionally, a related algorithm is developed that estimates entropy proximity, indicating whether two quantum states, ρ and σ, significantly differ in entropy. This variation utilizes identical mechanisms, integrating the effects of U and evaluating low and high eigenvalues, to approximate entropy distance with a cost of Õ(log^3(1/ε)|ρ|^3) operations, where ε represents the error margin, and it successfully generalizes to the case where the entropy of σ is constantly high. It's noteworthy that both algorithms resist various forms of interference from side channels. Finally, a second algorithm is introduced that uses less memory, specifically 1 log^2(1/ε) bits, to approximate entropy in the case where the entropy is constant, and it achieves this through a modified approach utilizing U and evaluating low and high eigenvalues. This algorithm achieves optimal generalization when employing a universal quantum monitor, eliminating the need for a classical monitor, thus enhancing its performance. However, using a universal quantum monitor is often economically prohibitive. To overcome this limitation, this study integrates a simplified quantum monitor into a quantum learning algorithm, making it feasible to implement in current quantum processing systems, such as superconducting processors. The study's results reveal that the combined effort of a universal and simplified monitor yields nearly optimal generalization performance. Moreover, when both monitors are classical, their combination produces generalization outcomes comparable to optimal methods, demonstrating the potential for improved results with quantum monitors. These findings are confirmed by running the algorithm on a hybrid quantum-classical system consisting of a superconducting quantum device and a classical FPGA board. This research presents a practical approach to leveraging quantum computers for learning tasks, providing an affordable pathway to leveraging the computational powers of quantum computers for learning applications. The study's findings also contribute to the understanding of how quantum monitors can be effectively utilized, an important consideration for the development of practical quantum algorithms. This research introduces a comprehensive music dataset combining three forms of music representation: sheet music, lyrics, and audio. The dataset is called MusicTM-Dataset. The development of this dataset is driven by the potential benefits of cross-modal learning where information can be shared and learned among different modalities. For example, recognizing song titles from sheet music or generating musical segments from lyrics requires the ability to learn and transfer information across modalities. The MusicTM-Dataset is designed to support research in cross-modal learning among complete multimodal music representations. It encompasses a diverse collection of 13,722 full songs, including visual representations, verbal descriptions, and audio recordings. Each music piece is represented by three modalities: $1)$ a set of $301$ dimensional vector tokens for the sheet music, $2)$ a set of $46$ dimensional vector tokens for the lyrics, and $3)$ a corresponding audio clip. A significant aspect of this research is the creation of the sheet music representation, which involves tokenizing staff sheets, converting them into vector-based information, and developing a neural framework for cross-modal learning. To demonstrate the effectiveness of the MusicTM-Dataset, we present a range of research findings, including cross-modal learning outcomes, based on established benchmark datasets. Furthermore, we show that our dataset enables the development of more effective models, measuring performance using benchmark datasets. Lastly, we employ various data augmentation methods to examine the influence of different modalities on cross-modal learning. The MusicTM-Dataset, along with accompanying code, dataset, and staff representation generators, are publicly accessible at https://musicm-tdataset.github.io/. Additionally, the dataset has been registered at OpenResearch and can be accessed using the repository ID opendr-15. A comprehensive guide on using the dataset is documented at https://musicm-tdataset.github.io/README.html. We investigate how aggregates made from different combinations of the same molecular components can spontaneously organize themselves. Our model reveals that, in systems involving multiple components with distinct interactions, hierarchical structures formed during synthesis are essential for self-organization. This self-organization capability is also reflected in experiments on DNA-generated complex structures. We present a partial Freiman type additive conjecture that lies between the k-summer and 1-summing instances, offering a stronger outcome than Freiman's 3k-4 conjecture. Specifically, for any sufficiently large integer k, this new conjecture asserts that if A and B are additive subsets of Z where |A|, |B|, and |A ∩ B| are all substantially larger than k, then there exist nonnegative integers a and b and an additive lexicographic sum over k elements such that the images of A and B under the map z → a + z + b exhibit significant overlap. It's observed that this new conjecture yields a strengthened version of Freiman's 3k-4 instance, along with a variant of the sum-product conjecture. Moreover, this new conjecture is shown to be valid in the context of cubic booleans, thereby implying a strengthened version of Freiman's 3k-4 conjecture within that context. Additionally, this new conjecture is demonstrated to be a stronger form of a previously established outcome in the context of arithmetic progressions. It's worth noting that this new conjecture may hold true for any k, but we are currently unable to verify that assumption. As such, our work does not provide a proof of Freiman's 3k-4 conjecture, though it does offer a stronger instance of the k-summer conjecture, as well as a strengthened version of Freiman's 3k-4 conjecture and the sum-product conjecture, all of which we establish through novel additive combinatorics strategies. Furthermore, our analysis yields several intriguing quantitative outcomes, alongside a few notable special cases in which the new conjecture yields nearly optimal results. It's expected that future research will build upon these findings, expanding upon the novel techniques presented here. As such, the present work is likely the most comprehensive documentation of the concept of 'helicity' to date. A novel approach uses measured eigenfunctions to establish a relationship between geometrically similar objects. Initially, an inner and outer radius are selected, then transmission eigenfunctions for several chosen frequencies are measured. Next, outer boundaries are calculated based on these measured functions and compared with designated reference boundaries. Finally, an metric such as the mean relative error is used to select the 'best fit' geometric shape for the boundary, allowing for the reconstruction of irregularly shaped domains via their probing transmission eigenfunctions. Our method's effectiveness is demonstrated through both numerical simulations and experiments involving artificially generated data sets. A key component in human-computer interaction, intent identification, plays a crucial role in understanding users' goals and has far-reaching applications in spoken language processing and beyond. Recently, researchers have explored leveraging pre-trained language models to enhance intent classification, particularly with semi-supervised and transfer learning approaches. However, existing initiatives often fail to provide a comprehensive comparison of different strategies. To contribute to this area, this study introduces a novel intent classification technique utilizing a pre-trained language model, incorporating both self-supervised pre-training and a comparative learning method for enhancing generalization on out-of-distribution (OOD) intents. The proposed approach builds upon the established BERT architecture but incorporates a novel comparative encoder that analyzes the comparative relationships within intent categories. When evaluated on six widely-used datasets, the proposed method demonstrated superior performance, achieving an average F1-score of 81.46% for the in-distribution intents and 52.66% for the out-of-distribution intents, surpassing the baseline pre-trained BERT model by 7.66% and 4.57% respectively, and showcasing notable improvements on datasets with more diverse categories and datasets requiring fewer training examples. The corresponding code and BERT-based Comparative Model can be accessed via the following GitHub repository: https://github.com/Chen-543/CL-BERT. A detailed open-source KajiPy library for intent classification is also available at: https://github.com/Chen-543/KajiPy. Experimental findings highlight the potential of leveraging comparative learning to enhance intent classification, particularly when data is scarce and distribution of intents varies. Future work may utilize reinforcement learning to develop intent classification models adapted to evolving goals. Moreover, the proposed model's capacity for analyzing comparative relationships can be utilized in numerous applications involving data reduction and summarization. The notion of a simplicial bundle was introduced as a refinement of the global simplicial structure, allowing for an equivalent description of the simplicial structure in terms of a classification theorem for simplicial spaces. This note reinterprets the simplicial bundle in a different light, treating it as a simplicial structure in its own right rather than a mere decoration of the global simplicial structure. Consequently, the simplicial bundle inherits a natural Riemannian metric and a metric comparison theorem can be applied to it. Additionally, this thesis examines the relationship between the global simplicial structure and the simplicial bundle, demonstrating that they are equivalent when the latter's fiber bundles are flat. Finally, a metric completion theorem is established for the simplicial bundle, yielding a complete Riemannian metric on the resulting space. Our methods build upon previous research, incorporating ideas from Geometric Group Theory and the study of metric spaces. Ultimately, this thesis emerges as a mathematical realization of the fundamental concept underlying Ralph Bott's 1958 paper, 'On the Lifting of Chiefly Local Simplicial Spaces'. Bott noted the connection between the global simplicial structure and the fundamental group of the resulting space, and posed the question of whether a metric could be defined on the resulting space in a way that respects its topological properties. Although Bott does not provide a solution to this problem, our thesis emerges as a positive realization of his inquiry. The Riemannian metric that we establish is inherently related to the choice of a measure, which in turn allows for the realization of the global simplicial structure as a geometric group with a well-defined word metric. Furthermore, the study of global simplicial structures is closely tied to the study of metric simplicial complexes, which have been examined by mathematicians such as Grigori Mubarsky and Nathan Miller. Our thesis emerges as a realisation of the fundamental ideas underlining these studies, and represents a geometric realisation of the ideas examined by Bott. Ultimately, the study of global simplicial structures, which are defined as a combination of metric simplicial complexes with a geodesic metric, represents a geometric realisation of the deep mathematical concepts examined by Bott in his 1958 paper. Our thesis emerges as a realization of the fundamental ideas underlying these concepts, and represents a concrete realisation of the ideas examined by Bott. These errors stem from inadequate training, misclassification, and ambigious visual features that facilitate the extraction of false positives. Consequently, separation of genuine and erroneous positive instances becomes necessary to develop reliable visual association detection methods. To accomplish this, we first employ a task-specific metric to filter out positive detections tainted by errors. Subsequently, we employ a technique called relative ranking maximization to learn a discriminative representation from visual data points. Notably, our proposed method overcomes the limitations of traditional classification models by overcoming their inherent weaknesses and achieving state-of-the-art performance in visual association detection on datasets like VOC 2007 and ImageNet V2. Additionally, our method demonstrates resilience in the presence of adversarial attacks and robustness in generalization. A message-passing algorithm called Graph Message Transmission has previously been used in computer vision for image segmentation. However, its application has been limited due to its slow speed in processing modern high-resolution images. A new and faster algorithm called the dynamic graph message transmission (DGMT) has been developed based on the graph message transmission principle. It uses a smaller and more efficient graph structure to rapidly transmit information and achieves faster convergence. In addition, by utilizing deep neural networks, the algorithm can learn optimal message transmission parameters, resulting in improved performance. When tested on the widely used CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets, the DGMT algorithm demonstrated superior identification results compared to existing computer vision models. Furthermore, the algorithm was successfully applied to visual identification tasks of multiple entities within complex scenes. A new dynamic graph structure was designed to efficiently transmit information and the optimization of the algorithm was fine-tuned. As a message-passing algorithm based on graph dynamics, the DGMT has the ability to simultaneously determine the identities and locations of multiple entities within complex scenes. A significant advantage of the DGMT is its ability to perform multi-person identification without the need for prior knowledge of the number of individuals or their locations. Therefore, the algorithm can be applied to tasks that involve identifying multiple entities or performing tasks that require the use of visual information. In experiments, the algorithm achieved higher overall accuracy and the performance improved as the difficulty of the task increased. Additionally, the algorithm demonstrated superior performance compared to models that use attention mechanisms or graph attention networks. A important extension of the algorithm has been made to enable the use of image regions as building blocks for message transmission. As a result, the algorithm demonstrates the ability to perform multi-person identification and has the ability to use regional information. In tests, the algorithm demonstrated improved performance compared to models that use different computer vision techniques. A new version of the dynamic graph transmission algorithm called the enhanced dynamic graph transmission (EDGT) has been developed. It uses a more advanced dynamic graph structure that incorporates regional information and results in significantly improved performance. Results showed a substantial improvement in accuracy for the EDGT compared to the DGMT. Additionally, the algorithm was successfully applied to tasks that require the use of additional information such as the identification of actions and their corresponding locations within scenes. In tests, the EDGT demonstrated improved performance compared to models that use different computer vision techniques and results showed a substantial improvement in accuracy for the EDGT. Efficient hardware implementations of numerical computations, such as multiplication, are crucial for various applications including signal processing and physics simulations. Researchers have developed methods, like DMAS, that ensure correct results but can lead to unnecessary hardware usage. In contrast, efficient hardware designs often prioritize speed over accuracy, but these approaches may result in system failures due to incorrect inputs. This paper primarily addresses the cost of hardware in direct multiplication and explores efficient methods for calculating N times M. These efficient methods, however, can compromise accuracy and sometimes lead to incorrect results, as calculated M times N may not equal N times M. This discrepancy poses challenges for applications requiring commutative property, such as polynomial evaluation or convolution. To bridge this gap, we investigate two primary areas: designing efficient hardware for non-commutative multiplications and obtaining identical results for commutative applications. Our analysis suggests that certain configurations can achieve accurate results for non-commutative multiplications at a lower cost, while specialized techniques, such as polynomial evaluation, can also help reduce hardware costs. Furthermore, we identify potential issues with hardware designs that attempt to rectify result discrepancies for commutative multiplications through additional calculations. These findings demonstrate that different objectives, speed and hardware costs, can conflict, resulting in unavoidable trade-offs between hardware efficiency, computational accuracy, and fault tolerance. Finally, we provide guidance on selecting the most suitable approach for specific application requirements. Our study is the first to examine the relationship between hardware efficiency, computational accuracy, and fault tolerance at a design-level for numerical multiplications. These findings are anticipated to extend to other design problems as well. Additionally, we verified our conclusions through rigorous hardware implementations, including FPGA designs. Our investigation is expected to pave the way for design decisions that take computational overhead into account, such as in the exploration of efficient neural network architectures. This hybrid approach not only leverages quantum computing's speed advantage but also potentially opens up new possibilities for modeling complex interactions. Despite the enthusiasm, numerous challenges need to be addressed before quantum deep learning can be utilized in practice. This article surveys existing research on quantum neural networks, highlighting their benefits, applications, and hurdles, and explores potential paths for mitigating these obstacles. Additionally, the article delves into the broader implications of integrating quantum computing in machine learning and discusses the current state of related projects. Lastly, the article concludes by emphasizing the need for interdisciplinary research that integrates expertise from physics, computer science, and mathematics to advance the field of quantum deep learning. perturbative dispersion relation for shear waves in relativistic viscous

appearing in the dispersion relation can only be meaningfully defined in cases

Our research assesses the significance of particle creation resulting from primordial black holes as a potential source of high-energy cosmic background radiation. We start by analyzing the most abundant PBH mass range, $10^{10}-10^{17}$ grams, and considering the standard cosmological scenario, we determine that particle emission from these PBHs would not sufficiently account for the observed cosmic background radiation. However, we do find that a narrow mass range, specifically $10^{12.5}$ to $10^{13.5}$ grams, could potentially emit radiation at levels compatible with cosmic background data, albeit still substantially lower than satellite measurements. It's crucial to note that a PBH mass spectrum with a significant fraction of PBHs in this range could accommodate LHC and PICSBee constraints. Moving on to dark matter comprised entirely of PBHs, we find that a mass range of $10^{12.5}$ to $10^{13.5}$ grams would result in radiation intensities compatible with cosmic background data, provided the fraction of masses within this range does not exceed 0.6. We highlight the interplay between cosmic background radiation, LHC, and cosmic microphysics experiments in constraining the PBH mass spectrum. Finally, as a novel prediction, we calculate the cosmic background radiation resulting from stellar collisions in the present day, which we find is below the measured signal. A plot showing the ratio of radiation intensity to the square of the PBH mass is provided for reference. It exhibits a peak at $10^{12.8}$ grams, indicating that collisions involving smaller or larger PBHs would result in weaker constraints, courtesy of their greater or lesser momentum, respectively. It's intriguing that both mechanisms exhibit a minimum PBH mass of $10^{12}$ grams with similar deviations. It demonstrates that neutrino decays would result in a slightly higher allowance, courtesy of a minimum PBH mass that exceeds $10^{12}$ grams. In the standard RAM model with addition, we examine the computational power of a single-bit addition operation. We show that executing a left shift by one position involves merely shifting bits and demonstrating the resulting bit is nonzero, a task that can be carried out using addition. Furthermore, we identify the specific conditions under which a particular arithmetic operation can be performed in constant time in this context, leading to an exploration of the robustness of this approach for more complex computations executed in RAM. Specifically, we investigate the additional steps required for simulated division and modulo operations, revealing that these operations can be performed in constant time with the assistance of a few additional operations not involving multiplication. We also consider the implications of having access to arbitrary RAM states and the impact when the input data is actually a zero, a scenario which significantly elevates the difficulty of executing certain operations in constant time. Lastly, we establish a fundamental relationship between the time and space requirements in the RAM model with addition. Ultimately, we conclude that there are specific operations that can be performed in constant time and others that require linear time, a distinction that cannot be predicted based on the problem's decidability. We address this issue by relating it to the computability of one-bit queries, a distinct combinatorial problem, and illustrate the distinction through a few concrete examples. Lastly, we contemplate the speculative consequences if all one-bit queries were to become computable in constant time. We propose a theoretical possibility of enhancing RAM's computational power, potentially resulting in a pivotal breakthrough in computability theory. Conversely, we also explore the possibility of proving a fundamental limit to enhancing RAM's computational power. We conclude by noting that these considerations remain theoretical and may not significantly alter the overall landscape of computability theory. Nonetheless, we envision a possible future development where RAM's computational power significantly surpasses its current limitations. We speculate that such an advancement could yield novel insights into the fundamental nature of computability. To tackle the inherent data scarcity problem in personalizing recommendations for specific users and situations, many advanced RE systems incorporate session information. Nonetheless, current RE methods mostly view users and sessions as separate entities, disregarding potential interconnectedness. Consequently, recommendations may lack the adaptability needed for different situations. To address this challenge, this study presents a new RE framework that utilizes multi-view correlative learning to enhance recommendation quality by leveraging user-session correlations. Specifically, the system derives user and session features from interacting data and blends them together, utilizing a self-supervised approach that utilizes internal and external guidance to produce relevant recommendations. Extensive experiments have shown the proposed method to be an effective enhancement over existing RE methods that utilize single-view data or those that view users and sessions separately. Additionally, an analysis of the results provides insight into how user-session interactions influence RE. The proposed method has been implemented and made available on GitHub. It has also demonstrated high performance in real-world scenarios, according to A/B testing results. Optimization techniques have become indispensable tools in various knowledge domains. Their wide-ranging applications have sparked research interest across different fields. However, academic publications and industry-driven projects have thus far failed to meet the growing demand for a comprehensive platform that can effectively demonstrate the core principles of these optimization techniques in a practical setting. To bridge this gap, we present LibOPT - a dynamic, open-source software framework designed to facilitate the implementation of original optimization algorithms in a practical, real-world environment. Leveraging its modular architecture and adhering to standardized interfaces enables seamless integration of new components and enables the simultaneous development of multiple optimization algorithms. Additionally, we highlight the potential benefits and diffusion possibilities of LibOPT, emphasizing its potential to enhance education, fuel ongoing research, and drive innovation in various fields. A primer on the software's architecture and development guide is also provided, along with a section showcasing the versatility of LibOPT through the implementation of seven optimization algorithms. Finally, we outline future development directions and invite the research community to collaborate in further enhancing this pioneering platform. A comprehensive tutorial and the software framework itself are available at https://optframework.github.io/ and https://github.com/optimization-toolbox/opttoolbox/tree/main, respectively. Please note that the OptFramework and opttoolbox GitHub repositories have been merged into LibOPT at https://github.com/libopt/libopt. You can also contact the authors at sriharsha.srinivasan@research.uts.edu.au or vamsi.kumar.palanki@gmail.com for further assistance. Social media platforms are facing significant problems due to the spread of hateful content, specifically gender-biased hate speech. Arab countries are particularly affected, with the most critical issue being the rise in misogynic hate speech, which threatens women's stability and security. To address this critical problem, this study introduces advanced neural architectures for detecting and categorizing misogynic content on Arabic social media. A large, manually curated dataset comprising 18,316 posts has been developed and evaluated to determine the efficacy of the proposed models in identifying misogynic hate speech. Our research shows that a multi-task neural system can significantly improve performance compared to single-task models, and, interestingly, fine-tuning a pre-trained language model enhances hate speech identification while decreasing misogynic detection performance. Additionally, the most accurate model achieved an F1 score of 53.46 for harsh content, 57.91 for severe content, and 42.67 for obscene content. Finally, the findings of this study could contribute to developing social media monitoring systems in Arab countries to combat the spread of misogynic hate speech. Pulsar wind nebulae are supernova remnant subcategories that result from the interaction of escaping pulsar wind and star-derived particles. A close correlation exists between the gamma-ray and radio emissions in these nebulae, indicating a common origin.
