Significant breakthroughs have been achieved in research on predicting the frequency and timing of software changes, particularly with the application of machine learning and deep learning methods. Despite notable advancements, the field still faces significant challenges related to data scarcity, variability, and the inherent unpredictability of release cycles. To address these issues, researchers often resort to supplementing existing datasets with artificially generated information or making presumptuous assumptions about system evolution patterns. Contrasting other approaches, this paper presents a novel framework that builds on previous work while incorporating new insights. It seeks to mitigate the drawbacks of existing methods and proposes a hybrid model that leverages the strengths of both Naive Bayes and latent variable models to predict when the next software release will occur. To develop and validate this hybrid approach, a comprehensive dataset is created by analyzing and visualizing data from multiple open-source systems, which enables researchers to study and compare the inter-arrival times of software changes. Experimental results demonstrate that the hybrid model outperforms Naive Bayes and other leading classifiers in terms of accuracy and performance features. Furthermore, the developed framework facilitates the exploration of various data scenarios, including different data sizes, densities, and distributions, which sheds light on the underlying risks and benefits of working with open-source and artificial data. To make the hybrid model even more effective, researchers can explore ways to further augment and diversify their datasets, which could potentially lead to more precise release time predictions. Ultimately, this research contributes to the body of knowledge on hybrid machine learning systems and provides new insights into the challenges and opportunities associated with software release forecasting. The presented work is expected to spark new research directions in software engineering and data analysis, which may lead to innovative applications in industries and organizations that develop and maintain their own software products. The complete dataset and experimental code are available on GitHub for reproducibility purposes. The latency model, R6spy, ScummVM, and XSTK datasets were consulted for analysis, and the results of our explorations are presented in Clementine. The Naive Bayes and other classifier results were compared with those of the hybrid model, which was trained on data from open-source systems. The luminance feature was extracted from the hybrid model, and the PAA and MAT datasets were consulted for comparison, which revealed new insights into software evolution patterns. The application of machine learning and deep learning methods has achieved significant advancements in research on predicting software release cycles. Despite these notable breakthroughs, the field still faces significant challenges related to data scarcity, variability, and the inherent unpredictability of system evolution.

Interactive systems, including browsing and searching tools, often involve users navigating a complex hierarchy of information. Users typically initiate sessions to accomplish specific goals, searching for relevant information or trying to achieve a particular goal. To facilitate goal achievement, interactive systems can provide suggestions, aiming to guide users efficiently. Nevertheless, existing suggestion techniques have notable shortcomings: (1) session suggestions fail to account for the sequential nature of sessions, offering uniform suggestions irrelevant to the current session context; (2) two-phase suggestion techniques, combining query-based suggestions with additional cues, fail to recognize that query suggestions and additional cues have distinct selection priorities; and (3) suggestions rarely take into consideration users' diverse preference patterns. To address these issues, we introduce CSRS, a new suggestion technique, addressing all the above shortcomings. (1) By leveraging session logs to identify frequently accessed items within each session, CSRS enhances suggestion relevance and contextual awareness. (2) By recognizing the distinct selection priorities of query suggestions and additional cues, and ranking them accordingly, CSRS ensures user-friendly interaction. (3) By incorporating user-specific preference patterns into suggestion processing, CSRS optimizes suggestion efficiency. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that CSRS surpasses current suggestion methods in relevant literature. Furthermore, we provide theoretical underpinnings for CSRS, analyzing its performance and confirming its optimality. To implement CSRS efficiently, we introduce CRS-RP, a novel rank representation technique. Empirical evaluations and rank representation validation demonstrate the practical effectiveness of CRS-RP. To facilitate research reproduction, we open-source CSRS and make available the necessary data. Additionally, we offer an interactive CSRS demo. Further details are available at csrs.systems. We investigate active particles moving through a activity gradient, focusing on how their movements are influenced by activity-induced forces and the presence of activity variations. When active particles can change their shape in response to activity levels, we find that they often travel in circular orbits around the area where activity gradients meet. However, if the area where activity gradients meet has a fixed shape, but the activity levels decrease away from it, we find that particles move towards it. When the shape of the area where activity gradients meet changes dynamically, we find that particles exhibit complex behavior, moving towards certain types of shapes, but repelled by others. These findings provide a framework for understanding how living cells arrange their cell membranes in response to changes in the activity levels of cells. It also suggests new ways in which artificial colloidal particles can be designed to move towards specific shapes, such as using changes in the size of gaps between particles. These findings have the potential to greatly expand our understanding of how active materials move and arrange themselves. The Seidel matrix $\mu$ for a graph $G$ with vertex set $V$ incorporates elements that equal $1$ if the distance between two vertices is an odd number and $-1$ otherwise. Our research focuses on characterizing the range of $\mu$ for a sequence of identical elements and determining its associated eigenvalues, energy, and diameter. We also establish a connection between the matrix's norm and these parameters, specifically showing that the norm squared of the matrix $\mu$ is equal to its energy multiplied by the number of unique eigenvalues. As a result, we can precisely calculate the range, eigenvalues, energy, and diameter of the Seidel matrix $\mu$ for a sequence graph $G_{m,n}$ with an infinite number of vertices and fixed parameters $m$ and $n$. We also present a formula for approximating the range of $\mu$ for a general graph and provide a figure illustrating how its range varies as the diameter changes. This research explores a controlled stochastic differential equation affected by a fractional Brownian motion with a small Hurst parameter. It demonstrates that under linear Gronwall growth and a moderate control constraint, a mean-field optimal problem for such an equation can be solved through both the classical maximum principle and the backward stochastic differential equation approaches. Additionally, the paper establishes the existence of a viable and optimal feedback strategy, which can be achieved by solving a related mean-field stochastic differential equation under certain conditions. This work extends the research on stochastic differential equations driven by standard Brownian motion, offering a first insight into the applications and properties of fractional Brownian motions in mean-field optimal control theory. Furthermore, numerical simulations are provided to demonstrate the impact of the Hurst parameter on the optimal state and control variables. It is noted that the solutions and properties of the system become more irregular as the Hurst parameter decreases, which is a notable characteristic. This research is part of a larger study on stochastic control theory utilizing fractional Brownian motions, which aims to establish a comprehensive framework for mean-field optimal control problems driven by these processes. This work is currently underway and will be presented separately. This research was presented at the 16th Applied Mathematics Conference, being paper 1.2. Specifically, the results in this study were discussed during the conference on December 14th, 2022. To achieve this result, a method is developed for calculating band edges via a trigonometric polynomial whose coefficients are constrained to have absolute values less than or equal to one, and it is shown that this polynomial converges to a neighborhood of the band edges as its degree increases. Additionally, it is demonstrated that its values, properly scaled, converge to the band edges of the operator, and a similar conclusion is drawn for the elliptic finite-band energies, leading to the error estimate. This work also addresses analogous problems in the scenarios of compact manifolds with not-necessarily periodic boundary conditions. However, the error estimate is found to be insufficient in these more general settings. It is hypothesized that the error rate could be $\mathcal{O}(N^{-1})$, but a definitive conclusion cannot be drawn due to the limitations of the current approach. The emergence of vehicular ad-hoc networks (VANETs) holds great potential for traffic management through data collection, but it is hindered by spotty coverage and connectivity issues, particularly in complex urban settings. To address these challenges, Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) communications incorporate vehicle, roadside outlay, and cellular network relays to ensure seamless and widespread coverage. To evaluate the effectiveness and reliability of 2-tier diverse vehicular networks, we analyze their multipath diversity order, channel conditions, and error rate performance under various factors, including node mobility, relay diversity, and network interference. Our examination reveals that VANETs benefit significantly from 2-tier relays, leading to enhanced error rate reductions and better signal quality. Our simulations demonstrate that by strategically using vehicle and roadside relays, diversity order and error rate performance can be improved, resulting in more reliable data transfer and faster data collection. Our analysis also shows that vehicle relays contribute more to error rate reductions, with node mobility and relay diversity in vehicular networks to the far greater extent. Finally, our findings suggest that VANETs with two-tier diversity relays can tolerate higher levels of network interference, ensuring a higher QoS and more efficient data collection. These examinations will contribute to the development of more resilient and high-performance diverse vehicular networks, promoting the practical application of VANETs. Ultimately, these findings will promote the practical utilization of 2-tier diverse vehicular networks. It is anticipated that by incorporating knowledge of these analyses into the design of vehicular communication systems, enhanced traffic management systems will be possible. Data collection streams will be minimized, and drivers will experience a reduction in data transmission delays, thereby promoting safer driving conditions. Traffic light systems will be modified to optimize traffic flows, and navigation systems will integrate spatial information to guide drivers through urban environments. By incorporating the diversity order and error rate performance of 2-tier diverse vehicular networks into GPS technology, users will benefit from a more reliable navigation service, and these systems will be enabled with cross-layer diversity. By combining the analysis of diversity order and error rate performance with vehicular social networks, traffic management will be further optimized, and drivers will take advantage of an alternative method for navigating through urban settings. It is also anticipated that the development of 5G V2X technology will be informed by these examinations, and next-generation vehicular networks will be enabled with numerous applications, including autonomous navigation, traffic control, and vehicle safety, all of which will be made possible by the diversity order and error rate performance

The public encyclopedia, Wikipedia, relies heavily on crowdsourced contributions, allowing anyone to edit its content. However, distinguishing between high and low-quality contributions is a significant challenge. Investigating the relationship between editing patterns and content modifications could help identify criteria for evaluating article materials. This study examines Wikipedia's lifecycle by analyzing page histories to identify sequences of contributions and their correlations. Edit sequences are used to develop a tagging system capable of automatically labeling materials on Wikipedia pages without manual intervention. The proposed method is validated by comparing its performance to existing algorithms using ten-fold cross-validation on a dataset comprising 1,500 pages. The results show that the proposed approach is a feasible alternative to manual tagging, and its accuracy surpasses that of alternative algorithms. This study presents a novel approach to transferring knowledge in a decision-based black-box framework. Without access to the underlying model, knowledge transfer relies solely on input-output mappings. Entropy-based metrics are established to assess task similarity, guiding the search for a mapping. A theoretical analysis estimates task similarity using metric entropy. A metric-based algorithm is developed, demonstrating effective knowledge transfer in simple scenarios. Consequently, this method is applied to a real-world image classification task, demonstrating the transfer of knowledge from a pre-trained model to a novel task with unknown input distributions. This approach offers a general solution to knowledge transfer in decision-based black-box frameworks. As such, it constitutes a useful tool for automated decision-making systems to adapt to evolving scenarios, where task definitions may shift suddenly due to changing priorities or limited computational resources. This dynamic scenario is common in systems designed to make decisions online, regardless of their complexity or simplicity. A knowledge transfer mechanism allows these decision-making systems to adapt to the changing environment by incorporating information from task definitions that may become available due to the nature of the dynamic environment. This transfer mechanism is unique in that it involves tasks to which the system has not been trained. This characteristic distinguishes it from traditional knowledge transfer methods, where knowledge is transferred between adjacent tasks defined by a training dataset. By contrast, the knowledge transfer mechanism presented here involves non-adjacent tasks, where knowledge is transferred from a pre-trained model to a novel task with unknown input distributions. This characteristic is highly relevant to decision-making systems operating in dynamic environments. This study offers a theoretical analysis of task similarity using metric entropy, providing a practical algorithm for knowledge transfer. Although the simple algorithm demonstrates effective knowledge transfer in our experiments, our approach can be improved by incorporating more sophisticated search methods, such as reinforcement learning, for more complex tasks. Additionally, the efficiency of our black-box framework can be increased using techniques like learning from web queries or learning from the output distributions. These modifications can further enhance the practical application of our knowledge transfer mechanism. To address this, we develop a novel method for learning co-observation interactions without requiring specialized data. Our approach utilizes existing human demonstrations of individual skills to generate synthetic co-observation interactions and develops a collaborative policy through offline reinforcement learning. We evaluate the efficacy of our method on a realistic driving task and compare it to existing methods, demonstrating that it surpasses interaction-specific learning methods and rivals a training method that requires human involvement. Notably, our approach successfully transfers driving behaviors learned from solo driving trajectories to co-observation interactions, achieving improved performance through more efficient use of data. Additionally, our method promotes robustness to various observability conditions and representation robustness, ensuring seamless interactions in various scenarios. Our work presents a pioneering solution for leveraging pre-existing individual skill datasets to create synthetic co-observation interactions, thereby expanding the applicability of interactive learning methods to diverse tasks. Encrypted data can be safely transmitted between two parties, or stored securely, using a particular type of code, known as public-arithmetical codes (PAC codes), which operate under a specific encoding/decryption paradigm. As numerical data can easily be encrypted using a one-way function, and both the encryption and decryption processes involve simple computational tasks, such codes offer an attractive solution for securely processing numerical information. Unlike conventional encryption methods, PAC codes don't add complexity to processing operations; instead, they rely on unique properties of public codes to ensure that an eavesdropper, unable to resolve parity checks, can never deduce the message. Our work focuses on measuring these parity check uncertainties and confirming the existence of codes capable of any predetermined level of eavesdropping risk. We also propose an efficient protocol for generating random PAC code vectors and present various numerical examples demonstrating the effectiveness of these codes in achieving high levels of security. To our knowledge, this is the first time a practical method has been developed for quantifying the uncertainty associated with parity checks in public codes, thereby enabling the reliable calculation of eavesdropping probabilities. As a result, PAC codes now offer a practical solution for processing numerical data at proven risk levels below a specified threshold. Our work includes an analytical estimation of eavesdropping risk, validated through extensive comparisons with randomly generated codes, and includes numerical examples illustrating how these codes can be applied in real-world scenarios to achieve specified levels of eavesdropping risk. Additionally, we propose an efficient protocol for generating random PAC code vectors based on our findings and provide an overview of various examples demonstrating the security benefits achieved through the use of these codes. It's worth noting that our work does not provide a new approach to achieving secure processing, as that concept has been well-established since the early public codes were first introduced by Diffie and Hellman in 1976. Instead, we overcome a long-standing limitation by simplifying the concept and proving that public codes can, in fact, offer proven security guarantees in processing operations. Our work includes an evaluation of eavesdropping risk, validated through comparisons with randomly generated codes, and is complemented by numerical examples illustrating the security benefits achieved through the use of these codes. As an example, when processing 10-bit numerical data and a desired eavesdropping risk below 10^-6, our findings show that a code requiring just 376 bits to achieve this level of security can be calculated directly. This means the eavesdropping risk can be quantified based on code statistics

It distinguishes from other approaches by simultaneously reconstructing the hand, joining hands, and estimating grip types, all within a dynamic Bayesian Network framework. HandInClud utilizes a versatile technique that integrates multiple sensors data, allowing it to adapt to diverse real-world scenarios. Even with modest resolution and sparse data, it achieves accurate engagement detection and tracks engagements continuously. Our system has been rigorously evaluated on a challenging dataset with intricate engagements and competitive representations. Additionally, it demonstrates its ability to differentiate various grip types, making it possible to identify activities based on the technique of grasping hands use. A pivotal component in robot learning involves adjusting the positioning of sensors, particularly when using multiple devices, as doing so manually can be a time-consuming and laborious task. Given the constraints of human limitations, automated calibration becomes essential for efficiently training robots in complex environments. This study presents an innovative approach to calibrating a robot's end-effector by utilizing data from an undetermined, freely-moving, laser-range-finding toy car, without the need for any initial setup. This calibration method is applied across various tasks, as the robot navigates through an unfamiliar space, collecting data on its surroundings in the process. Using a self-modifying neural network, the results demonstrate accurate calculations of the robot's tool position, with an average error of less than 2cm, using as few as 8 data points collected over the course of 2 minutes. Additionally, experimental findings showcase the advantages and reliability of this unmarked calibration method over other conventional techniques. This study's findings contribute to advancing the field of unmarked robot calibration, opening up new avenues for training robots in dynamic, changing environments. To assess the impact of treatment disruption, researchers use various methods, often relying on observational data and analytical tools like propensity score methods, instrumental variable analysis, or regression techniques. These tools assume treatment receipt is directly influenced by the treated individual's actions, an assumption invalidated by the notion of treatment disruption. This concept suggests treatment events can create "interference" that affect other individuals, potentially altering treatment outcomes. While theoretical frameworks for treatment disruption exist, the concept remains largely unexplored. This work introduces a novel interference framework, denoted as the k-neighborhood interference framework, wherein treatment receipt is influenced by the number and treatment status of their neighboring individuals. Under this framework, treatment disruption is identified through the existence of treatment-sensitive interferers, defined as individuals whose treatment status affects the treatment outcomes of another individual. This work utilizes the k-neighborhood interference framework to examine treatment disruption in two real-world settings: a health insurance program and a job placement program, utilizing survey data. Results indicate the presence of treatment-sensitive interferers in both datasets, empirically validating the concept of treatment disruption. The study further estimates treatment disruption rates, defining these as the proportion of individuals whose treatment status crosses a treatment threshold (induced treatment interference) or whose treatment status affects the treatment outcomes of another individual (causing interference). These rates are found to be relatively low, approaching zero percent in the job placement program and roughly 2% in the health insurance program. Ultimately, the study highlights the feasibility and utility of treating disruption as a latent variable, akin to treatment sensitivity and interference, with various statistical tests able to detect disruption (including the McFadden R-squared and a novel metric called disruption sensitivity). Lastly, the study uses a variety of counterfactual models to estimate treatment disruption's impact on treatment receipt and treatment-sensitive interferer incidence, revealing these effects to be relatively small but positive in magnitude. To address potential concerns surrounding treatment disruption's broader implications, the study employs two strategies: first, treating disruption as a latent variable above a certain threshold and second, using a statistical model that accounts for treatment disruption's potential spillover effects. In both scenarios, the study estimates treatment disruption's impact on treatment receipt and treatment-sensitive interferer incidence, again yielding relatively small but positive effects. To address a related concern involving treatment disruption's potential impact on treatment outcome homogeneity, the study utilizes a statistical model able to capture disruption-induced standard deviation within treatment groups. Results indicate this model yields a good fit, suggesting treatment disruption does not substantially contribute to treatment outcome variance

The ongoing UNIONS project is conducting a wide-field survey for galaxy clusters using CFIS on the VISTA Telescopes, an essential precursor to future all-sky surveys like the Roman Space Telescope. To enhance accuracy, UNIONS is utilizing the powerful DESHAPED data analysis pipeline, which leverages machine learning to create a reliable and efficient shape assessment tool. This new approach, known as ShapePipe, not only generates a dependable output but also offers transparent and understandable outcomes, fulfilling UNIONS' high data quality standards. Extensive testing using synthetic datasets confirmed ShapePipe's precision and robustness across diverse data types. Furthermore, the pipeline's real-world application to 181 deg^2 of CFIS data containing 254,849 galaxies has been completed, resulting in high-quality results that can now be utilized for weak-lensing analyses and other scientific applications. To ensure seamless integration with ongoing and future surveys, ShapePipe's source code has been carefully developed and is now freely accessible on GitHub. Ongoing UNIONS data reduction along with future all-sky surveys like the Roman Space Telescope are set to significantly benefit from ShapePipe's cutting-edge technology. To further enhance the tool's performance when dealing with noisier datasets, the ShapePipe project is incorporating noise modeling directly into its assessment process, thereby significantly increasing its accuracy across all galaxy samples. This research delves into the non-trivial interactions of two significant mathematical objects: the Kronecker-Weyl number $\alpha$ and the square root of $n$ for a large $n$. In systems exhibiting Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) phase transitions, the critical exponent associated with temperature vanishes as the dimensionality of the order parameter increases, signifying the transition's continuous nature. We investigate the BKT transition in the low-dimensional Heisenberg ferromagnet with a gyrotropic interaction term, which introduces a critical anisotropy strength above a specific field-adjustable threshold. As the threshold is surpassed, the critical temperature associated with the BKT transition drops to zero, thereby making the transition a first-order phase change. Conversely, decreasing the field below a certain level allows the critical anisotropy strength to disappear, thereby reinstating the BKT phase at all temperatures greater than zero. Our experimental results, obtained using single-crystal dilution refrigerator experiments, are substantiated by mean-field theoretical models, revealing that the critical anisotropy strength bears a direct proportionality to the gyrotropic interaction term's coefficient, as well as the square of the applied field. Moreover, our measurements reveal the presence of long-lived vortex-antivortex pairs near the critical temperature, despite the system exhibiting a magnetically ordered phase that exhibits short-range in-plane correlations and long-range out-of-plane order. Our research offers the first observational evidence of the suppression of the BKT transition through field-adjustable anisotropy in a 3D Heisenberg ferromagnet, thereby opening up avenues for exploiting this phenomenon in the development of versatile spintronic devices. Additionally, the observed period of the vortex-antivortex pair matches the predicted value derived from the BKT theory. Nevertheless, the temperature at which the period begins to deviate from the theoretical prediction is notably higher than the critical temperature, thereby indicating the presence of another critical temperature associated with the formation of the vortex-antivirus pairs. A diagram illustrating the various phases of the system across the temperature-anisotropy strength field has also been provided. Furthermore, our study sheds light on the relationship between the anisotropy of the gyrotropic interaction term and the type of transition exhibited by the BKT phase, thereby bridging the gap between previous numerical studies, which suggested the occurrence of a continuous transition, and experimental evidence revealing the presence of a critical anisotropy strength above which the BKT phase disappears. Lastly, our research demonstrates the feasibility of utilizing the anisotropy of the gyrotropic interaction term as a adjustable control parameter in the development of advanced spintronic devices featuring BKT transitions

We establish tighter limitations on the stabilizer rank of magic states, specifically the GHZ, cluster and topological cluster states. Our method for ranking stabilizers is streamlined and yields more efficient results. For example, our analysis indicates that the GHZ state cannot be condensed into a stabilizer state with a rank less than 7, representing a significant improvement over the previous lower bound of 13. Additionally, our study sets an upper limit on the stabilizer rank of magic states, demonstrating that the rank cannot exceed $O(\log^2 N)$ for states with $N$ systems. This finding broadens our understanding of the theoretical boundaries of quantum circuit complexity and generates new questions about the inherent characteristics of quantum states. Furthermore, our investigation reveals that the logical space of any pure state can be partitioned into polynomially many hypersurfaces, each defined by a set of independent stabilizer equations, thereby providing insight into the theoretical constraints of quantum computation. Finally, we explore the theoretical upper limits of the stabilizer rank that can be achieved through the execution of random unitary operations and demonstrate that the rank is conditioned on the number of applications, $t$, and is not constant but rather grows asymptotically as $t$ approaches infinity. This outcome indicates that the efficiency of stabilizer-based algorithms may decline as they approach convergence. This research has the potential to deepen our comprehension of the fundamental properties of quantum states and the underlying principles of quantum computation. It also offers a novel perspective on the quantitative assessment of quantum state preparation, thereby expanding our knowledge of quantum embedding. Ultimately, our study resonates with the current research priorities outlined by the Quantum Community Challenge. Creating truly random digits is crucial for generating high-quality pseudorandom numbers and seed values for statistical testing and simulation. Current methods for generating random numbers, widely employed in electronics and computing, are often plagued by shortcomings such as statistical biases or limitations that hinder their use in statistical testing and simulation. In particular, the lack of genuine randomness at high speeds and in low-energy applications hinders the advancement of random number generation. We present TuRaN, a novel approach based on under-scaling SRAM supply voltage that dynamically generates fully unpredictable 32-bit integers at frequencies exceeding 3.5 GHz while consuming as little as 0.25 pJ per integer. TuRaN's wide data rate and energy efficiency enable it to create fully unpredictable 26-bit integers at 11.5 Gbps, rivaling the best pre-existing methods. Furthermore, we demonstrate the feasibility of incorporating TuRaN into a SPWNN analog neural network, enhancing energy efficiency by a factor of 26 compared to traditional digital implementations. TuRaN's integration into analog neural networks, combined with standard SRAMs, enables the development of efficient analog machine learning circuits capable of training with genuine random gradients. In contrast to existing solutions, TuRaN leverages under-scaling for the first time to generate fully unpredictable data, making SRAM-based hardware generation of genuine random numbers accessible. We have thoroughly validated TuRaN's performance with both modeling and hardware analysis. The optical properties of $q$-deformed optomechanical systems can be explored through investigations of electromagnetic wave propagation. We analyze the transmission and amplification of optical pulses at both high and low frequencies within these optomechanical structures. For fast-paced light, increased optomechanical coupling strength leads to enhanced transmission and amplification, but the system undergoes decay due to the deformation. In contrast, slower-light scenarios reveal improved transmission and amplification, alongside reduced reflection, as a result of the deformation. We also examine how the type and magnitude of optomechanical deformation affect transmission and amplification patterns. We derive analytical formulas for transmission and amplification, as well as extinction, and conduct detailed numerical evaluations to illustrate how these properties can be manipulated through the optomechanical interaction. We conclude that, although isotropic deformation has a limited impact, anisotropic deformation offers the potential to design optomechanical structures with enhanced transmission, reduced reflection, and increased amplification of optical pulses at various frequencies. This work provides a foundation for future studies on designing unique optical properties at the quantum level. We also propose and examine another type of optomechanical structure, where anisotropic deformation originates from different masses for the cavity and mechanical modes. Our findings demonstrate that, by adjusting the ratio of these masses, we can achieve high levels of transmission and the largest amplification of optical pulses over a broad frequency range. Additionally, by correctly selecting the type of deformation, we can attain nearly complete transmission of optical pulses and experience very small levels of reflection. These outcomes illustrate the potential for $q$-deformed optomechanical structures to fundamentally modify optical pulse interaction and transmission, offering the potential for novel applications in optomechanics and opto-acoustics. Ultimately, these studies provide a foundation for future research on the theoretical properties of optomechanical devices. Experiments involving dipolar bosons in optical grids have demonstrated the ability to replicate bosonic or fermionic statistics through simultaneous application of grid dissipation and Raman transitions. Building on previous research, we investigated the unusual statistics of fermions and bosons in laser-cooled systems under grid dissipation. To investigate the impact of zero-point motion in small-scale clusters composed of sulfuric acid and water, we simulated the vibrational behavior of molecules using a classical and a quantum-based approaches for different cluster sizes ranging from 5 to 11 entities. Our results indicate that incorporating quantum behavior for smaller clusters, particularly those consisting of 5 or 6 entities, significantly affects their dynamics. However, this effect diminishes as the cluster size increases, suggesting that the influence of zero-point motion is mainly relevant to the earliest stages of cluster formation. Ultimately, our simulations suggest that the classical description is sufficient for describing the behavior of larger clusters, consisting of 7 or more entities, due to the decreasing importance of quantum vibrations within these systems. Our study's findings are expected to be applicable to various other clustered systems. We also observed that the rotational motion of these clusters, especially those consisting of 6 or more entities, becomes negligible due to conservation laws. Quantum corrections for rotational motion are also found to be insignificant for larger clusters. Our results imply that the utilization of classical-based Molecular Dynamics models can effectively facilitate the exploration of the energy landscape of these systems, thereby providing valuable insights into the thermodynamic properties and other characteristics of the clusters. Such insights include pair radial distribution functions, bond angles, and the distribution of cluster masses. Our research also estimates the influence of quantum behavior on the rotation speeds of these clusters, revealing the potential for sizable discrepancies between quantum and classical predictions for smaller clusters. These discrepancies are found to be most pronounced for small clusters consisting of 5 or 6 entities, with rotations speeds that could differ by as much as 2.4 kilometers per second. Conversely, we expect our results to be valid for other clustered systems, such as those comprising ammonia, ammonium hydroxide, ammonia water, hydrogen fluoride, hydrogen chloride, hydrogen, oxygen, sulfuric acid, and carbon dioxide. It is also anticipated that the influence of zero-point motion will be more pronounced in clusters exhibiting highly stretched shapes and involving the sharing of electron pairs, thereby displaying increased sensitivity to quantum vibrations. We observe that this effect is triggered by an unusual correlation between toroidal momentum and heat, which is caused by quasiparticle Hall measurements misleadingly suggesting a connection with the local energy density. Furthermore, the Thermal Hall effect contradicts the conventional correlations seen in charge or spin Hall phenomena. Additionally, we find that the Einstein relations do not apply in systems displaying toroidal momentum, even when quasiparticle Hall measurements are involved. We derive analytical equations to calculate the thermal conductivity using local and non-local correlations. Our findings are supported through numerical simulations based on the Kondo lattice model. We also explore the possibility of directly detecting the toroidal momentum by circumventing the associated measurement inaccuracies that lead to a false connection with energy density. It is hypothesized that an accurate detection of toroidal momentum will reveal an Einstein relation consistent with conventional physics. It is hypothesized that the Hall measurements are merely reflecting the system's inherent non-local nature, particularly in regards to toroidal momentum. During training, neural networks naturally develop simple architectures characterized by sparse representations, limited information flow and restricted control flow. The geometric complexity of their structure contributes to these properties by enforcing various constraints. For example, the interconnection pattern between neurons constitutes a graph that must be navigated during information flow, and the sequence in which neurons are visited determines the local computation order. Our work systematizes the diversity of these geometric constraints within different neural network architectures and investigates how they impose distinct regularization effects on the networks. We find that incorporating external regularizers often fails to match the quality of the inherent regularization effects, and these built-in restrictions also facilitate the discovery of meaningful representations within the networks. We demonstrate that geometric complexity is a significant factor in the regularization of neural networks, and our work identifies new possibilities for controlling the complexity of neural networks through the design of their architecture. By allowing the parameterization of geometric intricacy, our research enables the exploration of a vast array of relevant regularization effects, and ultimately, leads to the discovery of novel neural network designs that excel in learning simple and generalizable concepts. Our work also includes a vast collection of geometrically parameterized models for neural networks, known as the Geometric Neural Network space (GNNspace), and an interactive tool for navigating this vast collection based on the desired regularization effects of distinct neural network architectures. The automated composition tool, Omnimus, employs a deep neural network to assess musical compositions by measuring their coherence with the input melody. Omnimus relies on a Melodic Embedding Matrix that encodes melodic data but suffers from overfitting and limited generalizability. To improve its performance, we investigate data augmentation methods to enhance the stability of Omnimus. Specifically, we test three techniques - frame shifting, pitch shifting, and speed changes - to optimize the MeEM and improve the accuracy of the composition evaluation. Our results indicate that pitch shifting yields the greatest benefit, increasing the average accuracy of Omnimus by 15.46% compared to the baseline. Furthermore, we integrate Omnimus with the Transformer framework, incorporating attention mechanisms to regulate the flow of musical information, thereby augmenting the coherence measured by the attention weights. However, this substitution does not surpass the performance of the original model. To overcome this limitation, we explore the utilization of multi-head attention to enable the isolation of non-local dependencies in the melody, thereby enhancing the coherence measured by the attention weights. This modification yields a 4.71% boost in accuracy for the composition evaluation. To verify the efficacy of these data augmentation methods, we conduct a statistical analysis using the Wilcoxon signed-range test and discover that Omnimus' performance using pitch shifting outperforms prior research in composition evaluation while also facilitating the integration of the Transformer framework. Ultimately, the incorporation of data augmentation via pitch shifting, as well as the strategic selection of model parameters, empowers the deep neural network to surpass the performance of more complex, Transformer-based models. To validate these findings, the data augmentation methods and deep neural network designs are made publicly available on GitHub. This public repository enables researchers to replicate our data augmentation techniques and explore their applications in musical analysis and composition. Additionally, an interactive demo is available on Colab that allows users to input melodies and observe the resulting compositions using the augmented Omnimus model. This demo includes a range of data augmentation options, including frame shifting, pitch shifting, and speed changes, which can be combined in various configurations to examine their effects on the input melody. We anticipate that these data augmentation methods will contribute to the development of more robust and flexible musical analysis and composition tools. To expand the applicability of these methods, we investigate their application to other musical domains, notably chord progressions, while also exploring their application to non-sequential input data using the Transformer framework's multi-head attention mechanism. This analysis sheds light on the efficacy of data augmentation

Assuming a symmetric information environment allows the model to be solved as a Markov chain, which reveals that the optimal prospects have a specific spectral distribution and depend on the common distribution of individual abilities. The symmetry of wavefunctions under parity for particles of arbitrary spin is examined, leading to the determination of allowed combinations according to spin and parity, which in turn dictates the allowed combinations for the total angular momentum of particles. By correlating the combinations to statistics, we demonstrate how parity plays a crucial role in linking spin and statistics. This approach yields results consistent with Pauli's theorem for half-integer spin particles and deviates only for bosonic particles of integer spin greater than or equal to two. We further apply this method to investigate a particle exhibiting an equal mixture of spin one and spin zero characteristics, denoted as a "par Bose," as well as a particle that is neither a boson nor a fermion, denoted as a "bosfermion." Finally, we apply the formalism to the n-pion system, for which we determine the possible wavefunctions and identify the par Bose particle as pion. By examining the U(3) symmetry of the parity-conserving pion sector, we demonstrate how Pauli's theorem is inherently satisfied. This analysis reveals that any particle can be a boson if it has zero orbital angular momentum or if its orbital and spin angular momenta exhibit opposite polarization. Additionally, we show that any particle can be a fermion if its orbital and spin components are fully coupled and exhibit the same polarization. Ultimately, this linkage based on parity serves as the fundamental grounds for deriving the spin-statistics connection. Furthermore, we distinguish between two types of particle polarization: intrinsic polarization, which arises naturally, and facilitated polarization, which can be influenced externally. Consequently, we show that purely intrinsic polarization is a prerequisite for the derivation of the spin-statistics linkage. This study offers a new perspective on the origins of the spin-statistics connection, providing a basis for further investigation. Additionally, we examine the implications of Bell's inequalities on many-body systems, particularly focusing on the three-pion system as an illustrative example. Finally, we speculate on novel many-body phenomena that could arise from polarization effects. Lastly, we conclude by highlighting unconventional properties that can arise in systems where the ground state and first excited state exhibit opposite parity, a phenomenon that has no analog in single-particle systems. These properties are inherently connected to the inherent characteristics of bosonization. Moreover, we demonstrate that relativistic charge screening in the pion system owes its origins to bosonization. This work provides a novel framework for evaluating the robustness of solvers, particularly in the context of network communications. This treebank has undergone extensive evaluation and comparison with existing NLP systems. This project is poised to become a long-term initiative, with plans for expanding the treebank through incorporation of annotated data from various sources, including the Web, to create a comprehensive picture of UD Hebrew. A major challenge in clinical research lies in developing accurate models of disease progression, particularly when working with limited and unreliable patient data. This issue is compounded by the inherent variability in human health. Proficient medical doctors, who have spent years training and have extensive experience working with patients, are able to produce realistic outcomes for individual patients despite facing similar diagnostic challenges. To bridge this gap between medical expertise and complex data analysis, we establish a framework that enables the learning of accurate disease models by viewing treatment as a collaborative effort between multiple patients whose progress has been closely monitored. We utilize non-parametric Bayesian statistics to develop a speculative framework that mirrors the decision-making processes of experienced doctors. This approach results in a data-informed model that produces posterior predictive distributions for patient outcomes with minimal assumptions. Our model's performance in harnessing collaborative knowledge outperforms traditional statistical methods in both synthetic data experiments and a real-world study of HIV dynamics following antiretroviral therapy. This innovative technique not only enhances our understanding of collaborative dynamics but also increases the efficiency of patient monitoring, resulting in a more realistic and informative experience. Our software tools are completely translationally independent, allowing them to be used in conjunction with existing clinical monitoring systems. Our work lays the foundation for incorporating collaborative knowledge into disease modeling, ultimately informing treatment decisions. We envision a future where our software tools can optimize patient care at both an individual and a collective level. Our data-driven models are grounded in speculative collaborative ethics, as they merely reflect and interpret the outcomes of physician-patient cooperation. Our models do not control or dictate treatment; instead, they facilitate communication between doctors and their patients by providing essential context. Our models are therefore compatible with existing clinical monitoring systems and can be used by doctors and patients to better understand and navigate the dynamics of patient care. Our software tools are translationally independent, enabling us to replicate our findings in a range of applications, as demonstrated by our HIV case study. A novel coding technique utilizing Low-density Parity-check (LDPC) codes is proposed by integrating degree-degree connections into existing architectures. By systematically incorporating degree-degree connections, existing LDPC designs can benefit from enhanced performance. To maximize potential, degree-degree connections are strategically placed within the matrix structure, particularly at the edges of submatrices, where they contribute to a more compact and efficient storage format. Various density patterns, including square and rectangular formats, are examined and analyzed, resulting in the integration of degree-degree connections into LDPC codes. To verify the efficacy of this new approach, simulations were conducted using the Bernoulli Binary Erasure Channel and Binary Erasure Channel models. The data collected demonstrated that LDPC codes with degree-degree connections achieve better error-resistance and higher throughput rates compared to conventional LDPC codes. Specifically, these connections enabled the development of shorter-length LDPC codes with higher minimum Hamming distance, resulting in enhanced system performance and efficiency. Furthermore, degree-degree connections facilitated the creation of storage-friendly LDPC codes with the capability to store multiple parity check equations within a single node, resulting in a reduction in storage requirements and complexity. Examples of density patterns, along with their computational tools, are provided to assist readers in creating their own LDPC codes with degree-degree connections. The potential applications of this new coding technique are vast, encompassing areas such as satellite communications, deep space exploration, and data transmission, where LDPC codes have been successfully utilized for decades. Ultimately, the integration of degree-degree connections represents a groundbreaking advancement in the field of LDPC codes, enabling the development of more resilient and efficient codes that can outperform conventional LDPC codes in various channels and applications. The data presented in this paper is the first public knowledge on this topic and can be freely utilized by researchers and engineers to further enhance the performance of LDPC codes. A critical vulnerability in the decoy state quantum key distribution (QKD) system enables eavesdroppers to uncover partial information about signal states while launching full-scale attacks on the decoy states. Our proposed method involves randomizing the phases of signal states instead of their entire states, thereby limiting the eavesdropper's knowledge. The probability distribution of signal states, assumed to be coherent states with phase randomization, resembles the probability distribution of weak coherent states. The potential advantages of our method stem from the distinct non-Gaussian characteristics and more even probability distributions of the signal states, which could mitigate hacking attacks more effectively. Conversely, this method may exhibit decreased efficiency due to the increased variance of signal states, thereby requiring a more complex implementation to achieve the same level of security as the original QKD system. Our theoretical analyses, accompanied by experimental results, demonstrate that the phase randomization of signal states offers enhanced security against most common hacking attacks and is capable of generating secure keys at a faster rate than the existing QKD systems. Additionally, the proposed method can be further improved through the implementation of phase uncertainty to achieve even distribution and maximize key generation, thereby outperforming the original QKD systems in terms of efficiency. Recent research has demonstrated the effectiveness of leveraging large-language models through an approach called in-context learning, eliminating the need for extensive fine-tuning. However, the impact of varying training datasets on this method has not been thoroughly investigated. Our study examines how different foundational datasets influence in-context learning performance using a 13B-parameter language model and evaluates a wide range of diverse text datasets. Our analysis shows that utilizing relevant domain knowledge significantly enhances performance, but unexpectedly, incorporating unrelated data sometimes yields better results, potentially due to the diversity of tasks within such datasets introducing beneficial variability. Our code and dataset selection findings are publicly available. We also propose a statistical examination of a large language model's self-consistency that could guide future dataset creation to better exploit the potential of in-context learning. Our research presents a new perspective on dataset influence and offers new insights on building training datasets for maximal in-context learning effectiveness. We identify specific labeling strategies and text types that hinder or facilitate learning in-context and uncover a crucial challenge: ensuring data examples are sufficiently distinct to avoid semantic overlap. Our study compares various data examples and highlights models' capacity for learning diverse contexts (combination of text). Our research sheds light on enhancing language models by selecting training data that exposes the model to a broad range of context and promotes learning through repeated exposure to varied text across multiple tasks, as opposed to learning through associated knowledge. Our study delves into the theoretical underpinnings of dataset influence and the potential of in-context learning, and we plan to further explore these concepts in the future. Using three-dimensional numerical simulations, we investigated how wind from a central active galactic nucleus affects gas in a large galaxy cluster, focusing on cloud formation and destruction. We compared the impact of several physical processes: radiative cooling, magnetic fields, and thermal energy transfer between clouds. Initially, gas clouds form through cooling, but are soon disrupted by internal instability and external shocks. We found that for higher levels of magnetic field strength, clouds last longer and are more compact, while increased thermal energy transfer leads to more durable clouds. In one specific scenario, high-density clouds survived for 20-40 million years, but without magnetic field influence, they lasted only 1-6 million years. Our findings are consistent with observations of galaxy clusters, where such features are rarely seen. We suggest that a combination of these physical processes contributes to the diverse shapes and sizes of the gas distribution in galaxy clusters. Ultimately, this influences the efficiency of the intracluster medium in forming stars. If magnetic fields are present, a significant amount of gas may remain unreactive and uncollided, leading to lower rates of star formation. Conversely, whenotropic transport is dominant, more gas is involved in star formation, leading to higher rates. By considering all these processes, we can reconcile simulated and observed data, particularly regarding the amount of gas involved in star formation. Based on our results, we expect low levels of mass regulation and magnetic field activity below a certain threshold, above which they have a significant impact. This threshold aligns with the average magnetic field strength in our galaxy, suggesting that relativistic jets may only influence gas dynamics at distances comparable to their propagation speed. In the future, we intend to expand upon this research by incorporating galaxy jets that could further disrupt gas clouds and influence the overall process. Furthermore, we will re-run the simulations with an energy-based cooling function that may produce different results. With these enhancements, we aim to further understand the complex dynamics of galaxy clusters and the role of various physical processes. By combining our simulated findings with observed data, we can place constraints on the role of these processes and ultimately develop a more unified model of galaxy dynamics. In doing so, we can address the underlying questions of how galaxy clusters evolved and what roles different physical processes played in shaping their present-day structure. By examining mass regulation, magnetic field activity, and thermal energy transfer, we can reconstruct the timeline of galaxy cluster development and verify our assumptions about the role of these processes in shaping their overall structure. In the long run, we can use observed data to validate our simulated results

Beautiful and elegant theories, such as QCD and general relativity, are those that remain unchanged under CP, whereas more complex theories, like the strong CP theory, allow for CP transgression. This transgression gives rise to anomalous terms, as seen in the theta-term in QCD and the Einstein-Hilbert term in general relativity, which can be related to a Lagrangian multiplier. By imposing CP as an exact symmetry, we can determine if a theory is consistent, and any deviation from this condition would result in CP transgression. Based on this understanding, we examine the possibility of strong CP nonconservation arising from quantum gravity and find it to be unlikely. However, we do identify one potential exception - the case of fractal space-time. Furthermore, we propose an alternative method for determining CP transgression through the use of Taylor expansions in the Lagrangian parameter. This approach allows us to identify transgressive anomalies and establish relationships between different anomalous terms. Specifically, we demonstrate how theta-term and epsilon-term anomalies are interconnected. Lastly, we explore the possibility of strong CP nonconservation arising from matter field interactions and find that this interaction also gives rise to CP transgression. To address this uncertainty, we suggest that researchers focus their efforts on investigating the source of strong CP nonconservation, rather than the strong CP nonconservation itself. The success of future 5G networks depends on their ability to adapt to changing user demands and environmental conditions, which requires a more resilient and autonomous network management system. To achieve this, next-generation cellular networks need to transition from traditional management systems based on centralized decision-making. This article takes a step towards realizing such a system by detailing the key processes involved in core network administration, such as resource allocation and fault management, which could be implemented through a distributed computing method like cloud-fog computing. This approach not only enables 5G networks to dynamically adjust to varying service requirements but also promotes energy efficiency and environmental sustainability by minimizing energy consumption in network infrastructure. To further optimize this strategy, a multi-objective optimization algorithm is proposed to balance the trade-offs between energy efficiency, packet loss, and QoS constraints. The simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in achieving sustainable and autonomous 5G networks that can adapt to various user applications and network devices while ensuring optimal energy consumption. The outcomes of this research can be utilized by network operators to make informed decisions about 5G network design and can be integrated into future standardization discussions. The source code for the simulation experiments is available online at a public repository. This research can be further extended by exploring additional sustainability aspects in 5G networks, such as green energy integration and vehicle-to-everything communications. Additionally, the underlying concepts can be applied to other technical areas, such as software-defined networking and network function virtualization. To achieve a fully autonomous 5G network, future work can involve developing more advanced distributed algorithms for core network administration and exploring new distributed architectures, such as blockchain-based 5G networks. Finally, the effectiveness of this research can be validated through a practical implementation of autonomous 5G networks in real-world environments. To facilitate this, the source code for the demonstration is also publicly available. The study also identifies potential challenges and areas of investigation for the implementation of autonomous 5G networks, particularly in cases where some network functions may need to be implemented through hardware components. In such scenarios, the efficiency of the distributed management system could be impacted by the efficiency of the hardware. Therefore, future work can involve developing more efficient hardware components that can effectively support the distributed management of 5G networks. To achieve this, the source code for the implementation can be utilized to conduct simulations under different hardware scenarios. Additionally, the study can be extended by exploring other promising hardware technologies, such as non-terahertz radios, and investigating their potential to improve the efficiency of 5G networks.

The fundamental units of speech, speech sounds, are learned and distinguished without reference to written language, relying solely on auditory information. However, the most widely employed method for building speech synthesis systems involves using written spelling units. This study explores the possibility of developing a speech synthesis system based on auditory units, treating audio data as the primary source of information. First, the essential units of speech are identified through an analysis of speech that is free from external influence, and their boundaries are mapped out. This analysis is used to create a set of pre-recorded, short speech samples, which are the building blocks of a novel speech synthesis system. Furthermore, the system's voice is shaped by analyzing recorded human speech to establish relationships between the identified acoustic units and their corresponding auditory counterparts. This study presents a new approach to speech synthesis that doesn't require any additional information and achieves results comparable to those of systems that are influenced by written language. Importantly, the developed system's speech sounds are consistent with those of skilled human linguists, demonstrating the feasibility of developing highly natural speech synthesis systems without requiring extensive training data. This work draws on principles from linguistics, including the examination of speech patterns at both the overall sentence level and the individual sound level, and develops a range of innovative techniques to analyze and work with acoustic units. Ultimately, the developed system is blind evaluated and found to outperform speech synthesis systems based on written language units and systems that are trained on large datasets. This research demonstrates the possibility and effectiveness of developing speech synthesis systems that are influenced solely by auditory information and are therefore better equipped to capture the inherent sounds and patterns of speech. These findings have the potential to influence our understanding of speech patterns and to develop more natural speech synthesis systems. Optimization linked with motion planning techniques can be cumbersome due to the absence of an efficient formulation for paired decision variables. A novel multi-stage convex optimization framework, Ground-Truth Linked Convex Optimization, is proposed to overcome this challenge by creating a sequential plan consisting of ground truth-based linked optimization steps, ground truth-based sampling, and iterative paired variable matching. The proposed algorithm incorporates data-driven McCormick envelope relaxations to streamline the sampling process and a linked optimization formulation for paired variables. The GLCO framework is applied to solve a critical motion planning issue in autonomous driving. By leveraging a paired sensor data set, the optimization model ensures that the sensor plan is coordinated with the communication schedule, enabling the rapid deployment of connected automated vehicles. The implementation of the GLCO framework yields a substantial reduction in computational time of over four orders of magnitude when compared to alternative optimization methods. Moreover, the final optimized plans exhibit exceptional communication reserve capabilities, underscoring the significance of this research for autonomous vehicles. The proposed approaches can be extended to various other optimization linked with motion planning problems due to their broad applicability. As a result, the proposed techniques have vast potential for real-world implementation. Moreover, the method can be advanced by utilizing AI for obtaining paired sensor plan data through inverse planning. Our analysis indicates that these constraints are more stringent than previously thought, surpassing the limitations set by the quantum discord. In particular, we demonstrate that the total number of successful transformations is limited by twice the discord, rather than the discord itself. We also extend these results to the measurement process in the presence of noise, and find that the resulting entropy constraints align with our findings. In addition, we identify a specific scenario in which the discord is non-zero, yet no discord or error can be extracted from one state compared to another. Our study provides a thorough understanding of the boundaries of quantum state manipulation through probabilistic methods. Furthermore, we identify an important aspect to consider when applying the quantum discord metric, namely the amount of noise that can be eliminated. Our analysis also sheds light on the distinct characteristics of quantum discord that leads to successful transformations and noise reduction. In relation to resource theory, our results reveal that discord is not a sufficient condition for resource efficiency, but rather a necessary condition. Our study provides a deeper understanding of the interplay between entropy and discord, and highlights the potential of this analysis in the context of resource theory. Finally, we examine the relation between our findings and previous work linking discord to thermodynamic resources, and demonstrate that our results encompass and surpass the bounds of discord as a thermodynamic resource. In particular, we show that the total number of successful transformations is limited by twice the thermodynamic resource, rather than the resource itself. Our study provides a comprehensive understanding of the discord-entropy relationship, and highlights the potential of analytical techniques in the context of resource theory. Furthermore, we investigate whether our results can be generalized to the study of transformations involving multiple systems, and find that the total number of successful transformations in such scenarios is limited by twice the total discord, rather than the sum of the individual discords. In particular, we show that our results in the single-system context can be directly applied to multi-component systems, and that the total discord provides a stronger boundary than the sum of individual discords. In decentralized machine learning, multiple devices collaborate by sharing averaged gradient information via multiple communication rounds. However, this model has a significant limitation: it doesn't adequately handle local data distribution changes, which can cause slower convergence or even divergence. To address this issue, we develop a new method, distributionally resilient Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent, or DR-DSGD, which is capable of handling varying data distributions among devices. Our model relies on a communication-efficient sharing of local gradient estimates through multiple distributed networks. By leveraging a new performance bound that considers distributional differences, DR-DSGD achieves faster per communication round convergence. Furthermore, we tested DR-DSGD in image classification tasks using PyTorch and real-world datasets, and the results demonstrate its superior performance when dealing with data distribution changes. DR-DSGD outperforms traditional Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent by at least 30% in various scenarios. Moreover, DR-DSGD converges significantly faster, up to 2.5 times, when there are no data distribution changes. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/mimobott/drsgd. DR-DSGD is an open-source decentralized machine learning algorithm that is now part of PyTorch, with an issue ticket already filed (https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/76846). Powered by Public Autonomous AI, a large-scale AI experiment platform, we conducted a total of 145,200 GPU hours to develop and test DR--DSGD. This massive effort enabled us to extensively evaluate DR-DSGD's performance across various scenarios and data distribution changes. In summary, DR-DSGD is a robust, distributionally resilient decentralized machine learning algorithm that can effectively handle local data distribution changes and demonstrate superior performance. Our research focuses on how a high-speed jet interacts with a less dense cloud, particularly its lower-speed boundaries, and whether this high-speed jet can explain the entire movement of a protostellar envelope. Our high-resolution models, extending up to 10,000 years into the future, reveal two distinct types of movement: a high-speed jet that travels straight and a slower-moving layer around it. However, our findings contradict the idea that a high-speed jet alone can explain the entire movement of a protostellar envelope. Instead, we suggest that another movement mechanism, such as magnetic forces, is required to explain a protostellar envelope's movement that continues even after a high-speed jet has turned off. This research focuses on developing efficient equilibrium strategies for nonlinear systems with constraints. Current approaches, such as dynamic ORC schemes, often fall short due to their inability to address the following limitations: 1) they predominantly focus on the optimization of output power, 2) they assume knowledge of the system's parameters, 3) they typically use linear approximation models, and 4) they usually operate within systems' safe operating ranges. In an effort to address these shortcomings, this study proposes two novel methods: the Equilibrated ORC (E-ORC) and the parameter-adaptive E-ORC (aE-ORC) strategies, designed to maximize output power in nonlinear systems with restrictions using nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC). NMPC continuously adjusts the system's operating points to achieve an equilibrium between efficiency and stability. E-ORC optimizes the system based on local nonlinear models, while aE-ORC adapts to changing system parameters and identifies critical points, all within nonlinear systems' safe operating ranges. These strategies are evaluated using simulated cases of linear and nonlinear systems with various parameters and operating ranges. An algorithmic limitation prevents the utilization of more complex nonlinear systems in this study. During object recognition, Category-level perception (CLP) occurs when a partial visual cue identifies an object's general function or category (e.g., car, chair), without recognizing a specific individual object or its 3D shape. CLP is crucial for robots and intelligent systems that interact with diverse everyday items. This study proposes an innovative framework for resilient CLP, aiming to recognize categories from partial visual cues in the presence of uncertainty or limited information. We introduce two main challenges: predicting a 3D object's pose and shape from limited cues, which we then use for category recognition. Initially, we define and release benchmark datasets for Category-level object recognition, including new instances and established datasets with categories. Our framework utilizes a neural network to predict a 3D object's pose and shape from semantic keypoints, even when some keypoints are missing or ambiguous. This pose and shape estimation enables resilient category recognition, which can be achieved through deterministic or probabilistic methods. Our experiments demonstrate robust category recognition from minimal cues, either 2D or 3D, and with varying levels of uncertainty. Our proposed framework and benchmarks provide a framework for resilient category-level perception and can be used to develop more robust and adaptable visual recognition systems. The Cauchy distribution, characterized by a singular probability density function, poses challenges in calculating its statistical measures, particularly the variance of the sample mean. This article discusses how a standard approach using the sample variance yields biased results and presents a modification to obtain an unbiased estimate of the variance. Furthermore, the article derives formulas for constructing confidence intervals around the mean of the Cauchy distribution based on sample data, also exploring the behavior of these intervals as the sample size increases. Additionally, the article examines the square of the mean as a location parameter and derives the distribution of this new parameter, followed by the calculation of its statistical measures, such as the variance and correlation coefficients. Ultimately, the article presents a comparison of the results for the original and new (squared) location parameters, highlighting their relationships and similarities. The results in this article do not require any specific assumptions about the Cauchy distribution, making them applicable to a broader range of distributions as well. The mathematical proofs of the results are based solely on basic concepts in probability theory. The article concludes by exploring some interesting properties of the Cauchy distribution. A new statistical approach is developed for estimating the required sample sizes in clinical trials that study multiple subgroups within a single trial design, in order to achieve the same level of evidence previously established through separate trials for individual subgroups. This approach uses Bayesian statistics to combine data from ongoing trials, thereby allowing researchers to assess the progress of subgroup analyses as they accumulate data. We implement this method in a simulation study to determine accurate sample size estimates for subgroup analyses. The results indicate that using historical data in conjunction with sequential Bayesian sample size estimation leads to increased efficiency by reducing the necessary sample size compared to solely relying on ongoing data. Additionally, the approach allows researchers to utilize information from other subgroups' trials, thereby minimizing the needed sample size. However, increasing the difference in event rates between the treatment and control groups leads to larger required sample sizes. The approach yields precise estimates for two-group comparisons but exhibits slight deviations for comparisons involving more treatment arms. The findings from this study are disseminated to clinicians, researchers, and statisticians through an educational resource. The proposed approach is also illustrated through an example involving a basket trial designed to investigate multiple subtypes of non-small cell lung cancer. The method's associated software and a user-friendly guide for applying the approach in practice are provided. The statistical method presented in this work has been approved under the U.S. Food and Drug Administration's (FDA) policies by facilitating the simultaneous conduct of basket trials for multiple subgroups. Linear Parameter Varying (LPV) loop shutting is introduced as a motion control strategy to enhance accuracy and adaptability. This control method involves adjusting a first-order low-pass filter's cutoff frequency in real-time based on sensor data, effectively incorporating time-varying parameters into the control loop. This parameterisation enables the use of advanced nonlinear control techniques, specifically those employing the LPV framework, to achieve precise motion control. This study examines the effects of varying LPV loop shutting parameters on motion control accuracy, specifically in the context of a high-precision Moving Beam Scanner at CERN. A linearised SISO model of the system is constructed and a scheduled LPV state-feedback controller designed, resulting in a system with superior tracking capabilities and increased robustness. Experimental findings confirm that the LPV-controlled system outperforms its constant-gain counterpart, demonstrating state tracking errors reduced by approximately 75%. This motion control approach exhibits a 95% reduction in peak tracking errors compared to nominal values, effectively increasing overall system precision. This innovation has the potential to enhance the Motion Control accuracy at CERN's Large Hadron Collider and similar environments.
