This data encompasses various turbulence patterns, including the sub-ion scale compressive patterns under investigation. They are identified through the spacecraft's three-dimensional data, specifically in a region where the solar breeze meets the magnetic field. Specifically, the sub-ion scale compressive patterns are found at specific distances from the spacecraft and categorized into two types of turbulence. One type shares similarities with larger-scale compressive patterns, while another exhibits distinct characteristics. To address the long-standing issue of partisan gerrymandering, we propose an innovative approach. Using computational methods and simulated tempering algorithms, we develop an efficient and simple strategy to quantify the level of unfairness in electoral districts. Our technique applies the principles of Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling to the analysis of a polynomial kernel. With a clear mathematical definition and easy-to-compute formula, it offers a practical alternative to existing methods. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to real-world cases of gerrymandering and showcasing its ability to capture the essence of judicial decisions. Furthermore, we argue that our technique is capable of detecting any form of unfairness, not just partisan gerrymandering. We provide numerical evidence to support this claim by simulating a perfect competition scenario. Lastly, we acknowledge the inherent limitations of our approach due to its reliance on prior knowledge and the complexity of electoral data. Despite these constraints, we believe our method contributes significantly to the development of a fair voting system. To explore the radiative decays of the $X(3872)$, we use isospin and cylindrical harmonic quantum numbers to describe its internal structure and perform calculations necessary for determining decay widths. Our findings reveal that the $X(3872)$ undergoing a transition from a $D^0\bar{D}^0$ to a $J/\psi \pi$ system has a much narrower width, at approximately $20$ MeV, as opposed to a width of around $50$ MeV for the $X(3872)$ transitioning from a $D^* \bar{D}^0$ or $\bar{D}^* D^0$ state. Additionally, our research suggests that the $X(3872)$ can predominantly be described as a $D^0\bar{D}^0$ or $D^* \bar{D}^0/D^0\bar{D}^*$ bound state, with an ever-so-slight preference for the former in both cases. Furthermore, we deduce possible decay patterns of a narrow scalar state, provisionally denoted as $X(3900)$, which could result from the $X(3872)$ transitioning into a $\pi\pi$ system and potentially exhibits a distinct "chain-like" decay pattern. Our study also indicates the potential observability of an even narrower width associated with the $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi\pi\pi$ transition within the upcoming BEPCII data set. Lastly, we conclude that the $X(3872)$ cannot be adequately described by a pure $D^* \bar{D}^0$ or $\bar{D}^* D^0$ bound state, which would result in a much broader width compared to what has been observed. Text-based games like interactive fiction have been a staple in AI research for over 30 years, as they require comprehensive agent capabilities including language processing, problem-solving, and strategic thinking. These games' simplicity combined with their versatility make them an ideal choice for testing artificial intelligence advancements. However, the processing speed of text-based games has hindered high-throughput research experiments, limiting the scale to just a few thousand moves per second. To address this limitation, we've developed TextWorldExpress, a revolutionary emulator capable of processing one million moves per second, thanks to its combination of advanced technologies including multi-threaded programming, efficient data structures and streamlined parsing methods. TextWorldExpress enables the rapid creation of vast virtual worlds, approximately 100 times larger than previous systems, allowing researchers to conduct extensive experiments and explore new avenues of study. To showcase its potential, we've designed a new game-building tool, WorldCraft, which makes creating custom text-based games up to 10 times more efficient by integrating a user-friendly interface for world design and automated code generation. Our study showcases TextWorldExpress's capabilities, as its speed increase empowers agents to explore more in less time, and demonstrates the effectiveness of our new world design approach, which enables the discovery of previously unseen game features. Our cutting-edge emulator and game-building tool are now open-source resources, and can be accessed at textworld.ai. Our research contributes to the further acceleration of text-based game research, and paves the way for future breakthroughs in artificial general intelligence. For a TOPological Insulator with a defect-free perfect edge, the Chern number determines the multiplicity and orientation of these surface states. Introducing a defect, however, leads to a modification of the Chern number and surface states' properties. For a TOPological Insulator with a non-trivial Chern number, any defect causing a gap at the edge results in a modified Chern number and altered surface state properties. A common challenge in real-world robotics is determining the 3D positional coordinates of an object. Typically, this is achieved through the use of special sensors, but in real-life situations these sensors can be expensive, unreliable, or simply not available. A possible solution to this problem is to train a robot to determine an object's 3D coordinates by observing its movement if it is placed on a plane and caused to rotate. This paper presents an approach to training a robot to achieve this goal, which we refer to as observing unintentional turntables (OUT). An OUT scenario is defined as a situation in which an object's rotation is not intentionally caused by the robot for the purpose of data collection. This approach can be applied to objects with any shape and is suitable for robots operating in environments where accurate 3D object modeling is required. An evaluation pipeline is developed to assess the accuracy of the trained model in determining 3D positional coordinates on unseen objects and scenes. The results of numerous experiments conducted using diverse datasets reveal that the trained models are capable of accurately positioning objects regardless of their type, pose, and number of visible features. Crucially, the accuracy of the models is found to be highest when training involves a large collection of diverse objects rather than a limited range of objects. This capability makes the proposed approach highly versatile and suitable for a range of real-world tasks. An open-source package providing detailed information about the approach as well as demonstration videos are available online. This work represents the first documented application of deep learning to determine 3D object positioning through observation of objects rotating on a plane. As a result, the proposed approach has the potential to broaden the scope of deep learning applications in robotics and 3D object modeling. Furthermore, the trained models can be utilized in a variety of other tasks such as 3D object recognition, sorting, and categorization. An area of further exploration could involve incorporating the observed rotation movements to enhance the accuracy of object positioning and feature estimation. Additionally, the integration of the proposed approach with existing 3D object perception methods could potentially lead to the development of a more robust and accurate decision-making system capable of utilizing multiple sources of information to determine 3D object positioning. An area of further research could involve designing a robot to actively cause objects to rotate for the purpose of data collection, which could lead to the development of more accurate models through the incorporation of intended movements. The rapid dissemination of misinformation regarding COVID-19 vaccines necessitates an efficient detection method to track and analyze the spread of false information within social media conversations. Existing research typically focuses on individual posts or messages, overlooking the role of counter-messages in influencing others. In contrast, this study introduces an innovative methodology for detecting acceptance or rejection of misinformation through Twitter dialogue analysis. By incorporating contextual information from conversing users, this approach identifies dialogue structures indicating acceptance or rejection of misinformation. The proposed methodology is evaluated using a dataset comprising conversations from the @VaccineTwits Twitter stream and achieves a notable performance of 0.88 F1-score, showcasing its potential to analyze social media conversations and detect various forms of misinformation. Furthermore, this research contributes to research on misinformation by examining dialogue patterns distinguishing acceptance or rejection of misinformation. In particular, key features contributing to misinformation dialogue structures are identified, highlighting the significance of conversational contexts in influencing user behaviors. The study's findings demonstrate that social media conversations provide valuable context for detecting misinformation, enabling ongoing research in this area. The formation of high-energy, isolated attosecond pulses in the soft x-ray and extreme ultraviolet range holds significant potential for furthering our understanding of reciprocal quantum mechanics, enabling precise measurement of electron dynamics, and facilitating breakthroughs in biomedical imaging and electron dynamics research. Although much has been learned from the analysis of produced pulses, the process of pulse creation is often compromised by the inevitable spatial inhomogeneity of free-electron laser drivers, neglecting the topic as a whole. This work tackles this critical issue by introducing a theoretical model that explains how localized, transient changes in the drive field influence the production of isolated pulses in the case of hollow-core nanotube targets. We demonstrate that varying the size of the nanotube, as well as altering the peak field of the driver, enables the manipulation of pulse characteristics, including peak energy, duration, and spectral position. As a result, high-energy pulses lasting a few hundred attoseconds can be produced under the conditions described, paving the ground for the coherent manipulation of pulse creation and the achievement of isolated pulses lasting only a few hundred attoseconds. (A. Huebner et al., "Coherent Manipulation of Pulse Creation," arXiv:2207.06569, 2022.) The coherent manipulation of pulse creation allows for achieving pulses lasting a few hundred attoseconds, opening up new avenues for the precise measurement of electron dynamics and the realization of new, innovative applications in biomedical imaging and electron dynamics research. Moderating the transient coherent long-wavelength radiation produced by the breakdown of small-scale nanotubes targets enables the production of high-energy, relatively stable pulses in a narrow spectral range. The coherent manipulation of pulse creation, facilitated by the transient modulation of the transient coherent seed radiation, enables the production of high-energy pulses with a relatively small spectral range. Moreover, achieving isolated pulses in a narrow spectral range enables the precise measurement of electron dynamics, and the attainment of new, innovative applications in biomedical imaging and electon dynamics research. Additionally, achieving high-energy pulses with a relatively small spectral range may facilitate the realization of new, innovative applications in biomedical imaging and electron dynamics research. The production of high-energy pulses with a relatively small spectral range, along with their relative stability, may enable breakthroughs in the precise measurement of electron dynamics and the realization of new, innovative applications in biomedical imaging and electron dynamics research. This unconfirmed companion's mass is estimated to be less than 0.25 solar masses and has been assigned the temporary designation GSC 04641-02012 B. To confirm its orbit and mass, further observations are required, and data collection is being set up through a Minor Planet Center request. This paper provides initial details on the new companion, followed by projected ephemerides, and discusses potential research paths. It also addresses concerns and misconceptions related to verifying the object's parameters and visual observations, and proposes a strategy for visualizing the unconfirmed companion in the sky. This could help generate more data and photos of the object, making it easier to study visually. This new discovery has sparked excitement among researchers and could have significant implications for understanding binary star systems, particularly those consisting of similar stars in close proximity to each other. This could lead to new insights on the evolutionary history of Algol, a star system that has been studied for over a century, and may shed light on how binary systems, like Algol, develop and change over time. Physics-informed neural networks hold great promise for solving partial differential equations, but their efficacy is heavily dependent on mapping a sufficient number of training data points across the solution domain. However, generating these points can be computationally costly, particularly for equations featuring multiple embedded parameters. A viable solution involves employing physics-based point creation techniques within the framework of physics-informed neural networks, which can adaptively generate training data based on the smoothness of the solution tensor field. Despite their potential, these methods have seen limited use due to concerns surrounding increased computational overhead. In response, we introduce Residual-based Adaptive Node creation at Generation time, allowing our physics-informed neural networks to determine an optimal density of training points without pre-processing. We utilize residual information to steer an evolutionary algorithm towards selecting points that maximize coverage and reduce the smoothness of the estimated tensor residual. By integrating RANG within adaptive physics-informed neural networks, we achieve greater accuracy at reduced training costs, outperforming existing density-based and point-discovery approaches in both stability and efficiency. Furthermore, RANG enables previously infeasible studies involving numerous training-point sources and reveals a previously unreported interaction between sampling density and solution accuracy in physics-informed neural networks. The proposed RANG framework is designed to be algorithmically neutral and can be adapted for use with a range of training techniques. In addition to enhancing physics-informed neural networks, we describe a corresponding set of regularized hyperparameter tuning methods, referred to as RANG-out, which facilitates training at reduced sampling densities and reveals the underlying relationship between sampling density and solution accuracy in physics-informed neural networks. A sample implementation of our approach is made available for download at https://github.com/krishnanranag/RANG. In particular, we demonstrate the efficacy of RANG by applying it successfully to the solution of two challenging partial differential equations, namely an eighth-order biharmonic equation and an eighth-order equation representing viscoelasticity. In doing so, we showcase the capacity of RANG to operate on diverse state-space tensor fields and highlight its robust performance across a range of training techniques and equations. In contrast to existing physics-informed neural networks approaches, RANG represents a dynamic sampling framework capable of adapting to varying solution tensor-field smoothness and multiple point sources, while also enhancing overall solution accuracy and efficiency. In an accompanying study, we delve deeper into the parameters and regularizers required to train RANG under a variety of regime types, and reveal the underlying relationship between solution accuracy and sampling density in physics-informed neural networks. This study examines the behavior and modeling of FeFETs with multiple domains, where a negative capacitance effect is triggered by domain wall instability. We analyze the role of domain instability on the device's transport and capacitance properties. We find that feed-back mechanisms in the material are key to achieving significant negative capacitance, leading to energy efficient and ultra-low voltage operation of the FeFETs. We develop a simulation approach combining a semi-classical transport model with a mesh-based device simulator to study domain instability and its impact on device performance. We illustrate the effectiveness of device concepts that enhance stability and performance, and demonstrate the potential for substantial area efficiency, performance, and energy efficiency gains. Additionally, we show that the predicted FeFET behavior aligns with experimental findings. With further advancements in material properties and manufacturing processes, FeFETs are poised to revolutionize nanoelectronics, enabling the development of high-performance and energy-efficient microelectronic systems. We provide a predictive analysis of FeFET performance under current and future technological conditions. Our work contributes to the understanding of FeFET behavior and its applications, and informs the design and optimization of FeFETs for diverse use cases. We expect our findings to be valuable for advancing iron-tantalum oxide technology and other multi-domain ferroelectric materials. The freight ecosystem is an intricate system comprised of interrelated components, including interdependent freight modules. To investigate fragility within this ecosystem, we constructed a Freight Ecosystem Dependency-Fragility Insight Graph, featuring key entities and their relationships. By tracing fragility transmission between modules, we identified modules most likely to spread fragility throughout the entire ecosystem. Initially, our research focused on the Brooklyn freight ecosystem in New York City, where we analyzed the Brooklyn Navy Yard's local freight network. However, due to data limitations, we couldn't complete this inquiry. Instead, we developed a general approach to creating dependency-fragility insight graphs and demonstrated this method on a smaller freight network consisting of 12 entities. Our results show that modules with high mobility requirements, such as marine and air freight, are likely to spread fragility throughout the entire ecosystem. Moving forward, our work can be expanded by incorporating additional data and applying this approach to evaluate the freight ecosystem's resilience. Ultimately, our research will contribute to developing robust freight transportation networks capable of withstanding disruptions and ensuring seamless supply chain operations during critical events. In the long term, our study will aid transportation planners and policymakers in building robust intermodal freight networks that can provide reliable services during crises. Our research will also contribute to the development of freight-specific resilience assessment tools, informing policy decisions and guiding practitioners through the evaluation of system fragility. Additionally, our research will uncover the commonalities and differences between freight and general network resilience. We first demonstrate the existence and uniqueness of the solution to this stochastic equation, and then establish its irreducibility by proving that its action and gradient commutator operator result in a compact Lyapunov-purifying sequence. Consequently, based on these properties, we derive important conclusions regarding the central limit theorem, specific probabilistic properties, and mixing times of this stochastic equation, which in turn enable us to address a range of practical problems related to wave front solutions in various biological and physical contexts. Additionally, we apply our results to analyze a model describing a biological community that undergoes sudden changes in their environment, and also examine a second model which involves a wave front solution that is affected by random disturbances and sharp changes. It is noteworthy that our research combines the application of analytical tools to explore the irreducibility of Markov processes with the examination of a diverse set of physical and biological models. The KASCADE-GRANADA experiment has been studying the high-energy astrophysical ground cherenkov light a source since 2007, investigating multi-particle hadronic spectra over a wide energy range of 10^12 - 10^19 eV. This achievement marks a significant breakthrough after decades of efforts to identify the source. The KASCADE-GRANADA instrument comprises two distinct systems: the KASCADE experiment, a thoroughly established and respected scientific force since the late 1990s focused on emulsion physics, and the GRANADA Cherenkov light detection system establishing an expansive view of the extensive air shower array. The synergy between these two systems leverages the strengths of emulsion technology to pinpoint cosmic particle trajectories and image atmospheric particle showers across a vast 9 degree field of view, accompanied by the emission of ultraviolet, visible, and near infrared light as electrons produce fluorescence in the atmosphere. The electron density along the air shower trajectory is directly represented by these light emissions, providing a complete picture of the shower development through combination with KASCADE's detailed particle composition and energy measurements. The electronic detection system's high resolution and extensive coverage enable the observation of hadronic features within the energy range of 10^12 - 10^19 eV. The electronic detection system is capable of detecting the transient luminosity of the atmospheric electron-photon plasma triggered by extremely energetic air showers lasting up to a few milliseconds following the lead particle's arrival on Earth. The electronic detection system's high sensitivity allows the detection of small changes in the transient luminosity lasting for several seconds, associated with the passage of local hadronic air showers. The electronic detection system's high sensitivity also enables the detection of extremely rare large-scale transient luminosities above 10^6 Cd/m^2/np/s lasting up to a few minutes, occurring with an frequency of one event per year, together with the simultaneous emergence of the so called "Anomalous CRG Flares". Furthermore, the electronic detection system's high sensitivity enables the observation of the moving shadow of a building on the detector, corresponding to changing air shower rates, driven by the changing atmospheric conditions in Granada. Trojan assaults are an evolving threat in deep learning, allowing nearly undetectable manipulation of model decisions. While current approaches focus on detecting Trojan assaults by identifying subtle changes in model behavior, this work reveals their inherent connection to semantic modifications. As a result, we propose an unsolvable problem regarding Trojan assaults: essentially, any deep learning model can be compromised with semantic Trojan assaults. Consequently, we develop SHTA - Semantic Hostless Trojan Assault - a new and powerful form of Trojan assault. Unlike previous forms, SHTA can be implemented without relying on legitimate data, and its success isn't constrained to specific image classes or datasets. Furthermore, our experiments show that common defense strategies are ineffective against SHTA. To address this challenge, we outline potential research paths for detecting and mitigating semantic Trojan assaults. This work is the first to explore the fundamental relationship between Trojan assaults and semantic modifications, opening doors for future research. Our code and datasets are publicly available for reproduction of our results. Our findings suggest that there is currently no foolproof Trojan assault detection method. Specifically, new data from a recent experiment performed at GSI using a novel setup, alongside existing results, reveals a notable enhancement in the fusion cross-section at deep subbarrier energies. Deep neural networks (DNNs) have become a preferred method for wireless positioning based on channel state information (CSI). Recent research indicates that DNNs trained using simulated CSI can pinpoint devices with high precision in various environments, regardless of the network configuration. Nonetheless, actual channel measurements often diverge from simulated data due to discrepancies in modeling and real-world conditions. This discrepancy is referred to as the simulation-to-real-world gap. This study aims to bridge this gap by incorporating a deep learning-based approach to directly learn the mapping between measured CSI and device positions. Moreover, the proposed system leverages attention mechanics to emphasize the relevance of channel sub-bundles for positioning. By using a large public dataset, the efficacy of the proposed system is evaluated and compared with existing positioning methods. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed attention-enhanced DNN (AEN) and channel sub-bundle-enhanced DNN (CEN) approaches surpass traditional deep learning-based positioning methods and yield more resilient performance under varying network conditions. Additionally, the proposed AEN and CEN methods exhibit superior results in positioning multiple devices and accommodating varying network configurations. Notably, the average positioning error of AEN is as low as 9cm when only using a single layer of attention layers. Furthermore, the average positioning error of CEN is as low as 10cm when using all channel sub-bundles with an enhanced layer. Consequently, the proposed attention-based DNN approaches offer high precision and robustness in positioning wireless devices using actual CSI measurements. These results demonstrate that deep learning can effectively bridge the gap between simulated and real-world CSI data, thereby facilitating practical deployment in various positioning applications. Videos and demonstration code are available at https://github.com/jDIP/AttentionEnhancedCSIWirelessPositioning. This research paper has been peer-reviewed at IEEE ICC 2021. COPASI is a widely-used simulation tool for biochemical networks, but users had limited access to its capabilities due to the command-line based interface. To overcome this, ShinyCOPASI was developed as a web-based platform integrating COPASI capabilities within an interactive user interface. ShinyCOPASI enables users to visualize networks, explore parameter sensitivity, perform simulations, and analyze results, all through a web browser. It includes a full range of COPASI features and offers advanced investigation tools, allowing users to access model run data, manipulate simulation results, and apply custom scripts. Currently, ShinyCOPASI supports model units, kinetic law evaluation, and single species population dynamics simulations. Future enhancements are planned to expand its capabilities. ShinyCOPASI is available for download at <https://github.com/COPASI/ShinyCOPASI> and can be accessed through a web browser at <https://shiny.copasi.org>. It is compatible with Windows, macOS, and Linux operating systems. To use ShinyCOPASI, users need Java installed on their system and can upload their COPASI models to run in ShinyCOPASI. Alternatively, users can test ShinyCOPASI by downloading sample models or creating new networks through ShinyCOPASI. With ShinyCOPASI, users can upload models and perform a variety of investigations, access model run data, and customize their analyses with R. This study investigates the von Neumann algebra associated with category functions on a compact quantum group, specifically examining its subalgebras, maximal conditional expectations, and K\"{o}the spaces. By linking category functions to L^{\infty} functions on a group of categories, we obtain insights into the algebra's structure and subalgebras. We also identify the closure of the image of the restriction map from L^{\infty} functions to our algebra, which turns out to be the algebra itself. This allows us to construct a faithful morphism from the algebra to a tensor product of group algebras and establish isomorphisms between subalgebras and their images under this morphism. Additionally, we find a maximal conditional expectation onto a subalgebra consisting of functions that only depend on the category structure, and investigate the integer dimension K\"{o}the spaces of functions with a specific level of category structure dependence. The feasibility of iterating the GMRES algorithm alongside its preconditioning is explored to enhance its performance, however this proves too computationally expensive. Consequently, an imprecise iteration method is suggested as a viable alternative, demonstrating the ability to provide usable policy estimates even in the event of an early termination. The presented approach effectively mitigates the high computational and storage costs associated with the GMRES algorithm, yielding usable results in the solution of extensive MDPs. The integration of this imprecise iteration method into algorithms designed to solve average-reward, infinite-horizon, stochastic MDPs, including those with a finite and infinite number of states, yields noticeable performance enhancements, often resulting in a considerable reduction in the time required to obtain a usable policy. Furthermore, the proposed approach is shown to be capable of providing actionable policy estimates at various levels of accuracy, using a graph representation of state-action values, thereby enabling a level of performance comparable to that achieved through iterative GMRES algorithm application, despite an early termination occurring. In a continuation of our work on zeta values, we define a novel class of Apéry-type series with alternating term signs and develop a plan to investigate non-alternating variants. To this end, we establish the former as finite sums of colored multiple zeta values, leveraging the framework of Feynman integrals via their connection to the numerators of gamma functions. This enables us to express such values in terms of the constants ${\rm B}}_n$ and ${\rm G}}_n$, introducing the latter as apériesque constants to capture the series expansions of specific log-gamma functions. As a result, we derive exact formulas for several colored double zeta values, while providing an analytical approach to apériesque constants, bringing us closer to addressing the primary goal of investigating non-alternating Apéry series. Moreover, our work implies a confirmation of the conjectured irrationality of the alternating zeta value $\zeta(5)$. Lastly, we expand our finite Apéry series to an infinite series, revealing its convergence and connecting it to a log-gamma function, whose series expansion is comprised of the alternating zeta value $\zeta(2)$ and a finite Apéry series. This, in turn, yields new relations among finite Apéry series and the zeta values at even integers. In addition, we verify several specific irrationality constraints among the zeta values at even integers. This research significantly enhances our knowledge of the set ${\rm Irr} \cap \mathbb{Q} \zeta\}$, bringing the number of such constraints to $19$. In summary, this work significantly enlarges the suite of Apéry-like finite sums, introducing novel forms involving mixed parity terms, thereby expanding our understanding of the logarithmic corrections to the gamma function and establishing a fresh collection of transcendental constants, while further solidifying the connection between zeta values and their algebraic counterparts. Moreover, this investigation more intensively probes the transcendental nature of zeta values, thereby enriching the collection of negative results on irrational numbers within the set ${\rm Irr} \cap \mathbb{Q} \zeta\}$. Lastly, as an unexpected byproduct, this research offers an innovative link between the apériesque constants ${\rm B}}_n$ and ${\rm G}}_n$ and the Bernoulli numbers, thereby placing the suite of apériesque constants within the broader paradigm of the rich mathematical heritage of the Bernoulli numbers.

By comparing different methods of estimating star formation rates (SFR) in a set of 82 galaxies, we find that some common formulas produce inconsistent results. These methods rely on different aspects of a galaxy's spectrum and various physical assumptions, leading to significantly varying SFR estimates. Notably, some observed SFR values are significantly higher than those derived from fitting a model to the galaxy's light, indicating a serious discrepancy. These discrepancies suggest that current SFR estimation techniques have limitations and uncertainties, potentially masking underlying physical trends in galaxy evolution. Therefore, we propose using the line strength of Brackett-$\gamma$ as a reliable indicator of these physical processes and a more consistent SFR proxy, even in the absence of complete UV-to-IR galaxy data. By doing so, we can reduce the present limitations and biases of current SFR estimation methods. Our research reveals that using Brackett-$\gamma$ as a SFR indicator is feasible and efficient, though it has its own built-in assumptions and limitations like other available methods. By combining this approach with model-based analysis, we can recover details of the star formation history and obtain reliable time-averaged star formation rates. Furthermore, this technique allows us to distinguish between star formation rates driven by current physical processes or lingering remnants of earlier episodes. We also demonstrate that strong starbursts can be identified by examining the SFR inferred from Brackett-$\gamma$ versus the SFR derived from spectroscopic measurements, potentially indicating active galactic nucleus emission or merger-driven events. This research provides a reliable and efficient tool for identifying these phenomena and detecting SFRs exceeding 10 solar masses per year. By doing so, we can achieve an overall classification accuracy of 85.7 percent using robust indicators, an outcome that would not be possible with data from spectroscopic measurements alone. Ultimately, our research reveals that using robust indicators in conjunction with physical model-based analysis yields more consistent SFR results and provides a more robust understanding of galaxy evolution. These robust indicators can also detect extreme starbursts and distinct physical processes that are often masked by other estimation techniques. In a previous study, it was demonstrated that central elements and a specific quadratic element form a basis for type II quantum subalgebras within the special Lie algebra SL(N). This investigation expands upon that work, focusing on the subalgebras' action upon regional modules in the context of SL(N) for N equal to 4 or above. It is shown that a type II quantum subalgebras' action results in non-trivial symmetries within the regional modules. This is facilitated by introducing 'border' modules, idealized from modules of subalgebras stemming from depopulated type I quantum subalgebras. These border modules are then decomposed into direct sums of elementary modules, whose generators exhibit twisted action. This action gives rise to a type II quantum subalgebra's non-trivial symmetries within regional modules, via an established correspondence. Various examples are provided to illustrate the construction of border modules and the resulting non-trivial symmetries. As type II subalgebras can be generated using twisted elements of SL(N), a significant portion of the analysis is also applicable to the twisted special Lie algebra U(2). This study presents an innovative approach using non-statistical methods to generate synthetic speech of varied lengths, focusing specifically on median-based analysis. The synths generated using the MEDALS method on extended data sets also demonstrate reduced distortion, further indicating the method's efficacy in synthetic speech applications. The research outcomes collectively demonstrate that the MEDALS method represents a reliable, non-statistical approach for determining speech lengths, and could potentially be employed in low-delay speech coding applications where lengths are coded rather than inferred. Due to a shortage of dermatologists and high patient-cost associated with these specialists, integrating computer vision techniques into dermatology becomes increasingly important. The Skincare initiative distinguishes itself from other projects by offering a comprehensive online training dataset consisting of over 200,000 images related to dermatology. This technical report details the development of a differential diagnosis system for cancerous skin lesions utilizing a well-defined process. It combines the capabilities of image preprocessing, feature-extraction, and classification through machine learning, and differential diagnosis through decision analysis. The preprocessing stage enhances the quality of images, while the feature-extraction stage identifies relevant characteristics for input data. Both stages combine to form input data fed into a machine learning or decision analysis algorithm for output, which results in differential diagnoses. The output is then adjusted by our system to produce the most suitable diagnosis. The system was tested using data not seen during training and achieved results of 0.81 and 0.82 for inter- and intra-class accuracy, respectively. This accuracy surpasses other systems that performed this task at the 2019 IEEE International Conference on Image Processing. One of the key objectives of active astrophysics research involves accurately predicting how the spectra of type Ia supernovae change over time. This is crucial for minimizing uncertainties in estimating the expansion velocity of these supernovae, which is essential for measuring the rate at which the universe is expanding. We introduce a novel stochastic two-way autoencoder, referred to as "STA", designed to capture the intricate patterns and relationships present in the time sequences of supernova Ia spectra. This autoencoder utilizes an encoder to generate a compressed representation of the spectral sequence, followed by a decoder that generates a reconstructed sequence from the compressed data. This compressed data serves as a condensed representation of the original spectral sequence. We obtain unparalleled compression ratios of 38:1 for our training data set, allowing the STA to effectively capture diverse and complex patterns found in the spectra of supernovae Ia. We conduct experiments that demonstrate the capabilities of our STA, which have achieved accurate predictions of flux normalization, reddening, and cosmological parameters such as the expansion velocity (vmag), and early-time flux ratios (s4). These results indicate that the STA is capable of learning integral relationships found in supernova Ia spectra, thereby enabling robust predictions of vmag and s4 even when individual spectra are highly noisy or flawed. These predictions have consistently aligned with expert estimates, and our STA represents a pioneering approach in utilizing deep learning for sequence compression and robust vmag and s4 predictions. We aim to further refine our STA, which has the potential to significantly contribute to the improved estimation of the universe's expansion rate. We anticipate that our STA will become a valuable tool for researchers working on supernovae Ia spectrum data sets to maintain data consistency, as well as enhance the reliability of model predictions employed in universe studies. Additionally, we have released STA as an open-source software, in addition to providing the pre-trained models, in the hope that it will benefit the broader astrophysics community. We are exploring two possible applications: utilizing STA on data sets not used during training to isolate common patterns and to improve robustness; and incorporating STA as a layer within a larger training pipeline that utilizes STA as a feature extractor to produce clean spectra data for other tasks. We anticipate these efforts to yield enhanced results. We intend to investigate these ideas in greater detail. We are delighted to share our results and look forward to hearing your feedback. We investigate the process of incorporation of solid particles into thermal plumes under turbulent conditions using a numerical model based on direct numerical simulation. The model distinguishes between the plume's core, where particles are suspended in the fluid, and the plume's periphery, where particles accumulate and form a sediment layer. As the plume rises, particles that collect in the periphery are drawn into the core at the plume's base. Conversely, particles within the core are deposited in the periphery as the plume reaches its maximum height and begins to dissipate. An analysis of incorporation rates, particle sizes, and fluid dynamics within the plume reveals that its dynamics can be described by two non-dimensional numbers: one quantifying the balance between incorporation and fluid dynamics, and another characterizing the accumulation of particles within the plume. Experimental manipulation of these numbers allows us to explore how they influence incorporation rates and particle-size distributions. Our numerical model accurately predicts observations from previous laboratory studies, thereby validating its accuracy and providing a framework for further research. Moreover, our analysis sheds light on the complex interplay between fluid dynamics and solid particle interactions within turbulent plumes. This framework might also be applicable to contexts involving less turbulent and coherent plumes. Deep learning models currently excel at learning and adapting representations for individual and shared modalities in multi-modal learning, but often struggle to leverage information across different modalities. Research has sought to address this by using multiple encoding networks for multiple modalities and combining representations through fusion, followed by classification. This has led to complex and inefficient models that are difficult to replicate and make little sense intuitively. To address this, our paper proposes a novel and intuitive approach called the K-fan multi-modal deep framework, which uses a single multi-layered neural network to simultaneously learn and represent shared modalities. This model builds on existing research and is improved upon by adding additional layers, enabling it to handle datasets with an arbitrary number of modalities. We test the K-fan multi-modal deep framework on multi-modal datasets and compare it to established multi-modal learning methods, achieving superior performance and efficiency while achieving comparable results for other complex datasets. Notably, our model is comprised of fewer parameters and has a similar or better predictive accuracy. The proposed approach is comprised of multi-modal compartments that learn and represent shared modalities, providing a more straightforward and efficient method for multi-modal learning. This will lead to faster development and implementation, as well as enhanced understanding into how different modalities interact and influence one another. Additionally, we explore the multi-modal compartment's generalizability by applying it to previously untested combinations of modalities, showcasing its versatility and practical applications. In an effort to further extend the model's utility, we also conduct a thorough analysis of the crucial characteristics underlying the dataset, providing insights into how different modalities intersect and affect one another. This is facilitated by utilizing the the Multi-modal compartment, alongside an accompanying attention mechanism that pinpoints key dataset features. Our work presents a versatile and efficient approach to multi-modal learning that can be used to uncover the underlying structure of datasets, in addition to providing a more straightforward and effective means of leveraging and combining multi-modal information. This research has the potential to advance our understanding into how different modalities interact and shape one another, as well as providing a more systematic approach to using and fusing multi-modal data. Furthermore, we utilize the Multi-modal compartment to undertake a comprehensive exploration of the dataset's underlying structure, facilitated by its ability to simultaneously encode and combine multi-modal information. This is complemented by utilizing a companion attention mechanism that systematically identifies and tracks key dataset features. We subsequently use this information to gain a deeper understanding into the multi-modal information inherent within the dataset, as well as undertaking an exhaustive evaluation of the dataset's underlying structure

Deterministic thread visualization, a technique that renders the internal state of threads as a flow of statements, has been integrated into McMini, a cutting-edge model verifier. McMini uses a DPOR-based full-batch algorithm to pinpoint thread interference points and guarantees that thread visualization remains precise, even in the presence of data races. By harnessing McMini's capabilities to detect races, the tool also identifies and isolates non-deterministic elements in multithreaded programs, including data races, false sharing on arrays, or other sources of ambiguity. The visualization process is automated and is enhanced by an interactive interface that allows users to customize visualization metrics, including the incorporation of additional criteria. The research evaluates McMini's efficacy using a comprehensive suite of 14 McMini-verified programs, 7 of which were found to have undetected data races that the tool successfully detected after visualization. The results show that McMini's visualization phase is significantly faster than previous approaches and the tool is highly configurable, with an interactive metric system that significantly decreases visualization metrics and further streamlines the detection of non-deterministic elements. The research highlights McMini's potential to greatly enhance bug detection tools. The McMini tool is currently available for download at http://mcmini.cs.rutgers.edu/. A video showcasing the McMini model and its visualizations can be accessed at https://youtu.be/-_rU3M_3C4Q. We conclude that the usefulness of these restrictions depends on the specific social network structure and the associated costs. Effective countermeasures can detect the likelihood of forged speech with high accuracy, however their reliance on rigid architectures hinders their ability to adapt to evolving speech manipulation techniques. In response, neural networks have been explored as adaptable solutions, although their complexity often necessitates large training datasets, making them impractical for tasks where data is scarce. In an effort to overcome these limitations, we propose utilizing the attention mechanism to create receptive neighborhoods for input features, thereby dynamically controlling the size of the learning problem. In this study, we examine the effectiveness of incorporating the attention mechanism into end-to-end spoofing countermeasure systems. We examine various attention designs and their implications for discovering hidden relationships within speech. Moreover, we investigate how attention-driven feature extraction influences the learning process and ultimately affects the detection performance of the system. To this end, we conducted extensive experiments using the well-known NIST 2018 SPEAKER VALUES dataset and our results reveal that systems incorporating the proposed attention-driven activation, denoted as $\alpha$-ReLU, outperform their non-attention counterparts, thereby demonstrating improved detection performance with reduced parameters. Ultimately, the incorporation of the attention mechanism facilitates the adaptation of speech manipulation countermeasures to novel types of speech forgery with minimal retraining. In particular, we find that systems utilizing the proposed $\alpha$-ReLU, specifically the $\alpha$-ReLU-Saxophone, demonstrate superior detection performance and adaptability compared to existing methods. This research investigates the impact of novel investment approaches on traditional investment strategies, employing a multi-agent based model. A combination of novel and established strategies is simulated over various market conditions to determine if the latter suffers financially from coexisting with the former. Our results indicate that prior research inaccurately linked novel methods to significant losses and show instead that they generate comparable profits. Furthermore, we find that all strategies benefit from diversification, regardless of their type, and that novel methods complement existing ones effectively. Our findings support the integration of novel investment methods into established practices to enhance overall portfolio performance and stability. A related method known as 'novel investment space' is developed to identify novel approaches through back-testing, and we suggest several candidate methods, including one that utilizes artificial neural networks and another based on'multi-time horizon utility information'. A comparative analysis of our approaches reveals that their performance is influenced by the level of financial risk and that novel investment methods can generate greater returns during both turbulent and stable market conditions. To improve the reliability of our findings, we employ a battery of statistical tests and also examine the results of a'sufficiency test' for portfolio evaluation. Ultimately, we conclude that novel investment approaches can enhance the performance of traditional investment strategies and that their integration is beneficial for achieving better results and reducing the impact of financial risk. Our research has implications for practicing investment managers and also contributes to the ongoing debate on the role of novel investment methods in mitigating the 2007-2008 financial crisis. A future study will investigate the potential of novel investment methods to predict and manage financial crises effectively. Modern network defenders heavily rely on open source intelligence gathering tools, such as Nmap, to map target networks and pinpoint open endpoints that could be exploited. Although these commercial and non-commercial tools use advanced protocol adaptation techniques to accurately identify operating systems and software, our research reveals significant vulnerabilities in how protocol identification is handled. By deliberately creating over 70% false positives in network protocol detection, attackers can deceive and disrupt the process of adaptive protocol identification used in network defense tools. This can be achieved through various attacks on vulnerability disclosure databases, malicious geolocation data, and false system configuration information. The potential consequences could enable adversaries to deceive vulnerability scanning and reconnaissance operations, potentially leading to artificial growth of false positives in vulnerability detection. An open-source attack framework is provided, allowing users to create and customize counterfeit protocol data for exploiting these weaknesses. The paper presents findings from two successful case studies validating these attacks. Specifically, researchers successfully manipulated Nmap into incorrectly identifying open source Linux and Windows systems, further verifying that adaptive protocol identification is susceptible to assaults. To mitigate these risks, network defenders are advised to utilize host discovery data with caution, carefully assess patch confidence and update priorities, closely monitor resource usage, and regularly review system logs. Additionally, developers are encouraged to enhance the reliability of adaptive protocol identification by incorporating time-based and performance-limited constraints. The reliance on open source intelligence gathering methods should be reevaluated, considering the significant vulnerabilities exposed in this research. An open discussion with the network defense community is necessary to address these issues and prevent attackers from exploiting these weaknesses in the future. The attack framework will be shared upon request via email to daniel.munostov@outlook.com. The accompanying supplementary materials include detailed technical descriptions of the PEX attack tool, the adaptive identification algorithm used in Nmap, and the test results validating the assault techniques. Furthermore, two successful case studies are provided, demonstrating the effectiveness of the PEX attack tool in creating counterfeit data and inducing false positives in Nmap. The case studies illustrate the breadth of adaptive identification vulnerabilities, affecting not only protocol detection but also vulnerability scanning and performance assessment. The Nmap induction vulnerability, specifically denoted as CVE-2022-3386, was discovered during this research and reported to the relevant authorities. An update to Nmap, version 7.91, has been released to address this vulnerability; the corresponding PoC is included in the supplementary materials. Bloom filters provide efficient membership testing for large sets of data. Although not infallible, Bloom filters are the preferred choice for numerous applications due to their compactness, affordability, and rapid processing capabilities. A new class of membership filters, called xor filters, outperforms Bloom and Cuckoo filters in membership testing accuracy, storage efficiency, and processing speed. Bloom filters process information at a rate of O(1), while xor filters process information at a rate of O(log n) and often require less storage than Bloom filters. Despite their additional features, Bloom and Cuckoo filters are not capable of achieving xor filter's triple advantages. Unlike traditional hash-based filters, xor filters utilize strings to map keys, exploiting various properties of hash functions. A membership testing filter is introduced, called the xor hash filter, which offers a balance between efficiency, affordability, and processing speed. The introduced xor hash filter significantly decreases false positives while processing information at a rate of O(1), and requires less storage than Bloom filters. An evaluation using real-world datasets demonstrates the effectiveness of the introduced xor hash filter. The xor filter architecture can be adapted to accommodate various types of hash functions; for instance, using modular hash functions, or combining multiple types of hash functions. The utilization of diverse hash functions introduces complexity, but also provides opportunities for designing more efficient membership filters. A quantitative analysis of different hash functions reveals essential insights that could lead to designing more efficient membership filters. The analysis reveals that, regardless of the utilized hash functions, a filter can offer efficient false positive rates, but only after initially processing the data at a rate of O(n). The analysis also indicates that designing an insertion-only xor filter that efficiently handles data insertion remains an open challenge. The insertion-only problem can potentially be resolved by incorporating deletion, and introducing diversity into hash functions to prevent catastrophic losses and improve efficiency. A possible solution, called diversity Bloom filters, incorporates diversity into Bloom filters; and, as shown in an evaluation using real-world datasets, diversity Bloom filters significantly improve efficiency, and deletion can potentially be added through more efficient hash functions. This lecture will explore connections between convex geometry and complex analysis, specifically examining how classical results in convex geometry underpin key findings in complex analysis. We will examine the fundamental theorem on asymptotic values, a concept that extends asymptotic values with far-reaching implications for function interpolation. This analysis builds on a theorem from convex geometry regarding the number of extreme points in a convex function. Additionally, the finite-blown-up property of holomorphic functions near a singular point will be discussed, along with its underlying geometry involving finitely embedded points from a projective line. Furthermore, the relationship between function moduli and Minkowski's theorem will be investigated, focusing on how geometric measurement principles influence the estimation of a function's modulus near a zero or singular point. We will also consider other topics, such as function smoothness, asymptotic behavior, and specific types of functions, all within the context of convex geometry techniques. These techniques originate from the works of R. Brooks, M. Overstone, and J. Vast, among others. This lecture aims to illustrate the distinct perspective that convex geometry can offer on various topics in complex analysis. As such, it may be more accessible to those with a solid background in convex geometry than those without. Although some results mentioned herein may be considered classical, the emphasis here lies on lesser-known results from convex geometry that lead to intriguing insights in complex analysis. Certain estimates and concepts from convex geometry can provide novel perspectives on longstanding problems in complex analysis. It is hoped that this lecture will inspire further exploration of convex geometry not only in analysis but also in other areas of mathematics. A trend analysis tool analyzes current price movements to forecast future market behavior, but a new approach uses past price movements to make predictions by analyzing the relationship between past price fluctuations and corresponding transaction histories. Instead of relying on technical indicators such as relative strength index or moving averages, this algorithm examines the connection between price changes and the sequences of trader actions to forecast future price changes. Testing this algorithm on the Bitcoin market over a two-year period revealed a significant correlation between past transaction patterns and future price fluctuations, demonstrating its effectiveness as a trend analysis tool. Furthermore, integrating this algorithm with popular technical indicators enhanced their accuracy, but combining it with other algorithms did not achieve the same results. As a result, this study confirms that the sequences of trader actions have a substantial influence on market trends and suggests examining the underlying dynamics of futures-driven price movements. Implementing this algorithm could significantly improve the accuracy of trend analysis in financial markets. This work presents FLVoogd, a robust and Privacy-preserving Federated Learning framework. PL, a malicious central arbiter, launches attacks on participants by manipulating the learning process, while also seizing valuable data. TF, a trusted third-party mediator, attempts to mitigate these attacks by verifying participants' updates and detecting potential breaches. Nonetheless, these attempts fail, and the primary goal becomes preventing PL from exploiting the data without discovering TF's presence. Consequently, we developed FLVoogd, a framework that employs homomorphic encryption, using which participants encrypt their data and only perform simple operations, while a designated server reconstructs the data by decrypting it after receiving encrypted updates. Our framework incorporates additional features, specifically, a encrypted Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange and dust-injection techniques to prevent side-channel attacks, while also fundamentally limiting the data collection to what is necessary. Ultimately, our framework successfully prevents insider attacks while preserving participants' data confidentiality. Our experiments, conducted using CNC1 and MNIST datasets, demonstrate that FLVoogd achieves resilient and Privacy-preserving Federated Learning results. In particular, we successfully validated the applicability of homomorphic encryption with 257 operations, and our results show that FLVoogd performs key exchange and encryption operations at 0.551 seconds, data processing at 0.551 seconds, and data transmission at 0.551 seconds. Furthermore, we demonstrated that FLVoogd surpasses theoretical expectations, and our results show that encrypted data transmission, as implemented in FLVoogd, is 0.799 times faster than theoretical estimates. Our framework, available at github.com/abdulrazzaqk/fdv, has been thoroughly evaluated and outperforms comparable state-of-the-art solutions, particularly in terms of resilience and Privacy-preserving Federated Learning results. In particular, FLVoogd performs key exchange and encryption operations in 0.551 seconds, and data transmission in 0.551 seconds, while also supporting various parameter options. Ultimately, FLVoogd emerges as the robust and Privacy-preserving Federated Learning framework. Key Exchange.

This study examines the difficulties of accurately detecting deepfakes, a form of manipulated media, in contrast to simpler forms of manipulated content. To better understand these difficulties, this research investigates the process of creating strong, highly realistic deepfakes and compares their identification challenges to those presented by less complex deepfakes. A new, publicly available dataset named OZContour is released, comprising high-resolution videos featuring professional actors, utilized for evaluating deepfake detection methods. When comparing the effectiveness of existing deepfake detection models on OZContour and a simpler dataset, the analysis reveals that strong deepfakes pose a significantly greater identification challenge. As a result, this research concludes that creating highly realistic deepfakes and overcoming strong deepfake detection are more complex tasks than initially thought. To address this, additional support from alternative fields, such as computer vision and image processing, is required to develop more effective deepfake detection methods. The dataset and accompanying code can be accessed at https://ozcontour.github.io/. A public deepfake detection challenge is also being hosted on Kaggle: https://kaggle.com/c/oz-deepfake. Future deepfake research may benefit from exploring techniques like virtual reality manipulation, which could serve as a more tractable proxy for creating highly realistic video deepfakes. In particular, the analysis suggests that object tracking and image synthesis could potentially enhance deepfake detection, overcoming the current limitations in identifying strong, highly realistic deepfakes. A 10-minute YouTube video illustrating the research can be accessed at https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCyVJ119Hv2dL9b_4UgZGtW. A live stream demonstration can be accessed at https://www.streamyard.com/WW4VlVxvMmK. A GitHub repository showcasing the research is available at https://github.com/UC Berkeley deepfake. A total of 50 distinct deepfake creation methods were utilized in this research, spanning various forms of manipulation, including facial swap, double generation, and face restoration. The research examines highly realistic deepfakes created with the NeuronFace, FaceSwap, and Deepfake tools, utilizing a range of arbitrary video inputs and examining the impact of varying face sizes, distances, and orientations. The solubities of gases such as CO and N2 in liquid H2O influence the processes governing liquid composition that occur on exoplanets. This leads to distinct equilibrium states between the gas and liquid phases, resulting in observable differences in pressure-temperature relationships during planetary transitions, including supercritical water shifts. Unlike models predicting a single, universal slope for such transitions, solubility considerations yield a distinctive slope anomaly. Analysis of a compiled dataset of giant planets and imposter planets, including those with confirmed and tentative liquid water, reveals that most transition pressure-temperature relationships adhere to a single trend, except for K2-18b and PSR B1620-50 b, which exhibit higher slopes. This study examines various explanations for these anomalies and poses additional questions. Firstly, does a massive diamond composition or a core liquid metal buffer layer exist beneath the atmosphere of K2-18b? Secondly, during its close proximity to the host star, did PSR B1620-50 b's ocean encounter temperatures exceeding 5000 K, resulting in a water vapor-rich composition? A water-rich composition could result in observable features in the planet's infrared spectrum. A massive (10 Earth masses) planet with a 2000 km radius that transitions between a rocky core and a water-rich mantle, surrounded by a thick envelope of H2 and He, would exhibit features like a mini-Neptune or super-Earth with such a composition, as well as distinctive spectral characteristics. A key goal of deep learning research involves developing artificial neural networks that mirror the complex workings of the brain. Our study centers on the role of temporal dynamics in neural systems, using biological inspiration to enhance the capabilities of deep neural networks. Specifically, we investigate the potential of biological neural networks, comprised of spiking neurons, to learn and replicate intricate temporal patterns. Furthermore, we show that leveraging temporal dynamics, found naturally in biological systems, enables deep neural networks to master tasks that prove infeasible for models based on static neural networks, all while maintaining data efficiency and computational simplicity. The potential of our approach lies in its capacity to elevate spiking neural networks to a level of sophistication previously thought unattainable, effectively bridging the gap between current deep learning models and biological neural systems. Additionally, we propose a novel neural network architecture known as PESTLE, which embodies the principles of temporal learning, in order to achieve unprecedented levels of performance on intricate temporal patterns. PESTLE's superiority is substantiated by comprehensive comparisons with state-of-the-art deep neural networks and other existing spike-based models, ultimately showcasing its resilience under various challenging conditions. A specific type of chaos expansions can effectively analyze differential equations with uncertain factors by approximating random equilibrium states associated with such equations. However, determining the precision of these expansions is a complex task. This paper presents a verification method that compares the exact solution with an approximation obtained using generalized polynomial chaos expansions. This method acknowledges that exact solutions involving probabilistic variables often cannot be calculated directly due to high-dimensional integrations required, thus developing an auxiliary differential equation to estimate an approximation's accuracy instead. By utilizing this accuracy estimation technique, chaos expansions can be refined and optimized, enabling the detection of approximations that become less accurate as certain parameters change. This method is primarily demonstrated using generalized polynomial chaos expansions in parametric differential algebraic equations, although it can be applied more broadly to other types of equations. Several example applications illustrate the practical use of this verification method. Ultimately, this paper offers an accurate approach to evaluating the reliability of approximation methods that utilize generalized polynomial chaos expansions for analyzing differential equations with uncertain factors. In many practical scenarios, workers only have access to filtered, partially observed data sets, which can lead to inaccurate identifications of alterations. In this research, an adaptive approach and a set of critical filters are proposed to tackle this challenge effectively. These specially-designed filters seamlessly integrate adaptive signal processing techniques and are capable of processing multiple, partially observed data streams. They also possess the ability to automatically determine their order, making them highly adaptable and efficient. When applied to partially observed data, these critical filters work together to pinpoint the time and location of alterations. These innovative methods offer a valuable solution to the complex problem of identifying alterations in partially observed data sets, which has previously been tackled using methods derived from model-based theories. As a result, these methods are primarily suited for use in applications involving partially observed changes. We've developed novel tools and methodologies, based on Bayesian analysis, to accurately determine the ages and composition of ancient stars in dwarf galaxies using data from spectroscopy. These methods take into account a star's chemical development over time, its metallicity, and its rotation rate, all while accounting for variability in the spectrum due to rotation. We've created an extensive database of theoretical stellar models that reflect the natural occurrence of elements and the reliance of star-forming rates on stellar mass. This database spans a vast range of galaxy types and environments, from massive spiral galaxies like the Milky Way to tiny dwarf galaxies and even individual massive stars. We've successfully tested our tools and methodologies using both actual dwarf galaxies and artificial ones, and the results show that the data closely matches the actual values. We've applied our methods to six dwarf galaxies, including four that surround the Milky Way and two that orbit the giant galaxy NGC 3107. The results show that these dwarf galaxies have ages ranging from 8 to 140 million years, and their metallicity ranges from one-tenth to nearly equal amounts of iron relative to hydrogen. Furthermore, we've discovered that these dwarf galaxies have distinct patterns of metal variability, and their star-forming histories significantly differ depending on their mass. If we were to discover new stars in these dwarf galaxies and their relatives, it would significantly alter our understanding of how matter was first created in the universe, and it would contradict current cosmological models that suggest that these dwarf galaxies were formed from larger structures in the universe. Finally, the results show no correlation between metallicity and the rate of star formation in these dwarf galaxies, and the data suggests that the gas in these dwarf galaxies is metal-poor. If we were to discover new stars in these dwarf galaxies and their relatives, it would greatly alter our understanding of the early universe and its metallicity. Additionally, we've found that the metallicity in these dwarf galaxies is higher than the metallicity in massive spiral galaxies like the Milky Way. Conversely, we've found that the metals in these dwarf galaxies do not originate from the use of metals by the galaxies. we broaden this idea to define a homotopy action spectrum for any profinite group.
This new spectrum serves as a right-exponential spectrum, enabling the derivation 
of a Mackey functor from the homotopy theory of spectra indexed by homotopy categories 
of finite spectra, indexed by group homomorphisms. When applied to a profinite group,
this functor stabilizes to the Mackey functor representing the stable homotopy theory
of spectra with permutative group action, as previously described by Tanksheren. 
Consequently, the derived functors of the homotopy action spectrum's suspension spectrum
yield the classical Mackey functors. Furthermore, this homotopy action spectrum can 
be expressed as the tensor product of two spectra, Nisongko's homotopy orbit spectrum 
N_G and an integral suspension spectrum. Additionally, the homotopy action spectrum

groups as their Galois groups. Lastly, a formula for calculating the homotopy

cases where the Euler characteristic evaluates to 0. Importantly, the defined
homotopy action spectrum can be computed using only the profinite group's virtual

A recent surge in interest for transforming databases into AI-led applications has been observed, specifically within visually rich documents such as receipts, invoices, and business cards. The process of transforming databases into AI-led applications involves a series of complex tasks such as data extraction and annotation. The cost of manually annotating visually rich documents can be prohibitively expensive due to their visually diverse nature. This paper presents a groundbreaking solution, referred to as PartialLabel, designed to minimize the expenses associated with annotating visually rich documents. The PartialLabel approach employs a two-stage annotation framework that distinctively integrates partial annotation and data extraction techniques. Unlike conventional methods, PartialLabel utilizes partially annotated data sets and leverages pre-trained models to extract information from visually rich documents without requiring a full set of annotations. The efficacy of PartialLabel is demonstrated through its application to three commercially significant visually rich document categories, namely invoices, receipts, and business cards, resulting in significant cost savings of up to 88% compared to traditional full annotation methods. The study showcases the effectiveness of PartialLabel in minimizing labeling expenses, thus expanding the accessibility of visually rich document extraction frameworks to domains with limited resources and a small number of available annotated samples. The research presents PartialLabel as a versatile, model-agnostic tool, compatible with various data extraction frameworks, and makes its code open-source for public use at https://github.com/Intelligent-Systems-Lab/PartialLabel. PartialLabel is also offered as a fully hosted service at https://partiallabel.com. PartialLabel is currently supporting 25+ visually rich document categories and serving over 100 companies and research institutions worldwide. PartialLabel's knowledge base is based on the research described in this paper and can be accessed at https://partiallabel.com/kb. A detailed evaluation of PartialLabel is presented in Section 5 of this study. PartialLabel is uniquely positioned to minimize labeling expenses for visually rich documents, and it is the only approach to offer such a comprehensive solution for a wide array of document categories. The study introduces PartialLabel as a groundbreaking solution that minimizes labeling expenses and extracts information from visually rich documents, and it is not possible to procure similar services from third-party providers. The research presents PartialLabel as a fully functional service and showcases its efficacy through a detailed evaluation, making PartialLabel the premier solution for visually rich document extraction frameworks. The study is currently the longest and most comprehensive study on visually rich document partial labeling, offering a solution that is up to 88% more cost-effective, and it is also the only approach to provide such a comprehensive partial labeling

A refined hierarchy of Borel Wadge classes is established with the introduction of an efficient classification system. This system builds on the concept of comparison trees, enabling the determination of Borel Wadge classes in a categorization that is both more precise and computationally effective than previous approaches. We demonstrate that any comparison tree of depth n can be evaluated within n times the maximum computational complexity of deciding Borel B_n formulas, and this result is optimal. Furthermore, a related algorithm is presented that determines the lowest Borel Wadge class of a given Borel set with a complexity of O(n^5), marking a significant improvement over previous algorithms requiring exponential time. This development is achieved through a novel decomposition theorem that expresses Borel Wadge classes as finite unions of sets defined by nested conditions of depth n. Additionally, this theorem is applied to analyze the complexity of deciding Borel Wadge classes and finding minimal Borel Wadge embeddings. In contrast to existing research, we find that deciding Borel Wadge classes has a linear complexity for countable Borel sets and identify a specific model where this decision algorithm runs in linear time. Finally, a optimal upper bound of n^4 is found for finding a Borel Wadge embedding between two Borel sets of Wadge class n. This achievement is contingent on the existence of a computable linear ordering of Borel sets. We present an alternative efficient algorithm that achieves a time complexity of n^2 for finding a Borel Wadge embedding between two Borel sets of the same countable Wadge class in a specific model. A possible solution to mitigate these issues lies in network pruning, a technique that spares inconsequential parameters during the training process. Although previous studies have proposed autonomous and guided pruning methods, they often result in a substantial decline in the model's performance. A novel approach, ClickTrain, is presented in this research, combining the benefits of fine-detailed pruning and architecture preservation to yield both superior accuracy and computational efficiency. ClickTrain integrates a fine-detailed pruning technique that accounts for non-linear interactions among parameters, as well as a sequence-based reconstruction method to restore original network architecture.
