The 2017 detection of a gravitational wave from a neutron star collision by the LIGO and Virgo detectors marks a significant breakthrough in multi-messenger astronomy. Future detectors are expected to observe numerous neutron star collisions throughout the year. Identifying and classifying these events efficiently will be crucial for prioritizing follow-up observations. Although existing methods can analyze gravitational waves within a few minutes, they may become overwhelmed by the high event rate anticipated in the future. With the development of more sensitive detectors, the analysis of gravitational waves may become computationally demanding due to the vast amount of data that will need to be processed. To address these challenges, we have created a network of deep learning models capable of identifying and categorizing gravitational waves from neutron star collisions. Our model comprises a sequence of hierarchical classification layers that enable the rapid classification of events into distinct categories. Not only can our model handle the vast data volumes anticipated in future detection runs, but it also outperforms existing methods by classifying 90% of binary black hole and neutron star-black hole waveforms accurately, alongside achieving a 97% success rate for binary black hole waveforms without the use of Priestrapair features. Moreover, our model is versatile and can be adapted for detecting neutron star-neutron star collisions, well-suited for the anticipated detection of these events by the forthcoming third generation of gravitational wave detectors. With its ability to operate in real-time and classify events in real-time, our model paves the way for seamless application in future detection runs, thereby facilitating the exploration of numerous neutron star collisions throughout the year. Additionally, by enhancing efficiency, our model using neutron star candidate events will contribute to the reduction of unnecessary computations in the analysis of binary neutron star coalescence, thus accelerating the identification of events in future detection runs. Our work offers a significant breakthrough in the deep learning application to gravitational wave analysis and our code is publicly available for other researchers to utilize. With the upcoming launch of the LIGO O3 run, we are prepared to apply our model in real-time to enhance future detection runs, ultimately making contributions to various fields such as multi-messenger astronomy, astrophysics, cosmology, nucleosynthesis, binary merger analysis, gamma-ray burst activation, and more. We investigate a novel type of Markov Decision Process (MDP) known as Restricted MDPs (RMDPs), characterized by the accessibility of an approximate optimal policy through substantial computational efforts. Owing to their computationally demanding nature, solving RMDPs proves to be a resource-intensive task. To tackle this problem, we introduce a primary-dual algorithmic approach that generates a near-optimal restricted policy at a low cost, leveraging the pre-computed data of an RMDP. The core principle of our method revolves around the dual representation of RMDPs, where we capitalize on stationary values of state-action functions to develop a linear programming formulation that represents the dual problem. We employ constrained policy iteration to solve this dual problem, where each iteration yields a better dual solution, ultimately resulting in a high-quality restricted policy at minimal computational costs. Furthermore, we establish a primal-dual relationship, allowing us to derive a lower bound on the quality of the restricted policy, independent of the specific problem details. By minimizing the difference between the optimal and restricted policies using projected gradient ascent, we refine our restricted policy until it closely mimicates the optimal policy. We evaluate the efficacy of our proposed primary-dual approach through numerical experiments, revealing it to be substantially faster than state-of-the-art algorithms for RMDPs, while yielding a small degree of sub-optimality. The theoretical foundations of our method demonstrate a relationship between computation costs and the degree of sub-optimality, where higher computation costs result in smaller degrees of sub-optimality. Conversely, lower computation costs result in larger degrees of sub-optimality. We anticipate our primary-dual approach to be highly beneficial in settings characterized by resource-constrained environments, where a high degree of sub-optimality can be tolerated due to limited computation capabilities. On the other hand, we expect existing algorithms to be more beneficial in environments with abundant computation resources. The proposed primary-dual approach represents a novel algorithmic solution to RMDPs, distinct from prior works in restricted MDPs. We outline potential future research directions by highlighting the similarities and differences between the current understanding of RMDPs and the primary-dual approach. The main concepts of our method can be applied to various variants of RMDPs, such as MDPs with multiple objectives or interactive settings, where we introduce new paradigms for restricted MDPs. This study presents an advanced approach to recognizing handwritten mathematical symbols, symbols, and equations when not provided in digital form. Initially, the two-dimensional pen inputs recorded during handwriting are segmented into individual symbols or combined with other symbols to form expressions. Subsequently, a powerful offline recognition network, engineered using pre-trained Transformer blocks, is applied to translate these symbols into corresponding mathematical tokens. Ultimately, a sequential decoding technique known as Beam Search is employed to generate the final mathematical text from the symbolic data. Our method is meticulously evaluated using the Math and Science Challenge dataset. Specifically, our method achieves high overall accuracy in recognizing mathematical symbols, expressions, and equations with an overall Mathematising score of 42.97, surpassing the current best score of 41.6. Moreover, our method demonstrates exceptional performance in recognizing complete equations with symbol-only, symbol-plus-line, and mixed-line-symbol configurations, achieving scores of 34.88, 35.33, and 34.67 respectively. It's worth noting that our method also surpasses the current best score in recognizing symbol-only configurations by a significant margin of 9.44. Our contributions can be utilized to develop the underlying platform for offline handwritten mathematical notation recognition, with potential applications including mathematical expression translation and search. Reinforcement Learning has gained immense attention in recent years due to its wide-ranging applications in various fields. Actor-critic methods are extensively used for solving complex decision-making problems. However, these models often face challenges related to convergence, such as local optima and overfitting. To address these issues, we introduce a novel actor-critic algorithm that incorporates Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) simulations. This method employs Hamiltonian Dynamics for exploring beyond the limitations of Markov chains, utilizing kinetic energy to simulate trajectories. Furthermore, the introduction of a metacritic layer facilitates the transfer of knowledge across different tasks, effectively enhancing the robustness of the model. To evaluate the performance of our model, we conducted experiments on multiple Atari games, demonstrating its ability to achieve higher rewards and adapt faster across diverse tasks. Additionally, we provide visual representations of trajectories to illustrate the benefits of kinetic energy in identifying action patterns. The integration of HMC technology into actor-critic models offers exciting possibilities for future research and applications. The code for our model is available on GitHub at https://github.com/nirmalrajp/ACO.

The Twin Prime Hypothesis asserts that there is a finite, arbitrary gap between pairs of prime numbers. Demonstrating this hypothesis would show the infinite set of prime numbers contains pairs of the form (p, p+2). In this paper, a novel, straightforward proof of the Twin Prime Hypthesis is presented, leveraging a key concept known as the "Prime Number Theorem for Arithmetical Functions." This theorem describes the behavior of functions related to prime numbers as they relate to infinity, and has significant implications within number theory. A related statement, known as the Riemann Hypothesis, would result in the validation of the Twin Prime Hypothesis, as well as numerous other critical concepts within number theory. Therefore, this proof can be viewed as a validation of the Riemann Hypothesis. Additionally, results presented in this paper can be utilized to quantify the magnitude of gaps between prime numbers, and their associated distributions. A novel approach to infinite sums is introduced, referred to as "Infinitesimal Sums, Present and Past," which lends itself to generalizable techniques. In this context, numbers are viewed as combining the sum of all natural numbers preceding a given number. A related concept, "The Mirror,' serves as a mathematical operation that, when applied to a number, yields its companion mirror number - specifically, the smallest number resulting from reversing the digits of the original number, or a specified number greater than the original that is congruent modulo 10^k for any k. A fundamental relationship between prime numbers and their mirror counterparts, as predicted by the Twin Prime Hypothesis, would result in an infinite number of twin prime pairs, and is contingent upon the validation of the Riemann Hypothesis. Furthermore, this proof can be viewed as a validation of the Riemann Hypothesis, and resulting estimates for the magnitude of gaps between prime numbers, and their distributions, are provided. Autonomous navigation systems within encapsulating environments, such as marine robotics, require both forward and side-view perception to avoid obstacles and ensure safe movement. This research focuses on developing a navigation controller for underwater robots that utilizes forward-viewing sonar within a stratified structure and real-time side-viewing sonar data to adjust their trajectory accordingly. By incorporating a collision avoidance module using a biologically inspired method and adjusting the navigation controller's parameters through online regularization, the system demonstrates effective obstacle avoidance and path adjustments in lab tests using a low-cost, forward-viewing sonar. This results in a streamlined navigation controller that's both simple to implement and effective in navigating encapsulating structures. Furthermore, the paper explores potential applications of this system on mini-submarines and ROVs to enhance safety. To take the next step towards fully integrating the developed controller into existing autonomous navigation systems, the research also investigates its implementation on a submersible module equipped with a stratified structure and forward-viewing sonar, showcasing its capability to significantly improve safety by adjusting its path and avoiding collisions. This, in turn, contributes to the development of more robust and safe autonomous navigation systems in encapsulating structures. Time-stamped data and experimental videos are available on GitHub. We highlight a concern in the current learning algorithms for optimizing the treatment assignment policy in the dynamic treatment frameworks. Specifically, we show that existing algorithms do not adequately account for uncertainties in estimated model parameters when transitioning from a model-based to a model-free approach, particularly in scenarios involving multiple treatment options. This oversight leads to pessimistic outcomes in scenarios such as the theta-gram multi-armed bandit and the Q-Process. To address this shortcoming, we introduce a novel Bayesian learning strategy, known as C-cross, which incorporates uncertainty estimation for optimal treatment assignment policy in the dynamic settings. We prove that C-cross achieves a higher rate of convergence than previous algorithms and offer evidence from simulated trials to demonstrate its superiority. Furthermore, we outline a possible extension of our research to address uncertainty quantification in model-based reinforcement learning. Our study contributes to the active area of learning in the dynamic treatment frameworks by identifying an overlooked shortcoming and proposing a solution to address the issue. Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) with limited resources is challenging due to the scarcity of labeled data, character variability, and handwriting distinctiveness. The amount of useful information in each handwritten word is relatively low, which complicates training models. Moreover, systems dealing with composite characters (such as 'ch','sh', etc.) are limited in their ability to recognize them. To tackle these challenges, we introduce an innovative method that generates synthetic data from real labels, using a neural network trained on unlabelled data. This new method creates single-shot synthetic data at the character-level, taking into account the complexity of HTR systems' inputs. We compare it to traditional multi-line synthetic data creation and experimentally demonstrate its effectiveness on the datasets, IAM, Rimes, and BCSH, achieving notable improvement in model performance. Notably, our technique outperforms current synthetic data creation approaches, achieving state-of-the-art results on the IAM dataset. In addition, we introduce a novel benchmark for evaluating HTR systems that comprise multiple connected components within a single line. This benchmark, dubbed the Composite Character Recognition (CCR) benchmark, enhances the traditional HTR metric by incorporating a new character error rate that focuses specifically on composite characters. We utilize the CCR benchmark to simulate real-world testing scenarios, where models are faced with composite characters in a single line, and demonstrate its efficacy by achieving a 0.9% character error rate after training on synthetic data created using the single-shot method. In various fields, certainty must be guaranteed for decisions made based on uncertain knowledge, yet standard uncertainty measures fall short in providing absolute assurance due to their imprecision in quantifying uncertainty-related errors. We introduce a quantitative framework for measuring the reliability of uncertainty-based decisions in Bayesian networks by utilizing covariance-based error analysis. This precise metric allows us to develop a method, called stochastic certification, which guarantees a level of reliability for Bayesian network-based decisions through adjustable constraint tightening on the uncertainty structure. Similar to certification in stochastic programming, stochastic certification balances reliability and efficiency by controlling the tightening of probabilistic constraints, yielding an optimal trade-off. To achieve this, we separate the complex problem into two components, optimizing a robust variant of maximum a posteriori probability estimation under adjusted constraints and identifying the minimal tightening required to achieve a specified reliability level in the resulting robust optimization problem. We provide a comprehensive evaluation of our approach through case studies and experimental analysis, which offer a fresh perspective on reliance in machine learning, particularly for decision-making under uncertainty. This research is the first to address reliance in probabilistic knowledge structures, enabling the efficient and effective assurance of reliability for Bayesian networks. The diffusion model's unsupervised learning process generates substantial amounts of random text. To establish meaning within this text realm, we propose the Steady Creator, a dedicated encoder and prior distribution distillation process. By distilling the text realm's steady state, our approach enables the creation of an effective language-specific semantic model. We demonstrate the Steady Creator's potential in various applications such as unsupervised text classification, constrained text generation, and improving translation quality by bridging the gap between text summarization and unsupervised parallel corpora. The proposed method outperforms current state-of-the-art models in unsupervised text classification and constrained text generation tasks. Notably, it surpasses the performance of conditioned large-scale language models in these tasks, indicating the significance of targeted semantic models in generating relevant text. We also show that the steady text realm's semantic model enhances the quality of text-based translations, achieving top-ranked results in the TextAdvancement challenge. A novel method called U reversible steganography leverages the properties of unitary matrices to embed multiple messages within an input image without compromising its original content or compressing it. To develop a reliable message recovery algorithm, we construct a uniform unitary matrix whose columns are evenly spaced in the complex plane. However, creating such a matrix proves challenging, especially when messages are heavily embedded, as proposed methods fail to recover the full message with high accuracy. In response, we formulate a Bayesian neural network that embeds messages into unitary matrices while ensuring they remain reversible, and thus easily invertible. We find that a simple neural network comprising a single fully connected layer can effectively accomplish this task. Our message recovery neural network achieves exceptional performance, recovering the full message with high accuracy even when multiple messages heavily alter the input image. As an added benefit, we find that U reversible steganography offers stronger message confidentiality protection than traditional least significant bit steganography. Our research provides the first known implementation of U reversible steganography along with a detailed theoretical framework. We publicly showcase our steady message recovery performance in the provided images and videos. Furthermore, we make our generated unitary matrices and accompanying Python code accessible for others to utilize. With this research, we establish the potential for U reversible steganography to embed multiple messages into images while maintaining their full content and high image quality. As an interesting aspect, we observe that U reversible steganography can serve as an effective tool for protecting image content while also thwarting image compression. We hypothesize that U reversible steganography can also protect other forms of media, such as audio and video. As an interesting extension, we explore the possibility of employing U reversible steganography to embed encrypted neural network weights, effectively rendering the output unpredictable to unauthorized parties. We envision that U reversible steganography will emerge as a key tool for safeguarding image security. If the monopoles repel each other and are unable to hold onto the magnetic flux, they will not be able to explain the endurance of these galactic fields. Predicting climate variables over extended spatial and temporal periods is crucial, yet challenging due to the intricate interconnectedness of climate phenomena over large scales. Despite recent breakthroughs by large-scale neural network models, they often overlook the intricate local details, overlooking the importance of small-scale climate interactions. To address this, we propose the Shifted Window Cross-Focus network, an innovative model leveraging the power of attention mechanisms within a scalable and efficient framework, capable of capturing both large-scale and localized climate relationships. Extensively tested on prominent climate prediction challenges, including the ECMWF climate reanalysis dataset and the sub-seasonal to seasonal prediction dataset, it demonstrates exceptional performance with notable improvements over current state-of-the-art methods. Its code is freely available on GitHub. Notably, it achieved top-ranked results in SS3P challenge in 2020, later published in a research article. The code has attracted over 10,000 GitHub visitors and has been adopted by numerous industry and academic researchers. As a result, it has enabled the production of highly detailed climate visualizations, facilitating research and collaboration among climate and AI experts. To date, these visualizations have garnered over 1 million views on various platforms. Additionally, it has enabled the prediction of climate phenomena 30-90 days in advance with remarkable accuracy, surpassing conventional climate modeling methods. Its predictive capabilities have even extended to notable climate events such as hurricanes, droughts, and extreme rainfall events, demonstrating its potential to improve climate forecasting. To maximize its transparency and accountability, the model's source code, data, and model weights are freely available on GitHub, enabling anyone to reproduce its results and explore its potential applications in climate prediction. To date, its code has attracted collaborations from research institutions, companies, and organizations in the US, UK, India, China, Russia, Germany, and other countries. As a result, it has enabled the production of over 5000 models, collectively attracting over 5 million GitHub visits. We demonstrate that this hypothesis is true for all convex quadrilaterals formed by connecting pure states with maximal entropy along the asymptotic entanglement spectrum. As a result, the PPT hypothesis holds PPTd, which describes a PPT scenario for any local measurement outcome. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the PPT quadrilateral hypothesis is an integral aspect of the computational complexity of quantum systems, particularly in achieving a dichotomy between PPTd and PPTc. We also explore the related PPT rectangle hypothesis and establish its validity for certain instances, but left many cases undecided. We propose open questions for further investigation. The proof of our main result employs a novel concept called 'good' entropy, enabling a clear division between relevant and irrelevant information in the context of quantum systems. This distinction not only aids in understanding the PPTd and PPTc paradigms but also contributes to broader knowledge of quantum system behavior. Additionally, our work offers a straightforward generalization of the PPT rectangle hypothesis to higher-dimensional systems Arriva. The PPTd and PPTc paradigms have far-reaching implications, extending to scenarios involving random state arrangements and entanglement asymmetry, as we illustrate with specific examples. The integrality of the PPT quadrilateral hypothesis in achieving a dichotomy between PPTd and PPTc paradigms is demonstrated through the analysis of a local complementation operation. We also examine the PPT rectangle hypothesis in conjunction with its complement under local complementation, leading to the concept of PPTrachain, which describes a PPT scenario for any local measurement outcome in a specific chain of interconnected systems. Furthermore, our work in a complemented scenario demonstrates that the PPT rectangle hypothesis is associated with a fundamental concept in quantum complexity, particularly in understanding the behavior of quantum systems under local measurement. In brain tissue, the regulation of neurotransmitter levels is heavily dependent on the balance between the release and removal of these chemicals by nearby neurons. The rapid exchange creates a complex interplay influencing neural communication precision. We develop a unique mathematical framework, based on an optimization problem incorporating partial differential equations, to examine how neurons manage and exchange substances like neurotransmitters. This novel approach enables us to analyze the spatial distribution of neurons' response to varying levels of excitability and transport capacity. We demonstrate the model's utility by exploring how different transport mechanisms impact substance buildup and the effects of excitability changes through numerical simulations. The model has potential applications in studying neurodegenerative diseases caused by impaired transport and understanding the role of excitability in regulating brain function. Furthermore, this framework can be used to estimate parameters essential for understanding neural communication, such as the rate at which neurons release and absorb substances, by translating it into a related optimal control problem. We illustrate the process of estimating these parameters in a simplified setting. The study provides a foundation for further investigation into the design of experimental treatments aimed at modifying brain activity patterns by influencing excitability and transport processes. The associated data, including PDE implementation, numerical results, and transport estimates, are available for download at the designated repository. These transactions create a complex web of relationships.
To uncover hidden patterns within these relationships, researchers use the network motifs technique.
This approach enables the discovery of recurring patterns in transaction data, exposing the underlying structure.
By applying network motifs to real-world banking data, researchers identify distinct patterns.
These patterns differ from random connections and indicate the presence of meaningful relationships.
As a result, researchers can gain insights into the behavior of banking systems.
This approach offers a versatile tool for analyzing interconnected systems. 
It can potentially lead to new discoveries in fields such as social and information networks.
To further develop this method, researchers can explore the following challenges:
(1) efficiently discovering large patterns of high complexity,
(2) analyzing the statistical significance of detected patterns,
(3) uncovering the underlying causes of observed patterns.
Furthermore, researchers can envision various applications for this technique,
such as identifying correlated transactions or predicting transaction outcomes.
These ideas illustrate the numerous possibilities for which network motifs can be utilized.
This presentation outlines the background, research challenges, and potential applications for the network motifs approach.

Researchers are studying the process of a white dwarf star collapsing into a black hole through detailed simulations of the stars' interactions. When a white dwarf star nears the stage of its final death, it experiences a massive contraction that transforms it into a more compact object, such as a neutron star or black hole, depending on its original mass. In a recent study using sophisticated computer models, scientists observed the entire process of a 0.12 solar mass white dwarf star merging with a more massive 1.10 solar mass star, resulting in a 1.61 solar mass black hole. These simulations provide valuable insights into how the stars' material behaves during the collapse and how their interactions emit energy across a broad spectrum of the electromagnetic spectrum. In particular, the research reveals that during the stages of collapse, both stars emit large amounts of radiation, primarily as a result of chemical reactions that release energy, such as the formation of helium and iron. In addition, the team performed calculations to estimate the various amounts of energy emitted across different wavelengths, and observed that these emissions vary over time as the star undergoes different stages of transformation. Following the formation of the black hole, the team discovered that the star continues to emit energy mainly as a result of cooling processes, specifically the release of energy from falling electrons and the contraction of the star's innermost layers. In total, the research reveals that during the entire process of a white dwarf star collapsing into a black hole, the star emits an enormous amount of energy, primarily in the form of light and other forms of electromagnetic radiation, and also produces massive amounts of gravitational waves. In particular, the team estimated that a 0.12 solar mass white dwarf star and its companion, which is similar in size to the Sun, would release approximately 3.4 x 10^47 ergs of energy, and produce about 2.4 x 10^42 gravitational waves, all during the entire course of the star's final death. These findings could provide essential context for the study of supernovae explosions that result from the collapse of white dwarf stars, and potentially shed light on the creation of low-mass neutron star and black hole objects. Furthermore, the research reveals that the resulting 1.61 solar mass black hole would have an unusually small size, and that the accretion of material from a nearby star would lead to the formation of a bar-like or disk-like structure, potentially resulting in an uneven distribution of the star's mass, and potentially hindering the formation of a stable neutron star.

Recent advancements in movement deblurring have focused on addressing real-world challenges by incorporating priors learned from specific types of blurred images. However, existing methods still struggle to accurately recover original images when encountering unexpected blurring patterns. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel movement deblurring approach that learns to incorporate diverse blur patterns into its network prior. Our method utilizes a pseudo-blur generator to generate synthetic blurred images that mimic real-world movements, thereby broadening its applicability. Experimental results on standard benchmarks as well as medical and astronomical images demonstrate the superior performance of our proposed approach in restoring clear images, even in the presence of unusual blur patterns. The associated code will be made available for reproducibility purposes. Additionally, we introduce the BMoS dataset containing 500,000 blurred images that can be accessed via our website. This dataset is tailored to standard 2D movement deblurring methods, offering a valuable resource for evaluating performance and developing new approaches. Via ablation studies, we validate the effectiveness of our proposed model and the BMoS dataset in assessing model robustness and presenting training benefits. Notably, the BMoS dataset surpasses existing datasets in diversity, size, and application domains, offering a comprehensive 4,000-image validation set that mimics challenging real-world scenarios. Furthermore, we analyze and discuss the current state of movement deblurring, highlighting areas for improvement and potential avenues for future research. Lastly, we provide implementation details for our model and the BMoS dataset, thereby facilitating the reproduction of our methods and findings. To summarize, we introduce an innovative movement deblurring approach that incorporates diverse blur patterns into its network prior and present the BMoS dataset, a comprehensive benchmark of 500,000 blurred images. The associated code will be made accessible. Experimental results on standard benchmarks, medical, and astronomical images demonstrate the superior performance of our proposed approach in restoring original images, even in the presence of unusual blur patterns. Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) have gained significant attention for processing graph-structured data. Unlike traditional convolutional networks, GCNNs lack clear justification for their success. We present a novel perspective on GCNNs by interpreting the graph convolution operation as a matched filtering method for detecting latent subgraphs within an input graph. This analysis uncovers the equivalence between the graph convolution operation and the spatially weighted subgraph auto-correlation. Consequently, we derive the necessary and sufficient conditions for achieving graph convolution through auto-correlation correlation. Notably, we find that the current graph convolution operations used in GCNNs satisfy these conditions, thereby clarifying their effectiveness. This study provides a foundational understanding of GCNNs, thereby shedding light on their generalization capability in graph-based machine learning tasks. Most current programming systems rely on load-time or run-time mechanisms to address dependencies, leading to performance issues and insecurity vulnerabilities. Our study examines if compile-time specialization of run-time dependency resolution can improve system reliability, performance, and efficiency. The key compile-time dependency resolution techniques explored are template metaprogramming and auto-template instantiation. Through theoretical and practical analysis, we found that, although template metaprogramming allows for in-place code specialization, widespread use is limited due to complexity constraints. On the other hand, auto-template instantiation by default specializes code at compile-time, making it suitable for replacing traditional run-time dependency resolution. As a result, developers can leverage modern C++ compiler technology to enhance system reliability, performance, and efficiency. An open-source benchmark framework, called DepsBench, has been made available to facilitate further research into code specialization techniques. Ongoing research investigations have shown promising results, with potential to expand the scope to load-time dependency resolution and instantaneous specializations. An open question remains as to how code specialization techniques will develop and become integrated into the broader DepsBench framework. Moreover, the possibility of DepsBench being generalized into a dependable software component and toolchain remains a subject for future research investigation. An area to be explored is whether DepsBench can serve as a dependable software component and toolchain. As a consequence, the dependency resolution methods employed by programming systems will likely become faster, more efficient, and less prone to security vulnerabilities. Our research demonstrates that the direct detection of such low mass particles is feasible. Heart rhythms are measured in real-time through inter-beat intervals (IBIs) which are then analyzed to identify irregular heartbeats and assess cardiovascular risk. Accurate IBIs calculation is crucial yet compromised due to noise in electrocardiograms (ECGs). Filtering out this noise from ECG signals is essential yet challenging. Recent studies utilize deep learning to achieve this goal, yet most approaches make unrealistic assumptions such as requiring full dataset access or ignoring real-time applications. A novel deep learning technique, the Tiramisu network, is presented in this study to accurately remove noise and increase IBI reliability. Evaluations using human cardiac cycle markers reveal the Tiramisu method surpasses existing techniques with an average error reduction of 8.91%. Furthermore, the proposed method demonstrates exceptional time efficiency, processing 200 data points within 0.02 milliseconds. As such, the Tiramisu framework presents a highly viable solution for noise removal and IBI assessment in real-time cardiovascular risk monitoring applications. The Active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Particle (AOUP) is a simplified model of self-motile organisms that generates diverse movement behaviors, including random movement, smooth movement, and movement in response to attractants. Existing analyses of the AOUP have primarily focused on steady-state behaviors, but we investigate the dynamics of the AOUP during transient states, revealing complex and highly variable movement patterns. Our results indicate that, similar to animal movements, AOUP trajectories are characterized by distinct sections with differing characteristics. These regions are linked by abrupt changes, and the duration of the transition period fluctuates greatly. We also observe significant individual fluctuations in movement patterns, and demonstrate that these variations are necessary for producing complex, attractant-driven movements in a population. In the long-term, individual AOUP behaviors converge to exhibit similar patterns, but only when the organism's response to attractants is slow compared to the timescales of the environment. Our work establishes a connection between the steady-state behaviors of the AOUP and the diversity of movements exhibited by living organisms. Additionally, we provide a framework for evaluating the plausibility of different labor strategies in the context of the AOUP model. Based on our analysis, we propose that diverse movement behaviors may serve as a means of "division of labor" among AOUPs, with each organism exhibiting and utilizing its own characteristic timescale for responding to attractants in order to distribute workload and optimize performance in a population. This division of labor is environmentally-driven, yet also adaptable, as individual AOUP behaviors can adjust based on past experiences and changes in the environment. In the end, we identify a range of parameters under which a population's diversity in movement behaviors leads to enhanced collective efficiency. This research provides a foundation for exploring the concept of "labor variations" in collective, mobile populations. Additionally, our methodology is readily applicable to other collective animal groups, where diversity in movement behaviors may also be a means of "division of labor". Furthermore, we demonstrate the practical utility of our findings by successfully implementing "labor variation" in a simple bot designed to collect sugar in a digital environment. This research has the potential to contribute to the broader field of social biology by shedding light on the underlying mechanisms behind "division of labor" in mobile collectives. At the same time, we also identify novel avenues for exploring this topic, not only in biological systems, but also in synthetic entities such as robots. A well-established video super-resolution task known as Video Super-Resolution in a Temporal Framework was initially introduced in 2019 in the CVPR. This task was further refined in 2021 by a novel approach called BasicVSR, which incorporated self-attention and propagation techniques to extract spatial information from neighboring frames and leverage temporal context. However, the original BasicVSR approach had several limitations: it relied on a cumbersome alignment procedure that significantly increased computational costs and produced large output sizes; and it used a distinct set of convolutional layers for forward and backward propagation, which hindered efficient propagation and training. To address these shortcomings, a new approach called BasicVSR++ was developed in 2022. BasicVSR++ relies on a enhanced transmission model that utilizes self-attention to combine input frames with varying levels of convolutional layer iterations, and an updated propagation module that shares weights with the extraction module, resulting in efficient propagation and streamlined network design. Experimental evaluations of BasicVSR++ revealed a notable increase in SR and detailed PSNR metrics on test datasets, and demonstrated improved robustness to motion interference. Additionally, calculations showed BasicVSR++ to be the most compact solution among the top-performing approaches. Validations using other commonly used test datasets also revealed a notable increase in SSIM and FID metrics, and demonstrated reduced compression loss and improved restoration quality. As such, BasicVSR++ represents a simple yet effective approach to video super-resolution that surpasses existing methods in various evaluations. In complex settings with limited resources, training multiple tasks at once is more efficient, but the challenge is avoiding interference between tasks. We developed a novel approach called Multi-Task Modular Training, which improves upon existing methods by avoiding task dependency and allowing individual task modules to learn independently. We compared it to a sophisticated baseline called Meta-World, which implements a modular structure but suffers from interference and requires re-training when a task dependency is detected. Our method not only avoids interference but also significantly reduces training time, with a 10-fold reduction in steps required to adapt to a new task. We tested both methods in a variety of realistic robotic manipulations and found that they outperform a task-specific training method in settings with limited resources, while offering similar performance to a task-agnostic training method in settings with ample resources. Overall, Multi-Task Modular Training offers a reliable and efficient method for training multiple tasks at once. This suggests that energy infrastructure planners and operators need to be aware of the unique challenges posed by different weather events and take these into account when designing and managing energy systems for better resilience. Under the assumption that f is a non-zero eigenfunction of the Dirac operator in n-dimensional complex-valued functions on the complex projective space CP^n, we establish an extension of the Main Theorem from Kohn [6], which has been adapted for the context of Clifford analysis. It can be interpreted as a 'three spheres' theorem. In particular, if the zero set Z_f of f is composed of more than three disjoint spheres, then each of these spheres must be invariant under the action of a non-compact, solvable Lie group. This generalizes a previous result obtained by Jerónimo for the case of one sphere. The proof involves the use of a weighted integral operator, U_t f, which represents a Clifford analysis analogue of the Kohn layer potential. By establishing estimates for this operator, as well as its inverse, A^-1_t f, under certain conditions, we are able to derive the desired group actions. Additionally, our method allows for the construction of an explicit formula for A^-1_t f, which may be of independent interest. These findings are anticipated to be applicable in a variety of fields, such as complex algebraic geometry and PDEs in Clifford analysis. The article concludes with a discussion of potential future research avenues. In particular, we hypothesize that, under the assumption that f is an eigenfunction of the Dirac operator on CP^n with real eigenvalue, its zero set Z_f can be expressed as the disjoint union of at most three invariant spheres. Furthermore, we conjecture that, under the assumption that f is an eigenfunction of the Dirac operator on the complex projective space CP^n with real eigenvalue, its zero set Z_f can be expressed as the disjoint union of at most three invariant spheres, provided that f is also invariant under the action of the group SU(n+1). This hypothesis may be seen as a specialization of the 'three spheres' theorem' for functions invariant under SU(n+1), and thus represents an extension of a previous result obtained by Jerónimo for the case of one sphere. The proposed research will investigate the truth of these conjectured statements. The study will commence with an examination of the relationship between the action of SU(n+1) and the group action by which each of the spheres in Z_f is invariant. Subsequently, we will analyze the properties of the set Z_f when it comprises exactly three invariant spheres under the action of SU(n+1). Finally, we will discuss the relevant topological properties of Z_f.

We investigate two complex systems exhibiting heterochaos: the intrinsic dynamics of a planar kicked pendulum and a transverse nonlinear oscillator coupled with a linear oscillator. Both of these systems exhibit robust intermittently collapsing chaos characterized by intermittent occurrences of maximum entropy measures, which follow a predictable sequence in time. These maximum entropy measures can be understood as a result of mapping unstable periodic trajectories to an infinite Dyck system, which is comprised of arbitrarily extended sequences of strictly rising increments. This unique configuration leads to the possibility of two distinct measures, referred to as the forward and backward Hausdorff measures, which adhere to the requirements of uniqueness and ergodicity. We demonstrate that the forward measure represents the dominant invariant set in the system's dynamics and is responsible for its approachability, whereas the backward measure serves as a threshold for invariant measures based on ergodicity preservation, thereby effectively blocking approachability in these systems. In essence, we find that the forward measure is the target of approachability, but is rendered inaccessible due to the influence of the backward measure and the mechanism of intermittent collapse. This study introduces a new paradigm for understanding measure-theoretic dynamics, which could potentially be applied to other systems. This paper presents a novel network called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) that generates raw audio data using an autoregressive framework. Building on the success of WaveNet (WN) in generating high-fidelity audio, we propose QPNet as a WN variant that incorporates pitch-sensitive dilated convolutional neural networks. WN models raw audio signals through a conditional generative modeling approach, achieving remarkable results. However, as signal length increases, WN's training and sampling rates dramatically rise due to the network's sequential processing requirement. To overcome this limitation, we introduce QPNet, which achieves comparable performance to WN in generating periods, while also permitting parallel sampling across the frequency spectrum. As a result, the sampling rate per audio frame significantly decreases. Furthermore, we develop a novel training strategy that utilizes period lengths to enhance generated speech quality and decrease the training rate. The effectiveness of large-scale recommender systems heavily relies on their ability to handle the inherent issues of user preference fragmentation, scarcity, and subjectivity. State-of-the-art CF methods fall short in this regard, as they often disregard the interconnections between different user groups and their shared preferences. In an attempt to address these challenges, this study introduces a novel CF approach called user-centric bicluster CF. This innovative method combines user profiles and item profiles into biclusters through clustering based on shared preferences, effectively capturing the inherent complexities of user preferences. Furthermore, it incorporates the concepts of spatial autocorrelation and preference completeness to enhance recommendation quality. Our experimental results on multiple real-world datasets clearly demonstrate the superior performance of our approach, confirming its ability to produce more accurate and diverse recommendations that better reflect the inherent characteristics of user preferences. Specifically, UBCF outperforms existing CF methods by 10.61% and 20.45% in terms of accuracy and diversity, respectively. Our analysis also highlights the importance of managing preference fragmentation at the user level and shows that our proposed bicluster model achieves better results than CF methods that incorporate the bicluster concept in terms of diversity. In addition, the novel bicluster quality evaluation metric we introduced shows promise in capturing the essence of user preferences and can be utilized as an intrinsic evaluation method that complements the existing extrinsic evaluation. Our work offers a comprehensive approach to addressing the inherent issues of user preference fragmentation, scarcity, and subjectivity, as well as managing the subjectivity of these preferences through CF. Moreover, the proposed UBCF method can be generalized to incorporate various user preference models and can coexist with other CF methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhouzc2020/user-centric-bicluster-CF. In the future, we plan to expand our research by incorporating the concept of preference completeness in UBCF. For instance, we can utilize graph neural networks to predict user preference towards unrated items based on the shared preferences of users in the same bicluster. Another potential direction is the integration of UBCF and preference completion. For example, we can utilize UBCF to identify user groups and then utilize these groups and user preferences within a neighborhood-based CF method to complete the missing preferences. Additionally, we can utilize biclusters to generalize individual user preferences and merge them into a comprehensive preference profile for each item. This can aid in predicting user preference towards unrated items and enhance recommendation quality. Another possible strategy is the incorporation of UBCF

The presence of cool starspots and hot magnetic polar regions is reflected in various light variations detected by ground-based telescopes, including changes in solar radius, temperature, and line shifts. Previous studies have used HARPS-N data to analyze these variations in the Sun, but they have overlooked the impact of magnetic activity on spectral behavior. To address this gap, we used a new approach to characterize solar activity by selecting specific features in the spectrum that are sensitive to temperature and line shifts. Our key findings include the identification of specific markers in the Ni I 8103.8 Å line that track changes in these parameters, as well as the observation of distinct hyperspectral features near 6813 Å that are influenced by line shifts. Furthermore, we developed a new activity index based on the line core of the Ni I line, taking into account the fill-in and shift of this feature, as well as the nearby 8123 Å line. This index effectively separates active and quiet periods in the solar spectrum, as demonstrated by synthetic data and human evaluations. Our study's index values are comparable to those obtained from SDO images of sunspots and magnetic footprints. In summary, we have identified new spectral markers and an index that can be used to quantify the impact of magnetic activity on solar spectra, as well as demonstrate the potential for these features to distinguish between active and quiet solar periods. However, we also observe that magnetic activity indicators in HARPS-N spectra are not sufficient to capture the full extent of solar variability, as they fail to account for variations in line widths. Nonetheless, our study's results are relevant to other stars with visible starspots and are expected to be applicable to solar analogs with harmonic periods and close to the Main Sequence. Finally, we emphasize the significance of incorporating a comprehensive understanding of magnetic activity and its variations in solar spectra to ground-based telescopes, as well as photometric and spectroscopic observations of other stars. This understanding is crucial for avoiding biases in detecting and characterizing exoplanets, as well as constraining core parameters that reflect a star's average temperature and radius. In other words, we are advocating for the integration of magnetic activity modeling in analyses of super-Earths and hot Jupiters, as well as other stellar systems that are or are not bound to the Sun. To this end, we propose that detection techniques for exoplanets and core parameters should be adjusted to reflect variations in stellar activity, as demonstrated by the index values in this study that are tied to SDO imaging of sunspots and magnetic activity.

We introduce an innovative approach to image processing that enables seamless transition between realistic and highly detailed images. This style-extraction method utilizes a neural network to analyze a set of images and removes their specific details, replacing them with general styling elements to create new images. The transfer of this styling is instantaneous, affecting all images equally. To achieve this transfer, we developed dual neural networks that work in harmony to analyze image components and shift them from their original state to a stylized state. This process involves a forward direction, where we analyze images in their typical format and apply a grid pattern to identify regions to style, and a reverse direction, where we analyze images in a stylized format and extract features to apply to unstyled images. This unique partnership allows for the rapid and uniform transfer of styling elements from one image set to another. To validate our approach, we created a vast dataset of images and compared our results to state-of-the-art image processing techniques, demonstrating superior performance and more natural results. The implementation details are provided to allow for replication. In addition, we created an interactive tool that allows image editing and style exploration. This style extraction technique holds potential for various applications and domains, including image and video editing, graphics design, painting, and photo manipulation. During snowfall, the complex interaction between atmospheric turbulence and large snowflakes leads to a phenomenon known as selective sweeping, where larger snowflakes are transported faster than their smaller counterparts. While this process is often observed, its underlying mechanics have not been fully understood until now. Through a study using high-resolution wind simulations, the influence of atmospheric turbulence on snowflake transport has been investigated. By analyzing the movement of snowflakes in relation to the direction of wind velocity, it was discovered that larger snowflakes are indeed swept up more efficiently, but previous research suggested this was due to differing fall speeds. Using a novel statistical method, the impact of atmospheric turbulence on non-interacting particles was examined, revealing that directional variability plays a significant role in the acceleration of larger snowflakes. As a result, a greater accumulation of larger snowflakes occurs, potentially influencing global snowfall amounts and atmospheric cooling effects. This research represents the first evidence supporting the idea that directional turbulence aids in the transportation of larger snowflakes, ultimately altering the atmospheric circulation and snowfall patterns. As a result, this study can contribute to a better understanding of atmospheric processes and snowfall dynamics. A robot's capabilities are demonstrated through an examination of PAD's application to a complex grid-world environment, where the system learns and adapts to new concepts and skills, such as navigating obstacles, using tools, and incorporating external knowledge into its decision-making processes. This study validates PAD as a viable model for strong AI and highlights its potential for autonomous robot navigation in intricate and dynamic environments. PAD's non-linear and proactive methodology makes it an attractive alternative to conventional AI systems based on linear reasoning and reactive algorithms. This research opens up new avenues for exploring the application of PAD to a wide range of challenging tasks in complex robot navigation. Given the growing volume of data from these experiments, employing sparse data representation becomes essential to reduce the sheer data throughput. Convolutional AutoEncoders exhibit excellent capabilities in this regard, successfully capturing relevant data features and compressing data efficiently. However, existing CAE methods struggle to directly handle 3D data from TPC experiments and often require data transformation into 2D images. This, in turn, complicates data reconstruction and renders the process 1-way, i.e., data compression. This novel approach is evaluated using Real-world simulations from nuclear physics research projects, and the results demonstrate its superior data reduction capabilities when compared to traditional methods. Specifically, our Bicephalous Convolutional AutoEncoder achieves a remarkable 70% reduction in data size with only 5% accuracy loss compared to the original data. Similarly, in the vector potential formulation, a singular value decomposition approach is utilized to numerically conserve helicity without compromising spatial discretization methods. Numerical experiments are conducted to validate the analysis and demonstrate robust helicity preservation in both perfect and weather forecasting applications. Furthermore, extension of the analysis to magneto-hydrodynamics equations is considered, revealing the possibility of numerically conserving helicity in magnetic fields. These findings offer support for the development of numerical methods that can robustly preserve helicity, streamlining the design of vorticity-based baroclinic instability models and saving computational costs in meteorological forecasting. In the process, near-optimal entropy-stable schemes are designed and tested, also contributing to the development of more reliable and robust numerical methods for ideal MHD simulations that conserve helicity. Spreading events, such as rumors and viruses, take place on complex networks whose structure is unknown until the incident spreads. This hidden network architecture often stems from real-world phenomena, such as social or biological influences. As the incident spreads, we gain access to node information, but the network's underlying structure remains obscure. This problem is addressed by developing a method that uses incident time-series data to infer the incident's origin, identify critical network components, and estimate the incident's spreading rate. This task is complicated by the incident's dynamic nature, varying correlation lengths, and non-stationary fluctuations. To resolve this issue, we present a new method, CREDO, that uses deep learning and graph attention to detect incidents and map their propagation. This method is capable of estimating the incident's spreading rate, identifying the incident's starting point, and mapping the incident's flow through the network. As the incident continues to evolve, CREDO provides a dynamic estimate of the incident's average path length and key network components. This method is versatile and applicable to diverse networks, including random and small-world networks, as well as networks influenced by the incident's spreading dynamics. Notably, CREDO is the first method to use deep learning and graph attention to analyze time-series data and propagate this information to detect incidents and map their dynamics. As such, it outperforms existing methods by providing more accurate incident identification and flow mapping. This represents a significant breakthrough in incident analysis and network research. This method is further validated by analyzing the spread of malware through email networks, demonstrating its ability to estimate the incident's starting point, map its flow, and identify key network components. In the context of zero-error source encoding, we examine leakage in compressed data by relating coverage to graph concepts, specifically vertex cuts and matching. By doing so, we distinguish between intrinsic and extrinsic leakage, with intrinsic leakage corresponding to vertex cuts and extrinsic leakage related to matchings. Furthermore, we establish a connection between leakage and graph parameters, such as independence number and chromatic number. Finally, we explore how source encoding methods can disclose information about the source probability distribution through leakage, highlighting this risk in methods like Shannon folding and binary entropy folding. Our analysis also reveals instances where matching-based encoders surpass folding-based encoders in terms of leakage performance. To showcase the applicability of our theoretical findings, we conduct experimental comparisons of different encoding methods across various source distributions. These experiments align with our theoretical predictions, demonstrating the superiority of matching-based encoders under specific conditions. Ultimately, our study sheds light on the trade-offs inherent in zero-error source encoding and provides insight into the leakage consequences of employing certain encoding methods. These consequences can be mitigated by utilizing matchings, which exhibit superior leakage performance relative to other techniques. Nonetheless, matchings may not always be realizable or efficiently encodable; therefore, we identify the conditions under which simple matchings constitute optimal encoding strategies. Our analysis also raises questions about the realizability of specific vertex cut rates and the exact calculation of matching-based encoders, which we leave for future investigation. By approached leakage as a fundamental source encoding problem, we develop novel tools for bounding distortion distance and establish a metric that assesses leakage performance under specific confidence levels. These bounds are expressed in terms of graph and matching-based encoding parameters, ultimately leading to the introduction of leakage-bounded encoders. Specifically, we demonstrate how matching-based encoding can be modified to produce leakage tolerances, thereby resulting in leakage-degraded source distributions. These degradation levels are shown to affect the achievable distortion rates and, ultimately, the encoded data leakage. Consequently, we advocate for a more nuanced understanding of source encoding metrics, integrating leakage performance alongside traditional rate and distortion criteria. By doing so, we enable the development of leakage-aware encoding methods and provide a practical means for assessing leakage risks in source encoding scenarios.
